article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template
citation: Kate Place, Gregory Chojnacki, Virginia Knechtel, Andy Gothro, Megan Shoji, Lindsay Fox. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Seven-component structure of a complete M&E plan
description: The template enumerates what a complete M&E plan includes: "A description of a solution and theory of change"; information on prior research; detail on how priority communities were and will be involved; the study research questions; the measures and approach for answering them; "Ambitious targets (or goals) for each intended outcome"; and a timeline to carry out the work. This list defines the plan's organizing structure.
requirements: Each plan component must be completed for the plan to be complete, as enumerated by the template
target_learners: implementing organizations and funders developing evaluation plans
target_learning_goals: structuring a complete measurement and evaluation plan
examples: The template's own list of plan contents, from theory of change through timeline
key_sources: Kate Place, Gregory Chojnacki, Virginia Knechtel, Andy Gothro, Megan Shoji, Lindsay Fox. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-plan-template

article_title: Forming a Team to Ensure High-Quality Measurement in Education Studies
citation: Ellen Eliason Kisker, Kimberly Boller. (2014). Forming a Team to Ensure High-Quality Measurement in Education Studies. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Form a dedicated measurement team of staff and consultants to ensure high-quality data for answering a study's research questions
description: The brief recommends forming a team of staff and consultants with the needed expertise to make key measurement decisions. Its stated purpose is that such a team will "ensure high-quality data for answering the study's research questions." The brief is addressed to education studies that depend on sound measurement.
requirements: Team members must have the needed expertise to make key measurement decisions
examples: The brief outlines tips for forming a measurement team in education studies

Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Organizing Early Education for Improvement
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Pacchiano, D.M., Stein, A.G., Wagner, M.R., Luppescu, S., Park, S., Frank, E., Lewandowski, H., & Young, C. (2018). Organizing early education for improvement: Testing a new survey tool. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and the Ounce of Prevention Fund. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Measure organizational conditions in ECE settings because existing quality tools do not capture them
description: The report argues that ECE improvement efforts focused only on classrooms miss a key lever: the organizational climate and conditions surrounding teachers. It states that "The ECE field is missing a statistically valid tool that measures these organizational conditions in ECE settings and provides actionable information from which to design improvement strategies." Reliable tools exist for classroom structural quality, interactions, and administrative practices, but not for the interdependent organizational conditions that support or impede educators' daily practice.
requirements: Survey measures must be statistically valid and provide actionable information that program staff can use to design improvement strategies
constraints: Survey data are not expected to map perfectly onto other quality measures; they should provide consistent information while also identifying practices other tools do not capture
target_learners: ECE program leaders, practitioners, and stakeholders in school- and community-based preschool programs
target_learning_goals: strengthening organizational conditions that enable effective teaching and improvements in children's learning
examples: The Ounce and UChicago Consortium partnered to develop and test the Early Ed Essentials surveys to fill this measurement gap
key_sources: Ehrlich, S.B., Pacchiano, D.M., Stein, A.G., Wagner, M.R., Luppescu, S., Park, S., Frank, E., Lewandowski, H., & Young, C. (2018). Organizing early education for improvement: Testing a new survey tool. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and the Ounce of Prevention Fund. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/organizing-early-education-improvement-testing-new-survey-tool

article_title: AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218
title: Explain how AI works mechanistically, not through metaphors like human-like intelligence
description: The report recommends that explanations of what AI is and how it works 'not be couched in metaphors like "human-like" or examples of AI's powers, but rather be a mechanistic discussion.' Key points should cover how AI uses data, that models rely on statistics and identifying key features of data, and that generative systems synthesize new content by predicting outputs such as the next word or pixel. Explanations may be pitched at many levels of detail depending on the audience.
requirements: Explanations should cover how AI uses data, that models rely on statistics, and how GenAI predicts outputs such as the next word or pixel
constraints: Level of detail should be adapted to the audience
target_learning_goals: understand how AI systems work mechanistically
examples: The report provides a three-step explanation adapted from MIT Media Lab and MIT STEP Lab: obtaining and curating data, training a model, and using the model to receive outputs
key_sources: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Match methodological approach to research questions and broaden what counts as rigor
description: Teams must select the methodological approach that fits their research questions, and the field should extend rigor standards beyond causal impact studies. The note argues that "information about the usefulness of a product is as valuable as a study of the product's impact on learning outcomes," and that the field "needs to establish what rigor means for a wider range of methodological approaches beyond causal impact studies," especially as AI-based research methods emerge.
requirements: Both usefulness information and impact evidence are necessary to judge whether something will work and be used across implementation contexts
constraints: Especially important as new methodological approaches and tools, such as the use of AI in research methods, are introduced
examples: The note cites an emerging Digital Promise evidence framework for educational technologies as reference 2
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: Supporting School Improvement
citation: Hart, H., Young, C., Chen, A., Zou, A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2020). Supporting school improvement: Early findings from reexamination of the 5Essentials survey. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.5-essentials.org/
title: Schools working to improve on 5Essentials measures can expect outcome gains even before reaching strength
description: Because both starting the year strong on 5Essentials measures and improving on measures during the year predicted better student outcomes, schools below the strength threshold still benefit from growth. The report states: "schools that are working to improve in areas, such as Student-Teacher Trust or Teacher Influence, but have not yet reached a point of strength, can still see improvements in their students' outcomes such as GPAs, tests, and attendance." This makes measure growth a usable improvement signal for schools not yet strong on an essential support.
requirements: Annual survey administration so within-year measure growth can be observed
Analyses controlling for prior student achievement to attribute improvement beyond expected growth
constraints: In aggregate, most outcome improvement was better predicted by base strength coming into the year than by growth during the year, so growth benefits are reported alongside a strength advantage
target_learners: K-12 students in schools working to improve their organizational supports
target_learning_goals: Improvements in student outcomes such as GPAs, tests, and attendance while organizational supports are still developing
examples: The report's example: a school with strong measures in spring 2016 saw a larger Freshman OnTrack increase (4 percentage points) by spring 2017 than schools with average measures, beyond what students' prior performance predicted
key_sources: Hart, H., Young, C., Chen, A., Zou, A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2020). Supporting school improvement: Early findings from reexamination of the 5Essentials survey. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/supporting-school-improvement

article_title: Noncognitive Outcomes of Liberal Arts Education
citation: Key Questions. (2016). Mellon Foundation. https://www.mellon.org
title: Mellon Research Forum initiative on the value of a liberal arts education
description: The Mellon Research Forum is the initiative under which this paper was produced. The article states that "As part of the Mellon Research Forum initiative on the value of a liberal arts education, scholars are considering a range of potential outcomes of such an education, including knowledge development and critical thinking, health and well-being, civic engagement, and the economic returns to college attendance." This paper contributes the noncognitive-development strand of that multi-outcome agenda, and the article is published via the Mellon Foundation.
requirements: Functions as a scholarly initiative organizing consideration of multiple potential outcomes of a liberal arts education.
target_learners: undergraduate students in United States liberal arts education
examples: The article's publication tags are "noncognitive" and "college & post-secondary", and it links to the Mellon Foundation.

article_title: Systems Alignment and Coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's Early Care and Education System
citation: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Measure C and the Oakland Children's Initiative early childhood funding initiatives
description: Measure C is a countywide transaction and use tax–funded initiative passed in March 2020 that will generate an estimated $150 million annually for a Child Care, Preschool, and Early Education Fund, with aims of expanded access to high-quality care, improved provider wages, and promotion of wellness and kindergarten readiness. The Oakland Children's Initiative, established through Measure AA in 2018, is expected to generate approximately $30 million annually, with about 62 percent of the remaining amount allocated to early childhood and 31 percent to college persistence and success implemented by Oakland Promise. First 5 Alameda administers Measure C and is the contracted implementation partner for the Oakland Children's Initiative Early Education Fund.
requirements: Public accountability and demonstration of impact, which the report calls of paramount importance because the initiatives are funded by sales and parcel taxes that increase the cost of living
constraints: Measure C was delayed by multiyear litigation and is currently being launched; the Oakland Children's Initiative prioritizes families in the public education system
target_learners: Children from birth to age 12 in Alameda County (Measure C) and children birth to age 5 plus students to and through college in Oakland (Oakland Children's Initiative)
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness, school success, expanded access to high-quality early care and learning, and college persistence and success
examples: Measure C's initial investments include a 2-year Emergency Stabilization Fund as part of the initial investment of the 5-year plan
key_sources: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673491

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Metropolitan civil rights planning organized around three goals: diversification, stabilization, and revitalization
description: The report frames metropolitan civil rights planning as pursuing economically and racially diverse neighborhoods across a whole metropolitan area through three goals. It states: "Metropolitan civil rights planning can be roughly divided into three broad goals: 1. Diversification of affluent and white-segregated communities in outer-ring suburbs and exurban areas 2. Stabilization of diverse and integrated communities, particularly in inner and second-ring suburbs 3. Revitalization of economically distressed and nonwhite-segregated communities, particularly in urban centers and inner suburbs." Because government cannot force families to relocate, policymakers must indirectly increase the appeal of distressed areas, and the report calls well-designed magnet schools one of the few proven methods for doing so.
requirements: Policymakers must find indirect ways to increase the appeal of distressed or unstably integrated neighborhoods to wider socioeconomic groups
constraints: Stabilization and revitalization are harder than diversification because discrimination, disinvestment, and white flight push demographics toward segregation and poverty concentration
target_learners: Students and families across an entire metropolitan region
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to integrated schools and neighborhood opportunity
examples: The report builds on the 1968 Kerner Commission's recommendation of exemplary metropolitan schools designed to attract students of varying racial and socioeconomic backgrounds
key_sources: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312

article_title: Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase?
citation: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: Mentor Tech mentoring and support program at Texas Tech University
description: Mentor Tech is a Texas Tech program for underrepresented students pairing them with faculty mentors matched on "ethnicity, gender, hobbies, and career and academic interests," with required weekly contact and twice-monthly in-person meetings. It runs about 60 workshops a year on academics, career, and personal development, connects students to community groups, and awards $500–$1,000 scholarships. Started with 46 students in 2002, it now serves more than 1,000 students (45 percent black) with a waiting list.
requirements: Students must attend four workshop or social events each semester and maintain required mentor contact frequency
target_learners: underrepresented students at Texas Tech University, 45 percent of participants black
examples: Among black students at Texas Tech, graduation rates are now 56 percent, 19 points higher than a decade ago; Mentor Tech participants' first-year retention is 88 percent, 6 points above the university rate for underrepresented students
key_sources: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566672

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: Provide mentor teachers stipends and release time commensurate with the yearlong, intensive mentoring residencies require
description: Because residency mentors host residents 4 to 5 days a week for a full academic year and make significant instructional shifts, the report argues programs must "recognize the skill, time, energy, and specialized professional development required of them by providing mentor stipends and release time." This contrasts with typical student teaching, where mentors host candidates only 10 to 15 weeks with limited hours. Recognizing mentors as central influences on residents' learning also develops teacher leaders within schools and districts.
requirements: Funding streams for mentor stipends and release time, which the report suggests can come from reallocated professional development dollars
constraints: Mentor stipend levels vary by partnership district, as shown in the report's program table (e.g., $1,000 to $3,400)
target_learners: Experienced mentor teachers hosting residency candidates
target_learning_goals: High-quality clinical mentoring across a full academic year
Development of teacher leaders within schools and districts
examples: Highlighted programs pay mentors $1,000–$3,400 or offer course reductions and laptops; Fresno mentor teachers received release time to attend classes with residents and co-design integrated thematic units.
key_sources: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california

article_title: Ethical Generative AI Integration in English for Academic Purposes within Higher Education: A Mixed-Methods Study
citation: Alharbi, W., Hamid, S., Abbas, S., & Salieva, Z. (2026). Ethical Generative AI Integration in English for Academic Purposes within Higher Education: A Mixed-Methods Study. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/xwb6h668
title: Transformative learning theory combined with ethical decision-making frameworks as the design basis for GenAI professional development
description: The article grounds its professional development design in Mezirow's Transformative Learning Theory together with "established ethical decision-making frameworks in educational technology." This combined framework positions ethical reasoning as something educators develop through structured transformation rather than as a bolt-on compliance topic, and it guided how the study designed, implemented, and evaluated a program that "embeds ethical reasoning within a multicultural Global South institution."
requirements: Professional development activities must be structured so that ethical reasoning is embedded within technical GenAI training rather than separated from it
constraints: The framework was applied in one multicultural Global South higher education institution; the article states the model's adaptability to other contexts and its scalability remain to be investigated
target_learners: Higher education English for Academic Purposes educators
target_learning_goals: Ethical awareness of generative AI use
Academic integrity, transparency, and equity in AI-supported teaching
examples: The study designed, implemented, and evaluated a GenAI-integrated Professional Development program guided by this framework in a multicultural Global South institution

article_title: Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training
citation: Yang, L., Liu, H., Li, S., Jia, R., Xiao, Y., Chen, G., & Lu, L. (2026). Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10939
title: MeduAI-SP: a multi-agent LLM standardized-patient training platform with patient, tutor, turn-evaluator, and final-evaluator agents
description: MeduAI-SP is a web-based LLM platform for simulated clinical interview training built from specialized agents: "a patient agent for simulated dialog, a tutor agent providing Socratic prompts for history taking, clinical reasoning, and empathic communication without disclosing diagnostic information, and a turn-level evaluator agent that monitors clinical progress without revealing summative scores." A final evaluator produces post-encounter OSCE-aligned scoring. The platform also supports a structured non-LLM progressive-disclosure control mode and a patient-only examination mode, and logs all interaction data.
requirements: Structured YAML case materials reviewed by medical experts
tutor prompts triggered only when the turn evaluator identifies a meaningful need for intervention
constraints: the tutor was instructed not to directly reveal the final diagnosis, key differential diagnoses, or case answers
the final evaluator was not visible during the live examination interaction
target_learners: third-year undergraduate medical students beginning clinical history-taking training
examples: In the randomized study, students in the multi-agent condition completed two learning sessions with patient, tutor, and turn-evaluator agents, then an examination with a patient-only AI standardized patient
key_sources: Yang, L., Liu, H., Li, S., Jia, R., Xiao, Y., Chen, G., & Lu, L. (2026). Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10939

article_title: Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training
citation: Yang, L., Liu, H., Li, S., Jia, R., Xiao, Y., Chen, G., & Lu, L. (2026). Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10939
title: Expert-annotated clinical consultation corpus of 207 sessions and 4,815 messages with four annotation dimensions
description: The authors curated and released an open dataset derived from platform use: "The dataset contains 207 clinical history-taking sessions and 4,815 turns of human-AI dialog interactions between medical students and AI standardized patients." Three clinical experts annotated it along four dimensions: patient-message fidelity (script adherence and progressive disclosure), student dialogue intent, scaffolding need with recommended pedagogical strategy, and session-level OSCE ratings. Inter-rater reliability was highest for dialogue act (Fleiss' κ 0.84) and OSCE domains (ICC(2,k) 0.80–0.85).
requirements: annotation by three clinical experts using a multidimensional framework for clinical history-taking competence
constraints: agreement was lower for highly imbalanced labels: progressive disclosure κ = 0.31 and script adherence near-zero because almost all responses were classified as adherent
target_learners: medical students in early clinical training
examples: The corpus includes 118 multi-agent learning sessions and 89 examination sessions, with 2,350 student messages, 2,350 patient messages, and 115 tutor messages
key_sources: Yang, L., Liu, H., Li, S., Jia, R., Xiao, Y., Chen, G., & Lu, L. (2026). Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10939

article_title: Meta-Cognitive Insights into Cognitive Offloading: Mechanisms, Interventions, and Educational Implications
citation: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5
title: Beliefs-versus-experiences distinction as a two-component account of metacognition in offloading
description: The review's second organizing axis distinguishes metacognitive beliefs, which "encompass individuals ' general beliefs and knowledge about themselves stored in long-term memory," from metacognitive experiences, which "comprise metacognitive feelings aris- ing from speciﬁc information during the monitoring of of ﬂoading tasks" and are more sensitive to domain-specific and perceptual information. Beliefs dominate pre-task anchoring; experiences dominate in-task updating. The review argues this distinction reconciles contradictory feedback-intervention findings, because feedback targeting beliefs may fail during tasks while trial-by-trial performance feedback modulates experiences effectively.
requirements: Distinguishing which metacognitive component a feedback intervention targets (beliefs versus experiences) to predict its effects
constraints: The framework is argued from existing studies rather than tested directly in this review
target_learners: students using external aids and tools in technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: rational timing of cognitive offloading decisions across learning phases
examples: The review interprets Grinschgl et al.'s (2020) unexpected null effect of ranking feedback on offloading as belief-level changes being overridden by authentic task experiences
key_sources: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: The mediation gradient: five levels of interpretive agency transferred to AI, not volume of use
description: The mediation gradient organises AI use by "the degree of interpretive agency transferred to it" rather than by frequency or volume. Five levels are distinguished: access, preparation, co-interpretation, delegation and substitution. The level is diagnosed by five questions: who frames the question, who evaluates competing meanings, who chooses the response, whether a human encounter follows, and whether the student reflects afterwards. Timing interacts with the gradient: the same output may function as preparation, delegation or co-interpretation depending on when it is used.
requirements: Diagnosis requires asking who frames the question, who evaluates competing meanings, who chooses the response, whether a human encounter follows, and whether the student reflects afterwards
constraints: Access and preparation generally preserve agency; delegation and substitution may be justified for harmful friction but are most likely to erode learning when applied to productive friction
examples: A lengthy AI-drafted message that the student interrogates and rewrites may transfer less agency than a brief cultural explanation accepted without examination
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS)
citation: Yifan Liu, Jaime Arguello, Orland Hoeber, Chang Liu, Soo Young Rieh, Luanne Sinnamon, et al. (2026). Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS). ACM SIGIR Forum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08936
title: Three types of metacognitive laziness in academic search: plan-deficit, monitoring-deficit, and regulation-deficit
description: This framework, presented in a lightning talk by Song and Liu, identifies three types of metacognitive laziness during academic search behaviors: "plan-deficit, monitoring-deficit, and regulation-deficit". It characterizes ways learners offload metacognitive processes to GenAI systems, and it grounds two design challenges: evolving GenAI from fact-retrievers to problem-solving scaffolds at the strategy layer, and embedding metacognitive scaffolds to mitigate each type of laziness. The framework is used to foster adaptive collaboration and human-AI symbiosis in creative academic search.
requirements: GenAI systems should evolve from fact-retrievers to problem-solving scaffolds that help users break down ill-structured problems into manageable sub-problems at the strategy layer
target_learning_goals: metacognitive planning, monitoring, and regulation during academic search
examples: Song and Liu examined and identified the three laziness types from academic search behaviors, per the lightning talk
key_sources: Yifan Liu, Jaime Arguello, Orland Hoeber, Chang Liu, Soo Young Rieh, Luanne Sinnamon, et al. (2026). Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS). ACM SIGIR Forum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08936

article_title: Rethinking teachers’ diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis
citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: Meta-diagnosis: teachers' evaluative and integrative processing of AI-generated and self-generated diagnostic evidence
description: Meta-diagnosis is the cognitive process through which teachers critically evaluate and integrate two qualitatively different types of diagnostic evidence: their own judgments of student learning and AI-generated inferences based on algorithmic interpretation of student data. The article introduces it as the central diagnostic demand of AI-supported formative assessment, illustrated through contrasting case examples of subtraction teaching with and without a learning platform. It is 'not tied to a specific type of AI-supported assessment system but refers to the evaluative and integrative processes required of teachers.'
requirements: Teachers must have access to AI-generated diagnostic inferences that are accessible to them, so that these 'need to be evaluated and integrated into teachers' own diagnostic judgments'.
constraints: When explainable AI insights are limited, teachers must rely more strongly on their own classroom observations and observations of students' interactions with AI-supported learning environments.
target_learning_goals: formative assessment and adaptive instructional decision-making
examples: In the AI-assisted case example, the teacher weighs a dashboard's place-value error pattern against her own observation of the student's growing frustration before deciding to offer encouragement before addressing the misconception.
key_sources: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661

article_title: Math Education Digital Shadows for facilitating learning with LLMs: Math performance, anxiety and confidence in simulated students and AIs
citation: Esposito, N., Tricarico, A., Porzio, L., Aghazadeh Ardebili, A., & Stella, M. (2026). Math Education Digital Shadows for Investigating Learning with GenAI: Mathematics Performance, Anxiety, and Confidence in LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27618
title: MEDS dataset of 28,000 LLM runs across four mathematics-education tasks
description: MEDS is a multimodal, LLM-generated dataset mapping how large language models reason about mathematics under human-shadow and AI-assistant conditions. Each record includes prompts, psychological and sociodemographic metadata, and four tasks: interviews, three psychometric questionnaires, a cognitive network, and 18 high-school quiz items. The article states that "MEDS comprises 28,000 runs from 14 LLMs (i.e., Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, IBM Granite, Microsoft Phi, and xAI Grok) generated under human-shadow and AI-assistant conditions." Records are publicly available on GitHub as JSON files.
requirements: Runs must be generated under specified constraints: four tasks, prompting mode, and persona profile, with structured JSON outputs
constraints: The article states MEDS is not a proxy for human opinion and is not statistically representative of any specific country
examples: Each run completed four tasks: interviews about mathematics, MSES/AMAS/MSEAQ psychometric ratings, 50-cue-word semantic associations, and 18 multiple-choice problems with reasoning and confidence scores
key_sources: Esposito, N., Tricarico, A., Porzio, L., Aghazadeh Ardebili, A., & Stella, M. (2026). Math Education Digital Shadows for Investigating Learning with GenAI: Mathematics Performance, Anxiety, and Confidence in LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27618

article_title: MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training
citation: Zhiqi Gao, Huarui Luo, Guo Zhu, Bingquan Zhang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Yizhan Feng, Jiahuan Pei, Jie Li, Benyou Wang. (2026). MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17512
title: MedEasy: a multi-agent AI standardized-patient system for structured consultation practice
description: MedEasy is a web-based, multi-agent virtual standardized patient system that treats a virtual consultation as a staged process of patient dialogue, clinical action, decision submission, documentation, and post-session review. Its architecture separates "intent recognition, case-grounded patient response, action-contingent clinical findings, and trajectory-level evaluation." An Auxiliary Agent maps learner utterances to a 31-category clinical intent framework, a Patient Agent generates case-grounded responses, and an Evaluation Agent reviews the completed session against expert criteria. The Patient and Evaluation Agents use Gemini 2.5 Pro and the Auxiliary Agent uses Gemini 2.5 Flash.
requirements: A structured case library with expert-authored case records and a clinical intent framework must be authored offline before runtime consultation.
constraints: The Evaluation Agent's review "applies the scope defined in the authored teaching case" and is used for formative post-session review rather than formal grading.
target_learning_goals: clinical consultation skills including history taking, examination selection, diagnosis, treatment planning, patient education, and medical-record writing
examples: The case library contains 20 clinical cases selected by a panel of medical experts, balanced by patient gender and spanning three age groups, seven major organ systems, and 16 diagnoses.

article_title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
citation: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao, Xun Lin, Hongqiu Wu, Longfei Gou, Yixiao Liu, Ann Sin Nga Lau, Qi Dou. (2026). MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570
title: MedGame dual-engine framework: Medical Narrative Designer plus Story Director for case-to-game transformation
description: MedGame is a generative framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. It "adopts a dual-engine architecture that decouples clinical narrative ideation from technical orchestration": a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes raw patient summaries into a hierarchical Clinical Storyline with Acts, Scenes, and Decision Nodes, and a Story Director maps that storyline into a directed acyclic graph of multimodal generation primitives for rendering. The storyline serves as the interface between the two engines.
requirements: Generated storylines must be faithful to the source case, expose meaningful decision checkpoints, remain medically plausible, and stay machine-executable (enforced via a Pydantic schema and medical rubrics).
constraints: The linear storyline formulation is motivated by the deterministic source case format, not by an assumption that clinical reasoning itself is linear; branching story graphs are discussed as an extension.
examples: A 15-year-old boy's ER case was adapted into a storyline with Acts such as 'A Bloody Alarm' and Scenes for laboratory and imaging decisions, with decision nodes asking which diagnostic tests to order.
key_sources: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao, Xun Lin, Hongqiu Wu, Longfei Gou, Yixiao Liu, Ann Sin Nga Lau, Qi Dou. (2026). MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570

article_title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
citation: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao, Xun Lin, Hongqiu Wu, Longfei Gou, Yixiao Liu, Ann Sin Nga Lau, Qi Dou. (2026). MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570
title: MedGame Bench: 5,000-case benchmark for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction
description: MedGame Bench is a case-grounded benchmark and evaluation protocol built from public patient summaries in the PMC-Patients Dataset. The authors "sample 5,000 cases balanced across eight medical specialties" and partition them into a fixed 4,000/1,000 train–test split. It contains two evaluation tracks aligned with the dual-engine design, scored on structural validity, story adaptation, medical accuracy, educational quality, and task reasonability, with structure checked by rule-based validation and content indicators rated by LLM-as-a-Judge on a 1–10 scale.
requirements: Evaluation uses automated rule-based checking for structure validation and GPT-5.2 LLM-as-a-Judge scoring with rubrics for content-oriented indicators.
constraints: The benchmark is built from PMC-Patients case-report-derived summaries; high-similarity patient variants across the train–test split are tracked and analyzed for related-case effects.
examples: The benchmark samples 5,000 cases across cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, hematology/oncology, nephrology, neurology, respiratory and critical care, and rheumatology, with 625 cases per specialty.

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: A taxonomy of 17 cognitively-grounded flashcard interaction types across three learning categories
description: Memdora's central design contribution is a taxonomy of 17 interaction types across three learning categories: Language (6 types), By Heart (1 type with 3 retrieval modes), and Exam (10 types). Each type is paired with a primary cognitive-science citation, e.g. Vocabulary is grounded in "retrieval practice [15]" and Concept in "elaborative interrogation [7]". The taxonomy is built on three principles: "retrieval effort produces retention", "format should match learning goal", and "transparency builds metacognition".
requirements: Each interaction type must be grounded in peer-reviewed cognitive science research with per-type citations and design rationale documented
constraints: The efficacy of these types within Memdora, and in combination with FSRS-6 scheduling, has not been empirically evaluated
target_learning_goals: vocabulary and phrase acquisition in a target language
examples: The paper documents all 17 types in Table 1 with interaction descriptions and primary citations, e.g. Cloze: supply missing word in target-language sentence, grounded in Bransford & Johnson [4]

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Memdora: cross-platform AI spaced repetition system with single-gesture capture and FSRS-6 scheduling
description: Memdora is a cross-platform SRS deployed on iOS, Android, Web, and browser extensions for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. Its capture layer offers four modalities including "using the browser extension to highlight text on any web page", collapsing card-creation context-switching cost to near zero. All cards are scheduled with FSRS-6, which "maintains per-card estimates of memory stability (S) and retrievability (R)" and runs client-side on mobile for offline scheduling.
requirements: A large language model generation pipeline with structured output prompting and content-type classification routing items to appropriate interaction types
constraints: The AI generation pipeline may produce cards of variable quality in highly specialized domains
target_learners: readers capturing content from web pages
target_learning_goals: long-term retention through spaced retrieval practice
examples: The browser extension supports in-context vocabulary recall: hovering over a word already in the user's deck displays the card with its current FSRS-6 retention percentage without opening the application
key_sources: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Collaborative deck layer with live synchronization and independent per-follower scheduling
description: Memdora's collaborative layer lets users publish decks publicly, to friends, or privately; published decks appear in a Discover feed where users follow them. When the deck owner adds, edits, or removes a card, "all followers' copies update instantly—no re-follow required", while "each follower maintains independent FSRS-6 scheduling state, learning at their own pace". The infrastructure uses a publish-subscribe model with server-side scheduling state.
requirements: A publish-subscribe infrastructure with each follower maintaining independent scheduling state server-side
constraints: The collaborative deck features have not yet been evaluated in a formal educational setting; deployment may reveal unmet needs around teacher workflows and institutional authentication
target_learners: students following a teacher's shared deck
target_learning_goals: shared vocabulary learning with teacher-curated content
examples: The paper describes classroom use: a teacher publishes a shared vocabulary deck, students follow it, and the teacher can push new cards or corrections that propagate to all students automatically
key_sources: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Effort-based behavioral reward system incentivizing cognitive engagement rather than app presence
description: Memdora rewards cognitive effort through two mechanisms: a Study Time Reward granting bonus AI generation credits for "completing 5 continuous minutes of active card review", and a Volume Reward for reviewing 100 cards in a day. A Streak System tracks consecutive days of actual card review rather than app opening, providing continuity motivation through loss aversion. This contrasts with presence-based rewards the paper says produce superficial engagement.
requirements: Rewards must be tied to actual card review (5 continuous minutes of study, 100 cards per day) rather than mere app interaction
constraints: The effort-based reward system has not been evaluated; a future study is planned comparing learning depth metrics between effort-rewarded and presence-rewarded conditions
target_learners: daily SRS users needing engagement continuity
examples: Users earn AI generation credits for completing 5 continuous minutes of study and for reviewing 100 cards per day

article_title: Can Generative Artificial Intelligence Reliably Score Open-Ended Question Assessments in Undergraduate Medical Education?
citation: Olvet DM, Kruidering M, Fulton TB, Truong B, Endo K, Lucito R, Willey JM. (2026). Can Generative Artificial Intelligence Reliably Score Open-Ended Question Assessments in Undergraduate Medical Education? Medical Science Educator 36:1539–1552. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40670-026-02638-2
title: Med2Lab platform for feeding vignettes, rubrics, and student responses to GPT-4 for automated OEQ scoring
description: Med2Lab is a platform through which case vignettes, questions, rubrics, and deidentified student responses were entered into GPT-4 for automated scoring of open-ended exam questions. The article states that "The Med2Lab system was specifically engineered to manage rubric integration and automate prompt workflows." For each student response, GPT-4 generated a score and an explanation of 3–4 sentences of feedback. The model used was OpenAI's GPT-4o-2024-05-13, accessed via OpenAI's cloud platform through the Med2Lab interface at ZSOM and via a localized HIPAA-compliant deployment at UCSF.
requirements: Deidentification of student responses before inclusion into the system
A scoring rubric and instructional prompt defining the grading task
constraints: Student answer texts were stored in a secure password-protected AWS database accessible only to designated personnel
target_learners: medical students in undergraduate medical education
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of open-ended exam responses with generated feedback
examples: The instructional prompt used read: YOU = a medical educator grading the QUESTION below, based on the RUBRIC

article_title: College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias
citation: Ren S (2026) College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias. Front. Psychol. 17:1926110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1926110
title: Metacognitive dependence: a descriptive framework for perceived–behavioral reliance mismatch in AI-assisted decisions
description: The article introduces "metacognitive dependence" as an integrative conceptual label for a specific mismatch: students' observable reliance on generative-AI advice may diverge from their awareness of how strongly that advice shaped their judgment. The authors state the term is "not treated here as a validated unitary latent trait"; it organizes four theoretically related but distinct indicators — behavioral reliance, perceived reliance, decision confidence, and attributional responsibility. The framework also distinguishes overreliance (acceptance of incorrect AI advice) from trust calibration and metacognitive monitoring accuracy.
requirements: Behavioral reliance, awareness calibration, confidence, and attribution are analyzed separately rather than as one psychometric construct
constraints: The framework is descriptive; evidence that the measures change together is not psychometric proof of a single latent construct
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for academic decisions
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of AI influence on judgments and decisions
examples: In the experiment, open ChatGPT support produced a negative mean signed discrepancy (behavioral reliance exceeding perceived reliance), while reflection brought signed discrepancy near zero.

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Messick's unified validity framework used to map six facets of GenAI threat to assessment validity
description: The article applies Messick's unified validity framework as its organizing analytic axis, systematically mapping GenAI threats across six validity facets. As the abstract states, the authors "use Messick's unified validity framework to systematically map the ways in which GenAI threatens content, structural, consequential, generalisability, substantive, and external validity". This gives assessment designers a structured taxonomy for diagnosing which facets of validity a GenAI-vulnerable task loses.
requirements: Users must be able to analyse an assessment task against each of the six validity facets named in the framework.
target_learning_goals: validity-focused evaluation and redesign of assessment tasks
examples: The framework is used to organise the article's analysis of how GenAI undermines each validity facet before the twin approach is introduced.

article_title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
citation: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942
title: MedQA semantically equivalent user-cohort benchmark for measuring prompt privilege
description: A benchmark construction methodology that instantiates prompt privilege on the MedQA benchmark: for each original MedQA question, four additional semantically equivalent prompt variants are generated representing distinct user cohorts — Low Literacy, Everyday User, Educated User, and Prompt Engineer. Variants are produced with GPT-5.5 under rewriting instructions that preserve all clinically relevant information, answer choices, and the original ground-truth label, so observed performance differences can be attributed to prompt formulation rather than task difficulty or information content.
requirements: Clinical facts, symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, and reasoning cues may not be added, removed, or altered — only linguistic characteristics such as vocabulary complexity, terminology, sentence structure, and communication style are modified to match the target user cohort.
constraints: The Prompt Engineer cohort does not represent a linguistic population; it augments the original question with explicit reasoning instructions as an upper-bound performance reference.
target_learners: users with limited health and digital literacy
typical adults without formal medical training
college-educated individuals without professional medical training
target_learning_goals: comparing model performance across users who share identical information needs but communicate differently
examples: Prompt Engineer variants keep the clinical question unchanged and prepend explicit reasoning instructions to isolate the effect of prompt-engineering expertise
key_sources: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942

article_title: Applying psychometric methods to distinguish between human and generative AI responses to multiple-choice assessments
citation: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713
title: Build AI-cheating detection systems on educational measurement theory rather than ad-hoc text-similarity methods for closed-form items
description: For MCQ-based assessment, where text-similarity detection tools do not apply, the authors recommend grounding detection in psychometric theory: "We propose building systems based on educational measurement theory, specifically IRT and PFS, to model assessment behaviors using metrics that are sensitive to the differences between human and artificial intelligence behavior." This extends anomaly-based cheating detection from text-rich outputs to the most common closed-form question format.
requirements: Assessment instruments with enough items (at least 20) for PFS to show reasonable variance
Access to response-level data from the assessment platform
constraints: Effectiveness decreases as GenAI use becomes more prevalent
Retrospective rather than real-time
Misfit may reflect legitimate conditions such as learning disabilities
target_learners: examinees on large-scale standardized and high-stakes MCQ assessments
target_learning_goals: preserving the validity and integrity of MCQ-based assessment of learner ability
examples: The authors demonstrated the approach on two authentic contexts — a formative high-school chemistry diagnostic and a summative psychometric entrance-exam chapter — using premium versions of three leading chatbots.

citation: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808
title: Structured metadata framework for annotating components of educational knowledge base repositories
description: The article proposes structured metadata for describing all components of hybrid AI-driven knowledge bases, intended to annotate objects stored in specialized repositories for personalized tutoring (ontologies, mappings, rules, tools) and their representation in an ontology. Its purpose is to support searching and reuse of developed knowledge base components, thereby reducing development time, effort, and cost. The article states that "This metadata framework can support the development of an ontology that facilitates the discovery, selection, and reuse of appropriate ontologies, rules, mappings, and tools stored in specialized knowledge repositories for educational purposes."
requirements: Specialized repositories must exist to store previously developed components of educational knowledge bases
constraints: The article notes weak standardization and coexistence of multiple standards in the field as a challenge for reuse
target_learners: developers and maintainers of knowledge-based intelligent educational systems
target_learning_goals: ontology and knowledge component reuse for personalized tutoring development
examples: The framework classifies entities used in the systems based on the proposed knowledge base architecture

article_title: Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance
citation: Fan, Y., Tang, L., Le, H., Shen, K., Tan, S., Zhao, Y., Shen, Y., Li, X., & Gasevic, D. (2025). Beware of Metacognitive Laziness: Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Motivation, Processes, and Performance. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13544
title: Metacognitive laziness: dependence on AI assistance that offloads metacognitive load and weakens association of metacognitive processes with learning tasks
description: The article defines metacognitive laziness as "learners' dependence on AI assistance, oﬄoading metacognitive load, and less eﬀectively associating responsible metacognitive processes with learning tasks". It extends cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert) and disfluency accounts (Alter et al.): reliance on AI-generated outputs removes the cognitive difficulty that triggers deeper analytical processing. The authors ground the construct empirically in the AI group's process maps, which centred on consulting ChatGPT with relatively fewer metacognitive processes such as evaluation and orientation.
requirements: Learners must have access to an AI agent that can take over monitoring and evaluation during learning tasks
constraints: Observed in a single lab-based English writing-revising task with university students; the authors call for multi-task and cross-context studies to test generalisability
target_learners: university students learning with generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and metacognitive engagement in writing tasks
examples: AI-group learners predominantly relied on consulting ChatGPT during revision, forming a loop between revising, evaluating and interacting with the agent

article_title: Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education
citation: Ido Roll & Ruth Wylie. (2016). Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 582-599. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0110-3
title: The mentor metaphor: a new vision for ILEs beyond the two-sigma human-tutor benchmark
description: The article proposes replacing the human-tutor metaphor — which frames ILEs as one-on-one, time-limited, and space-constrained — with a mentor metaphor. ILEs have unique affordances: they can be "collaborative, omnipresent, and portable", supporting learning anytime, anywhere, by anyone. An appropriate metaphor offers a vision and concrete evaluation goals; the authors do not argue the two-sigma problem is solved or irrelevant, but want that level of improvement across tasks, contexts, and goals, including life-long skills, peers, and learners' life problems.
requirements: The metaphor serves two stated functions: offering a succinct inspiration and offering concrete goals against which progress can be evaluated.
constraints: The article explicitly does not claim the two-sigma problem is solved; the mentor vision is aspirational rather than demonstrated by reviewed data.
examples: The article opens with Henry Ford's faster-horses quote and characterises 25 years of AIED as building faster classrooms — similar learning gains in reduced time.
