article_title: Guidance during mathematical problem solving.
citation: Ahmad Tarmizi, Rohani. (1991). Guidance During Mathematical Problem Solving. Doctoral thesis, University of New South Wales. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/69310
title: Means-ends analysis as a problem-solving strategy that inhibits learning
description: Means-ends analysis is a general problem-solving strategy in which the solver reduces the difference between the current state and the goal state by applying appropriate operators, creating subgoals when operators cannot be applied. The thesis reviews evidence that most novice problem solvers use it, hypothesizes that it imposes heavy cognitive load and misdirects attention compared to studying worked examples, and therefore treats it as a mechanism that can inhibit schema acquisition during learning.
requirements: A problem with a defined goal state and operators that reduce differences between current and goal states
constraints: Applied mainly by solvers not highly familiar with the subject matter; the thesis argues its search for operators consumes working-memory resources that could otherwise go to schema acquisition
target_learners: novice problem solvers in mathematics and science
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition and rule automation rather than mere solution of a given problem
examples: GPS, the General Problem Solver, solving Tower of Hanoi and other transformation problems via means-ends analysis; water-jug experiments showing move selection governed by the means-ends heuristic
key_sources: Ahmad Tarmizi, Rohani. (1991). Guidance During Mathematical Problem Solving. Doctoral thesis, University of New South Wales. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/69310

article_title: Development and Plasticity of Cognitive Flexibility in Early and Middle Childhood
citation: Buttelmann F and Karbach J (2017). Development and Plasticity of Cognitive Flexibility in Early and Middle Childhood. Front. Psychol. 8:1040. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01040
title: Metacognitive EF training: qualitatively changing how children engage executive functions to support flexible adaptation and transfer
description: The review proposes metacognitive training as a promising new approach to promoting cognitive flexibility in childhood. Unlike training that enhances the quantity of EF children can engage, it would "change qualitatively how they engage EF as a function of task diﬃculty", training children to reflect on how to approach new tasks by weighing the costs (e.g., mental effort) and benefits (e.g., rewards) of available control strategies. Because this approach is relatively task-unspecific, the authors argue it may support transfer of flexibility training to untrained tasks and abilities.
requirements: Training should encourage performance evaluation, including error detection and feedback processing, which are still gradually developing in young children.
constraints: The approach is proposed on the basis of a few recent studies; the review states metacognitive instructions have rarely been applied in cognitive-training research and mechanisms of training and transfer effects are not fully understood.
target_learners: typically developing children from preschool to elementary school age
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility and executive function development
transfer of training to untrained tasks
examples: Espinet et al. trained 2- to 4-year-olds with corrective feedback and reflection instructions; Moriguchi et al. had preschoolers explain task rules to a puppet.
key_sources: Buttelmann F and Karbach J (2017). Development and Plasticity of Cognitive Flexibility in Early and Middle Childhood. Front. Psychol. 8:1040. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01040

article_title: The development of metacognitive ability in adolescence
citation: Weil L.G., Fleming S.M., Dumontheil I., Kilford E.J., Weil R.S., Rees G., Dolan R.J., Blakemore S.-J. (2013). The development of metacognitive ability in adolescence. Consciousness and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.concog.2013.01.004
title: Metacognitive ability as a dissociable monitoring component measured by type II signal detection theory
description: The article treats metacognitive ability as "how accurately participants' confidence in their performance tracks their actual performance", operationalised via type II signal detection theory as the area under the type II ROC curve (Aroc). A psychophysical staircase clamps first-order performance so that confidence judgments can be studied independently of objective accuracy. This dissociation is presented as critical for developmental studies, where performance and awareness are otherwise confounded.
requirements: A task in which objective performance can be dissociated from metacognitive judgments, e.g. by staircase-clamping accuracy
constraints: The measure concerns the confidence–performance relationship on a perceptual task; the authors note they do not test how this corresponds to other forms of metacognition or mentalising
target_learning_goals: awareness of one's own cognitive processes and performance monitoring
examples: Participants performed a Gabor pop-out interval judgment, then rated confidence 1–6; Aroc was computed from the type II ROC after excluding the first 100 staircase-stabilisation trials.
key_sources: Weil L.G., Fleming S.M., Dumontheil I., Kilford E.J., Weil R.S., Rees G., Dolan R.J., Blakemore S.-J. (2013). The development of metacognitive ability in adolescence. Consciousness and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.concog.2013.01.004

article_title: Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge
citation: Kate Cain, Jane V. Oakhill, Marcia A. Barnes, and Peter E. Bryant. (2001). Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge. Memory & Cognition, 29(6), 850-859. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03196476
title: Mental models account of children's text comprehension difficulties: poor comprehenders construct incomplete, poorly integrated representations of text
description: The article interprets children's comprehension difficulties within the mental models framework, in which skilled comprehension requires building a coherent, integrated model of a text as a whole rather than only local links. The authors state that "poor comprehenders construct incomplete representations of text: They are often able to integrate information at a local level but are unable to produce a coherent integrated model of the text as a whole." In this study the framework motivated the distinction between coherence inferences, needed for cohesion, and elaborative inferences, which enrich the representation, and the finding that inference failures leave a poorly integrated text model.
requirements: Assessment of inference making must separate inferences essential for textual coherence from merely elaborative ones
Relevant background knowledge must be available to the learner for knowledge-based inferences to be possible
constraints: The account is applied to children with age-appropriate word-reading and vocabulary skills whose difficulties arise at the text level
The study tested 7- to 8-year-olds listening to a multiepisode story, so scope is limited to that age band and auditory presentation
target_learners: 7- to 8-year-old children with specific reading comprehension deficits despite adequate word-reading skills
target_learning_goals: Inference making during narrative listening and reading
examples: Children heard a six-episode story about an imaginary planet after learning a 12-fact knowledge base, and answered coherence, elaborative, literal, and simile questions after each episode
key_sources: Kate Cain, Jane V. Oakhill, Marcia A. Barnes, and Peter E. Bryant. (2001). Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge. Memory & Cognition, 29(6), 850-859. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03196414

article_title: Numbers in the Blind's “Eye”
citation: Salillas E, Grana´ A, El-Yagoubi R, Semenza C (2009) Numbers in the Blind's ''Eye''. PLoS ONE 4(7): e6357. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0006357
title: Mental number line account of the SNARC effect (amodal spatial-numerical representation)
description: The article frames its study with the mental number line account of the SNARC effect: an internal representation of magnitude in which "numbers are represented along a left-to-right oriented mental number line", whose automatic activation produces faster responses to small numbers with the left hand and large numbers with the right. The study uses this framework to test whether number semantics are modality-neutral, arguing that a spatial organization of number representation in people deprived of visual world experience indicates a modality-neutral, hardwired core number representation, and extends the account to attention shifts in auditory space.
requirements: Numerical input culture with left-to-right written numbers, per the article's framing of the SNARC effect
constraints: The article treats the representation's left-to-right orientation as shared by blind and sighted groups but attributes differences in its manipulation (working-memory dependence) to the modality of numerical input
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude representation and number-space associations
examples: Auditory number cues (1, 2, 8, 9) followed by lateralized dichotic targets in seven blind and seven sighted adults produced congruent-trial detection advantages in both groups
key_sources: Salillas E, Grana´ A, El-Yagoubi R, Semenza C (2009) Numbers in the Blind's ''Eye''. PLoS ONE 4(7): e6357. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0006357

article_title: Working memory and number line representations in single-digit addition: Approximate versus exact, nonsymbolic versus symbolic
citation: Xenidou-Dervou, I., van der Schoot, M., & van Lieshout, E. C. D. M. (2014). Working Memory and Number Line Representations in Single-digit Addition: Approximate versus Exact, Nonsymbolic versus Symbolic. VU University Amsterdam. https://www.vu.nl
title: The mental model for simple arithmetic
description: The mental model holds that "performance variations across different simple arithmetic problem formats occur because different presentation formats place different demands on one's WM". Before age six, children solve nonsymbolic problems more easily by representing quantities in a readily accessible mental model in the VSSP, while symbolic problems require phonological storage or transcoding via the CE. The study extended the model by adding domain-specific coding, i.e. nonsymbolic and symbolic mental number line representations, tested alongside WM components.
requirements: Predictor tasks must differ from the addition tasks only in storage, manipulation and representation, so mechanisms can be distinguished
constraints: The study tested kindergarteners at the end of the school year in the Netherlands; transcoding direction varied with format familiarity and the authors call the alternate-transcoding interpretation tentative
target_learning_goals: single-digit mental addition (approximate and exact, nonsymbolic and symbolic)
examples: Four computerized addition tasks differing only in stimulus and response type were administered with Corsi Blocks, digit span forwards/backwards and two computerized number line estimation tasks
key_sources: Xenidou-Dervou, I., van der Schoot, M., & van Lieshout, E. C. D. M. (2014). Working Memory and Number Line Representations in Single-digit Addition: Approximate versus Exact, Nonsymbolic versus Symbolic. VU University Amsterdam. https://doi.org/10.1080/17470218.2014.977303

article_title: Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change
citation: Cortes, R. A., Peterson, E. G., Kraemer, D. J. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., Dinh, N., Weinberger, A. B., Daker, R. J., Lyons, I. M., Goldman, D., & Green, A. E. (2022). Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change. Science Advances. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abo3555
title: Mental model theory: spatial processes covertly underlie verbal reasoning, implying spatial education can improve verbal ability
description: Mental model theory (MMT) posits that ostensibly verbal information is processed by co-opted neural resources that evolved to support visuospatial operations, with the spatial process of "scanning" supporting mental model–based reasoning. It further holds that reasoning depends on developing the effectiveness of spatial resources and their integration with executive resources, e.g., functional connectivity of posterior parietal cortex to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The article uses MMT to derive the educational hypothesis that curricula fostering spatial cognition, especially spatial scanning, should transfer to verbal reasoning, and tests its behavioral and neural predictions in real-world classrooms.
requirements: Curricula must develop the effectiveness of spatial resources (e.g., spatial scanning) and their integration with executive resources, not merely engage spatial processing
constraints: MMT-based improvement is predicted to depend on developing spatial resource effectiveness, not just engagement; the article notes a curriculum focused on three-dimensional rotation might be needed for mental rotation gains
target_learners: high school students in STEM courses
examples: The Geospatial Semester curriculum was designed around scanning maps to identify key spatial features and determine how features relate across maps, operationalizing the MMT-based educational hypothesis
key_sources: Cortes, R. A., Peterson, E. G., Kraemer, D. J. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., Dinh, N., Weinberger, A. B., Daker, R. J., Lyons, I. M., Goldman, D., & Green, A. E. (2022). Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change. Science Advances. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abo3555

article_title: The role of metacognition in human social interactions
citation: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123
title: Metacognition comprises implicit and explicit forms serving monitoring and control of cognition
description: The article defines metacognition as the processes by which we monitor and control our own cognitive processes, distinguishing an implicit form that is rapid, automatic and without awareness from an explicit, slow and deliberate form that generates reportable knowledge. It applies the same distinction to mentalizing (metacognition applied to others). This framework organizes the review's argument about social interaction.
requirements: Distinguishing monitoring (reflection on memory/perception) from control (regulation based on that knowledge)
constraints: The article notes the question remains open as to whether the implicit form of self-monitoring should even be called metacognition
target_learning_goals: understanding metacognitive monitoring and control of one's own cognitive processes
examples: Tip-of-the-tongue states illustrate monitoring; alphabet-search strategies illustrate control; skilled typists slowing after corrected errors illustrate implicit monitoring
key_sources: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123

article_title: Metacognition in Later Adulthood
citation: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/
title: Metacognition as monitoring plus control in a reciprocal relation, forming the basis of self-regulated learning
description: The article defines metacognition as "thoughts, beliefs, and other cognitive processes devoted to assessing and controlling one's own cognitions." Monitoring evaluates information from an ongoing cognitive process, such as a retrieval search, while control uses that monitoring to decide whether and how to change cognitive processing, such as restudying what one cannot access. Monitoring and control are in a reciprocal relation and are viewed as critical components of self-regulation. The framework organizes the review's evidence on aging, JOLs, FOKs, and intervention design.
requirements: Monitoring must be empirically validated against objective measures of the judged processes, such as comparing JOLs to later paired-associate recall performance
constraints: The review focuses on relative accuracy (resolution), typically computed as within-person Goodman-Kruskal gamma correlations between judgments and criterion performance
target_learners: adults across the life span ages 18 to 81
target_learning_goals: self-regulated study decisions such as selective restudy
examples: Older adults learning diabetes symptoms monitor whether they can retrieve studied facts about nutrition and blood glucose so they can further review inaccessible information
key_sources: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/

article_title: Metacognition in Later Adulthood
citation: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/
title: Memory-quality account of episodic feeling-of-knowing resolution: FOK accuracy derives from the diagnosticity of cues produced by encoding quality
description: The article advances an explanatory account in which FOK judgments are informed by cue familiarity and by partial information accessed during attempted retrieval, and the resolution of FOKs depends on the quality of the underlying memory representation. As the article states, "rich encoding experiences produce cues that are more diagnostic about the availability of a sought-after target in memory; hence, using these cues will produce more accurate FOKs." Apparent age deficits in episodic FOK resolution may therefore reflect poorer memory representations rather than a monitoring deficit. The account explains why equating memory performance across age groups matters.
requirements: Investigations of age differences in retrieval monitoring should attempt to equate older and younger adults on memory performance to rule out this explanation
constraints: The account applies to FOK judgments for episodic memory tasks where underlying memory quality varies
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of whether sought-after information is available in memory
retrieval decisions such as whether to continue search or restudy
examples: In the Hertzog, Dunlosky, and Sinclair (2010) experiment, older adults with a 30-minute delay had better memory performance and better FOK resolution, attributed to more diagnostic encoding information rather than superior monitoring
key_sources: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/

article_title: Adherence to a Mediterranean diet and cognitive function in the Age‐Related Eye Disease Studies 1 & 2
citation: Keenan Tiarnán D., Agrón Elvira, Mares Julie A., Clemons Traci E., van Asten Freekje, Swaroop Anand, Chew Emily Y.; AREDS and AREDS2 Research Groups. (2020). Adherence to a Mediterranean diet and cognitive function in the Age-Related Eye Disease Studies 1 & 2. Alzheimer's & Dementia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8328271/
title: Recommend Mediterranean-type dietary patterns in evidence-based dietary guidelines to support cognitive health in aging
description: The article concludes that its findings "may help inform evidence-based dietary recommendations, adding strength to evidence that Mediterranean-type diet patterns may maximize cognitive reserve against impairment and dementia." The principle is that population dietary guidance for older adults should feature Mediterranean-type patterns, with emphasis on fish intake given its additional association with slower decline. It rests on observational associations, not trial evidence.
requirements: Dietary assessment via validated food frequency questionnaires to index adherence (the modified aMED score over nine components)
constraints: Associations are observational and post hoc; residual or unmeasured confounding (e.g., physical activity) is a stated limitation
Generalizability to populations with different dietary patterns or without age-related macular degeneration is not certain
target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive function and reducing risk of cognitive impairment in aging
examples: In AREDS and AREDS2, aMED tertile 3 versus tertile 1 yielded odds ratios for cognitive impairment of 0.36 and 0.56 respectively, and fish intake quartile 4 showed consistently lower impairment odds in both cohorts
key_sources: Keenan Tiarnán D., Agrón Elvira, Mares Julie A., Clemons Traci E., van Asten Freekje, Swaroop Anand, Chew Emily Y.; AREDS and AREDS2 Research Groups. (2020). Adherence to a Mediterranean diet and cognitive function in the Age-Related Eye Disease Studies 1 & 2. Alzheimer's & Dementia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8328271/

article_title: Effects of age on metacognitive efficiency
citation: Palmer E.C., David A.S., Fleming S.M. (2014). Effects of age on metacognitive efficiency. Consciousness and Cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4154452/
title: Meta-d′/d′ as a performance-controlled measure of metacognitive efficiency
description: Meta-d′/d′ is a signal detection theoretic measure that quantifies metacognitive efficiency independently of primary task performance. The article explains that "Meta-d′/d′ is a relative measure: given a certain level of processing capacity (d′), meta-d′/d′ quantifies the extent to which a metacognitively optimal observer is aware of their performance." A value of 1 is metacognitively ideal; values below 1 indicate a failure of metacognitive awareness. The study uses it to dissociate metacognitive efficiency from age-related changes in task performance, which confound measures such as the gamma correlation.
requirements: Requires confidence ratings collected on each trial alongside a primary task, and computation of both d′ and meta-d′ from the same data
constraints: Values greater than 1 may occur when the initial judgment is made under time pressure, as the article notes
target_learners: Adults aged 18–84 in laboratory studies of perception and memory
target_learning_goals: Quantifying the efficiency with which confidence ratings discriminate between correct and incorrect trials
examples: Applied to a staircase-controlled perceptual task and a 2-AFC word recognition memory task in adults aged 18–84
key_sources: Palmer E.C., David A.S., Fleming S.M. (2014). Effects of age on metacognitive efficiency. Consciousness and Cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4154452/

article_title: Metacognitive scaffolding boosts cognitive and neural benefits following executive attention training in children
citation: Pozuelos, J.P., Cómbita, L.M., Abundis-Gutiérrez, A., Paz-Alonso, P.M., Conejero A., Guerra, S., & Rueda, M.R. (2019). Metacognitive scaffolding boosts cognitive and neural benefits following executive attention training in children. Developmental Science, 22: e12756. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12756
title: Metacognitive scaffolding amplifies brain plasticity and cognitive efficiency effects of process-based training
description: The article proposes that adding metacognitive scaffolding to process-based training changes how training affects the brain and cognition. It frames its results as showing that "metacognitive scaffolding boosts the influence of process-based training on cognitive efficiency and brain plasticity related to cognitive control", with the N2 ERP component associated with conflict processing serving as the neural marker of this amplified plasticity. The framework links educational scaffolding and metacognitive strategies to computerized training outcomes.
requirements: A computerized process-based training program whose effects can be indexed at cognitive and neural levels, with scaffolding layered on top
constraints: Proposed on the basis of one training study in typically developing preschoolers; the abstract presents it as an interpretation of the reported results
examples: Preschoolers in the metacognitive group showed both larger intelligence gains and increased N2 responses, and N2 change predicted intelligence gain within that group
key_sources: Pozuelos, J.P., Cómbita, L.M., Abundis-Gutiérrez, A., Paz-Alonso, P.M., Conejero A., Guerra, S., & Rueda, M.R. (2019). Metacognitive scaffolding boosts cognitive and neural benefits following executive attention training in children. Developmental Science, 22: e12756. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12756

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A 50-minute metacognitive strategy instruction lesson on divergent thinking for visual arts
description: A single 50-minute lesson providing explicit instruction on metacognitive knowledge about creativity, twelve divergent thinking activities and strategies for originality in visual art products, and metacognitive skills for regulation (monitoring and control). The lesson "contained five lesson-phases" covering orientation on metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive strategy instruction, divergent thinking strategy instruction with exercises, and evaluation. It was delivered by the first author with a second teacher assisting, within a 14-week photography project on the theme of 'Time-grasping'.
requirements: Requires an instructor trained in the divergent thinking strategies and metacognitive instruction approach
Requires visual art examples to illustrate the twelve divergent thinking strategies
constraints: Tested as a single 50-minute lesson within a 14-week visual arts project with Grade-11 pre-university students in the Netherlands
target_learners: Grade-11 secondary school students aged 16–17 in pre-university visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Understand why, how and when to use specific divergent thinking activities and strategies to generate original ideas for visual art products
examples: Students exercised with an alternative uses test for a tablet computer, practised generating many different kinds of original ideas, and evaluated the originality of their own ideas in dyads and whole-class discussion
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: The Development and Evaluation of a Self-Questioning Study Technique
citation: Marli E.D.A. Andre and Thomas H. Anderson. (1978). The Development and Evaluation of a Self-Questioning Study Technique. Center for the Study of Reading Technical Report No. 87. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Development+and+Evaluation+of+a+Self-Questioning+Study+Technique
title: Levels-of-processing plus metacognitive monitoring account for self-questioning effectiveness
description: The article offers two explanations for why self-questioning works. First, the levels-of-processing notion holds that "increasing 'depth' implies a greater degree of semantic or cognitive analysis and hence greater retention"; determining main ideas and transforming them into questions entails deeper semantic analysis than rereading. Second, the technique combines metacognitive and cognitive components: it forces the reader to pause frequently, deal with an understanding question, check whether comprehension occurred, and decide on the next strategic action, promoting active monitoring of the learning activity.
requirements: The student must generate questions based on main points of the text, requiring comprehension of the text to answer correctly
constraints: The article presents these as possible explanations, not tested mechanisms
target_learners: high school juniors and seniors studying prose material
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of expository prose
examples: The authors attribute the superior criterion performance of question-constructing groups to deeper semantic analysis of the text than reading and rereading
key_sources: Marli E.D.A. Andre and Thomas H. Anderson. (1978). The Development and Evaluation of a Self-Questioning Study Technique. Center for the Study of Reading Technical Report No. 87. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Development+and+Evaluation+of+a+Self-Questioning+Study+Technique

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: Metafora dual-interaction space: construction space plus argumentation space supporting learning-to-learn-together
description: The article describes the Metafora system, designed via design-based research by Schwarz and colleagues to support learning-to-learn-together. It pairs "a construction space and an argumentation space": the construction space offers domain-specific modeling applications forming a mutually visible "joint problem space" for collective reflection, while as one member acts, others assess the action in the argumentation space, "either affirming it or questioning it." A sophisticated planning/reflection tool prompts planning steps (collective agency) and team reflection (collective responsibility), going beyond simple chat-plus-construction dual-interaction systems.
requirements: A culture of collaboration: appropriate motivations/rewards, careful training in collaboration and subtle mentoring
constraints: The article states success "also depends on a culture of collaboration" beyond the software itself
target_learners: small groups of students in mathematics or science inquiry
target_learning_goals: argumentation, collective reflection, peer assessment, meta-learning
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4

article_title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
citation: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6
title: MEPA production rule system for automatic dialogue act coding
description: The Multiple Episode Protocol Analysis (MEPA) computer program hosts a production rule system that automatically categorizes utterances into dialogue acts. "A set of if-then rules uses pattern matching to look for typical words or phrases, in this case for discourse markers or clue phrases." It comprises "a rule system for automatic segmentation of combined utterances in single messages (300 rules) and a rule system for dialogue act coding (1,250 rules)", and "MEPA is able to code a protocol consisting of 1,000 utterances in less than a second." A segmentation filter splits chat contributions on punctuation, connectives, and starting discourse markers, with exception rules preventing erroneous splits.
requirements: Uncoded InfStm? messages (about 10% of a protocol) must still be checked and coded manually by the researcher
constraints: New discourse markers encountered may need to be added to the DAC filter
Filter rules must be specified when coding needs to take preceding or following utterances into account
target_learners: researchers analyzing CSCL collaboration protocols of secondary students
target_learning_goals: automatic identification of dialogue acts in online collaborative learning protocols
examples: The DAC filter assigns the InfStm? default catch-all code to messages for which no matching discourse marker is found, directing the researcher to check them.
key_sources: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6

article_title: Mediating and perspective-taking manipulatives: Fostering dynamic perspective-taking by mediating dialogic thinking and bolstering empathy in role-play and reflection for microteaching
citation: Mochizuki, T., Sasaki, H., Wakimoto, T., Kubota, Y., Eagan, B., Hirayama, R., Yamaguchi, Y., Yuki, N., Funaoi, H., Suzuki, H., & Kato, H. (2022). Mediating and perspective-taking manipulatives: Fostering dynamic perspective-taking by mediating dialogic thinking and bolstering empathy in role-play and reflection for microteaching. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09382-w
title: Dialogic microteaching supported by two complementary manipulatives: mediating puppets and perspective-taking animation
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that achieving dialogic microteaching requires overcoming two challenges: role-playing various imaginary students plausibly, and appropriating their viewpoints in subsequent reflection. Grounded in Bakhtin's dialogism, in which utterances are formed "in anticipation of what the listener will say," the design pairs mediating manipulatives (tangible puppets whose psychological distance reduces anxiety and elicits multivoiced performances) with perspective-taking manipulatives (3D first-person viewpoint switching in reflection). Previous work showed puppetry alone left reflections returning to pre-role-play perspectives, motivating the combined design for immediate transfer of imaginary students' perspectives.
requirements: Student teachers must overcome self-consciousness and evaluation apprehension that makes unaided role-play normative and unrealistic
Reflection must follow the puppetry performance; puppetry alone was "not found to be sufficient" for diverse student perspectives in reflection
constraints: The 3D animation effect was studied as a companion to puppetry role-play in a three-session sequence, not as a stand-alone intervention
examples: The quasi-experimental class design gave all triads puppetry in Session #2 and varied only the reflection medium, then tested persistence in a Session #3 self-performed microteaching without manipulatives

Mediating and perspective-taking manipulatives: Fostering dynamic perspective-taking by mediating dialogic thinking and bolstering empathy in role-play and reflection for microteaching. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09382-w

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Mentalising in shared meaning-making as Bayesian reasoning under uncertainty
description: The article presents shared meaning-making as requiring 'mind reading' (mental state inference, or mentalizing): hearers infer the concept meant by a peer's word, using contextual, para-verbal and non-verbal signals, world and cultural knowledge, and dialogically established common ground, since a word's conceptual meaning remains hidden beyond its registerable use. The authors propose formalising this as probabilistic inference in a Bayesian framework, computing P(concept | utterance) from the prior P(concept) times the likelihood P(utterance | concept), normalised.
requirements: Listeners must have their own conceptualisations (not necessarily propositional) to compute likelihood of alignment with the speaker's conception; a more knowledgeable listener such as a teacher would know multiple conceptualizations
target_learners: students in collaborative groups; teachers as more knowledgeable listeners
target_learning_goals: shared meaning-making and negotiation of conceptual meaning in dialogue
examples: Applied to a peer saying "force" in a science class: listeners compare the utterance against their own conceptualisations of force to infer the speaker's conception.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
citation: Sebastian Strauß, Isis Tunnigkeit, Julia Eberle, Arlind Avdullahu, Nikol Rummel. (2025). Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09430-7
title: Meier et al. rating schema adopted as the domain-agnostic model of productive collaboration with five aspects and nine dimensions
description: The study's model of productive collaboration is the rating schema by Meier et al. (2007), chosen because it overlaps with PISA 2015 and ACT21S skill frameworks and, unlike the domain-specific FINCA framework, is domain-agnostic and adjustable to specific tasks. It identifies "five aspects of successful computer-supported interdisciplinary collaborative problem-solving processes: communication, coordination, joint information processing, relationship management, and motivation", decomposed into nine dimensions such as sustaining mutual understanding, information pooling, and reaching consensus. It served both to score collaboration knowledge in the tests and to rate interaction quality in the videos.
requirements: Can be adjusted to the specific collaboration task
Supports rating interaction quality at multiple levels
constraints: Originally developed to assess quality of interaction in groups; some dimensions were further differentiated into subcodes for the study's coding manual
examples: Used as codes for the knowledge test scoring (Cohen's κ = 0.74 on 20% of answers) and for two-stage video-based interaction-quality rating (weighted κ = 0.87 on a 20% subset)
key_sources: Sebastian Strauß, Isis Tunnigkeit, Julia Eberle, Arlind Avdullahu, Nikol Rummel. (2025). Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09430-7

article_title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
citation: Zhou, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Ryan, Z., Stiso, C., Murphy, D., Danish, J., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2025). Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09438-z
title: MEME: a networked collaborative modeling tool with evidence linking and commenting for peer critique
description: MEME (Modeling and Evidence Mapping Environment) is a CSCL tool supporting students in creating, sharing, evaluating, and revising qualitative models, "organized around entities, processes (mechanisms), and outcomes." Students can access an evidence library of brief reports and simulations, explicitly link evidence to model components with rationales, rate evidence strength, and justify ratings. Its commenting feature lets students comment on specific components of peers' models, select the most relevant evaluation criterion from a menu of class-shared criteria, and reply to comments — creating a shared space for collective, evidence-based modeling with integrated feedback.
requirements: A comment box prompting students to "select the most relevant criterion for their comment from a menu including options aligned with class-shared criteria for model evaluation."
target_learning_goals: Building and revising mechanistic models of complex ecosystems using evidence
examples: During the gallery walk, students used MEME to evaluate other groups' models, leave constructive comments, and address received comments synchronously and asynchronously.
key_sources: Zhou, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Ryan, Z., Stiso, C., Murphy, D., Danish, J., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2025). Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09438-z

article_title: Productive dissent in learning communities
citation: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0
title: Melser's account: learning is subordinate to communal belonging
description: The article highlights Melser's (2004) extension of Vygotskian scholarship, in which "the human drive to learn or to teach is better understood as a drive to act in concert with others." A child sees community members engaged in shared activity and desires to join, and in that way learning happens; thus "learning is subsumed by and subordinate to communal belonging." This predicts that even logic-like domains are subject to social approval, so individual traits like critical thinking are best developed by joining communities that value them.
requirements: Participation in a community whose valued activities make learning salient and inviting
constraints: The account predicts community values can trump individual isolated observations, so what a community does not value may not even be seen
examples: The article cites Doebel and Munakata's demonstration that self-control, typically viewed as a fixed individual trait, can be influenced through group dynamics
key_sources: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0

article_title: Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law
citation: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3
title: Metaconceptual processes framework: awareness, monitoring, and evaluation
description: The article builds on Yürük's (2005) framework of metaconceptual processes, which target reflective thinking operating explicitly on learners' conceptual structures rather than cognition generally. The article states: "Three main categories are used to evaluate these processes: metaconceptual awareness, metaconceptual monitoring, and metaconceptual evaluation." Awareness is further divided into first-order (recognizing current mental representations) and second-order (recognizing previously held ideas); monitoring tracks understanding, consistency between new and existing ideas, and idea change; evaluation involves commenting, finding attractive, and defending a chosen idea among competing alternatives. Table 1 details these categories, subcategories, and their educational significance with social studies examples.
requirements: Activities must externalise students' internal conceptual structures so the three processes can be activated and observed
constraints: Framework as applied here is limited to conceptual understanding of social studies concepts over a four-week curriculum period
target_learning_goals: Correcting alternative conceptions of civic concepts
examples: The Elif and Yağız population-density episode illustrates evaluation: after hearing reasoning that density means crampedness as well as crowdedness, Elif judged her initial idea not useful
key_sources: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3

article_title: Noticing and weighing alternatives in the reflection of regular classroom teaching: Evidence of expertise using mobile eye-tracking
citation: Keller, L., Cortina, K. S., Müller, K., & Miller, K. F. (2022). Noticing and weighing alternatives in the reflection of regular classroom teaching: Evidence of expertise using mobile eye-tracking. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09570-5
title: Mobile eye-tracking (MET) video feedback with think-aloud protocols for teacher self-reflection
description: MET devices worn as glasses record the teacher's field of view and fixation point during regular lessons; teachers later watch their own footage from their own viewpoint and freely comment aloud (video-stimulated recall). The study used the ASL Mobile Eye Tracker with 37 teachers and coded commentary for noticing and alternative strategies. MET "allows teachers to 're-live' their teaching from their own viewpoint instead from the perspective of a classroom observer" and rarely shows the teachers themselves.
requirements: Teachers wear the eye-tracking glasses during regular lessons and complete a think-aloud session watching their footage within days of recording
constraints: Recording occasionally started late or stopped early due to technical issues; three recordings were unusable due to device failures
examples: In the study, 37 teachers wore the ASL Mobile Eye Tracker during a regular class period and commented on their footage 2–10 days later in a research lab
key_sources: Keller, L., Cortina, K. S., Müller, K., & Miller, K. F. (2022). Noticing and weighing alternatives in the reflection of regular classroom teaching: Evidence of expertise using mobile eye-tracking. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09570-5

article_title: Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer
citation: Saba, J., Kapur, M., & Roll, I. (2025). Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer. Instructional Science, 53, 1603–1632. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09726-7
title: Mechanistic reasoning as a four-component framework underlying MVC reasoning assessment
description: Drawing on Krist et al. (2019), the article treats mechanistic reasoning as "a crosscutting form of thinking across multiple scientific practices that guides students’ decision-making, evaluation, and reflection as they build and test scientific ideas". It comprises four components: considering events at a scalar level below the observed phenomenon; identifying and characterizing relevant elements at that lower level; coordinating these elements over space and/or time into chains of cause and effect; and examining how these elements give rise to the observed phenomenon. The study adapted this framework into a bottom-up coding scheme (Describing, Unpacking, Linking) for students' open-ended MVC reasoning responses.
requirements: Responses must be coded bottom-up against the Describing/Unpacking/Linking scheme, accounting for the number of factors addressed in students’ reasoning
constraints: The framework was applied in this study to open-ended written responses about virus spread and predation simulations with undergraduate participants
target_learners: undergraduate students in science and engineering programs
examples: The coding scheme scored responses from Non (no description or unpacking) through combinations such as U3L, unpacking three factors and linking them to an observed outcome
key_sources: Saba, J., Kapur, M., & Roll, I. (2025). Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer. Instructional Science, 53, 1603–1632. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09726-7

article_title: Measures of relative metacognitive accuracy are confounded with task performance in tasks that permit guessing
citation: Vuorre, M., & Metcalfe, J. (2021). Measures of relative metacognitive accuracy are confounded with task performance in tasks that permit guessing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09257-1
title: Meta-d' as a performance-normalized measure of metacognitive efficiency
description: Meta-d' is a signal detection theoretic measure of relative metacognitive accuracy, attributed in the article to Maniscalco and Lau (2012), that explicitly models the relation between primary task performance and metacognition. The article notes it "allows normalizing metacognitive performance with primary task performance", yielding a metacognitive "efficiency" measure (meta-d'/d') that is not inherently constrained by primary task performance or bias. The article presents it as an otherwise attractive measure whose general implication matches its own results: in certain tasks, resolution metrics are inherently related to performance.
requirements: The primary task must be conducted in a manner analogous to a signal detection task, such as 2AFC, as the article states.
constraints: Not suitable as a measure of metacognition in free-response tasks, or, in its current implementation, multiple-choice tasks where the number of choice alternatives exceeds 2.
target_learners: adults completing recognition or general-information tasks in laboratory or online experiments
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of metacognitive resolution independent of task performance
examples: The article discusses meta-d' in its conclusions as an existing measure whose approach aligns with its own demonstration of the guessing confound.
key_sources: Vuorre, M., & Metcalfe, J. (2021). Measures of relative metacognitive accuracy are confounded with task performance in tasks that permit guessing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09257-1

article_title: Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection
citation: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1
title: Metacognition as competence and disposition: meta-strategic knowledge and epistemic understanding as two meta-level forms supporting strategic argument performance
description: The article frames metacognition, following Kuhn, as "a competence and as a disposition". As competence it involves meta-strategic knowledge — awareness of available strategies, their power relative to task goals, and control of their application — which is proposed to be fundamental for strategic performance. As disposition it involves epistemic understanding of the point of an intellectual task, valuing it as worth cognitive effort, connected to motivation. The study hypothesizes that reflection during dialogic argumentation develops both forms, which in turn support strategic-level argument skill.
requirements: Engagement in tasks involving the targeted strategies, so that application at the cognitive level informs meta-level knowing in a continuous cycle
constraints: The article notes understanding of how to support metacognition development is still limited, and even adults may fail to have good judgments of their own knowing
target_learning_goals: argument skill: constructing counterarguments and using evidence to weaken opposing positions
examples: Participants in the experimental condition reflected on their own dialog transcripts using reflection sheets while waiting for the opposing pair to respond, with a same-side collaborating partner
key_sources: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1

article_title: Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities
citation: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5
title: Meijer et al. taxonomy of 56 metacognitive text-studying activities in four superordinate scales
description: A taxonomy for coding think-aloud protocols of secondary school students studying a history text, developed by Meijer et al. and described as "theoretically based and data driven" and tested on new protocols "in a cyclic fashion". Its revised form "discerned 56 specific metacognitive activities that adhered to four superordinate scales, orientation & planning, execution, monitoring, and elaboration & evaluation." In this article it directly formed the basis of the task-specific questionnaire, with each taxonomy category tapped by one questionnaire item.
requirements: Think-aloud protocols of text studying to code, and raters trained in the taxonomy's categories
constraints: The four-scales distinction is theoretically based; the article reports students may not perceive the items as interrelated within the expert scales
target_learners: secondary school students studying history texts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive learning activities during text studying
examples: In Study 1, 2,817 activities were coded in 16 protocols, with the maximum (541 occurrences) for the subcategory 'error detection (plus correction), keeping track'
key_sources: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5

article_title: Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research
citation: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y
title: Competing taxonomies of metacognition: Flavell's four areas and later two-factor, self/other, and three-factor modifications
description: The article organizes metacognitive theory as a landscape of competing taxonomies. Flavell's original theory "divides metacognition into four areas: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals, and actions." Later modifications include Brown's division into knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition, Schraw and Dennison's addition of information management and debugging as regulation subcomponents, self-versus-other taxonomies, and a proposed third factor of metacognitive beliefs or attributions. The review uses this landscape to frame why so many different self-report questionnaires exist.
requirements: The article states that evaluating a generalizable structure of metacognition requires participants representing the general population, with widely applicable questionnaires.
constraints: The article states there is a lack of consensus regarding a theoretical organization of metacognition, and available self-report questionnaires reflect this lack of consensus.
target_learners: general population across primary school, secondary school, and university students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and regulation of cognition
key_sources: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y

article_title: Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research
citation: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y
title: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis of metacognitive self-report measures (24,396 articles screened; 22 factor-structure studies; 37 correlation studies)
description: This element is the article's own evidence base: two PRISMA-conducted systematic reviews and a meta-analysis of self-report in metacognitive research. Searches in seven databases located studies from 1982 through 2018, with "24,396 articles from 1982 through 2018 were screened for inclusion in the study." The first review tabulated 22 factor-structure studies; the second analyzed 37 studies, in which "the 37 articles reported 328 correlations between factors and/or subcomponents of metacognition," with instrument type and timing coded for moderator analysis.
requirements: Included articles had to statistically evaluate metacognition in the general population using widely applicable measures, or compare at least two pure metacognition measures with correlational effect sizes in a within design.
constraints: Articles were excluded when participants had a condition or disability, when questionnaires targeted a specific subset of the population, when measures included other skills such as motivation, or when articles could not be obtained in English.
target_learners: general-population learners from primary school through university and adults
target_learning_goals: measurement of metacognitive knowledge, regulation, and their subcomponents
key_sources: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y

article_title: Testing pays off twice: Potentials of practice tests and feedback regarding exam performance and judgment accuracy
citation: Nick Naujoks, Bettina Harder, Marion Händel. (2022). Testing pays off twice: Potentials of practice tests and feedback regarding exam performance and judgment accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09295-x
title: Meaningful classroom practice-test setting: voluntary participation, lecture-aligned content, criterial-test format, and corrective feedback
description: The article synthesizes features that prior classroom testing-effect studies share and that its own practice tests met. Such a setting in the context of a lecture is characterized by features including "voluntary participation in practice tests" and "practice tests of same format as the criterial test (multiple-choice)". In both studies, four online multiple-choice practice tests of 12 items each were offered after each thematic block, drawn from the lecture content of the previous weeks, with exam items never reused from the practice tests.
requirements: Practice-test content must reflect the material of the respective lecture/exam
Students should continue to process the content of the tests and not merely seek insight into exam difficulty and structure
constraints: Participation is voluntary, so uptake varies widely; in both studies many students took none or only the last test before the exam
target_learners: undergraduate students in regular lecture courses
target_learning_goals: course-relevant knowledge measured by a final multiple-choice exam
metacognitive monitoring of one's own performance
examples: Four online practice tests per term on a university learning platform, each available for ten days, with items saved as PDF after completion
key_sources: Nick Naujoks, Bettina Harder, Marion Händel. (2022). Testing pays off twice: Potentials of practice tests and feedback regarding exam performance and judgment accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09295-x

article_title: Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses
citation: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x
title: Coding framework of metacognition intervention components and instructional methods
description: The article develops a fine-grained coding framework for metacognition interventions, distinguishing intervention focus (primary vs. secondary focus on metacognition), four metacognition components, and six instructional methods. Components are defined temporally: "Before starting a task, children are encouraged to think about how they could approach a task or set goals for themselves" (planning), monitoring during tasks, control during tasks, and reflection after tasks. Instructional methods include informed instruction, modelling, prompts, practice, feedback, and peer activities. This framework enabled the first meta-analytic tests of which components and methods drive effectiveness.
requirements: Interventions must include aspects of metacognition such as planning, monitoring, control, or reflection, and consist of more than one session with a control group
constraints: The article notes the motivational-orientations outcome category is rather heterogenous and groups concepts from different theoretical traditions
target_learners: typically developing pre- and elementary school children up to 12 years of age
target_learning_goals: metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, control, reflection) and related self-regulated learning and academic outcomes
examples: Studies were coded with Cohen's Kappa of .84 (89.5% agreement) between two coders for intervention focus; Fuchs et al. (2003) is given as a primary-focus example and Artuso et al. (2019) as a secondary-focus example
key_sources: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x

article_title: Motivating children to (pre)monitor: positive effects on monitoring accuracy?
citation: Sophie Wacker, Claudia M. Roebers. (2024). Motivating children to (pre)monitor: positive effects on monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09351-0
title: Memory-metamemory interplay account of children's overconfidence
description: The article organizes its manipulation and interpretation around frameworks in which "memory and metamemory are no longer considered separated, independent constructs, but rather to be closely intertwined". Monitoring and control processes rely on retrieval from long-term memory, and early retrieval coupled with early monitoring regulates later monitoring. The unexpected overconfidence increase after pre-monitoring is interpreted through this coupling, confirmation bias, and cue-based heuristics such as ease of accessibility.
requirements: Interpretation assumes monitoring judgments are entangled with memory retrieval processes rather than isolated confidence reports
constraints: The article questions whether a confidence judgment can be considered an isolated, memory-independent process at all
target_learning_goals: calibration of confidence in memory recognition
examples: The paired associates task with a pre-monitoring phase was designed to weaken the influence of a single prepotently selected memory trace before recognition
key_sources: Sophie Wacker, Claudia M. Roebers. (2024). Motivating children to (pre)monitor: positive effects on monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09351-0

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Mesosystem linkages shaping belonging (Table 1)
description: Table 1 maps common mesosystem linkages in higher education—such as advising-financial aid coordination, faculty-counseling referrals, disability services-academic department consistency, and Title IX responses to harm—alongside their mechanisms and potential impacts on belonging. The article states 'mesosystem connections are not just the sum of individual settings but the infrastructure that links them, shaping whether students experience campus as coherent or fragmented.' When systems reinforce one another they create coherent opportunities for belonging; when siloed, students face contradictory messages.
requirements: Cross-unit coordination and alignment for coherent belonging opportunities
constraints: The article notes meso-level connections remain underexplored in higher education research compared with microsystem factors
target_learners: higher education students, including low-income, disabled, racially minoritized, and international students
target_learning_goals: institutional coordination that supports students' sense of belonging
examples: When academic advising works closely with financial aid, low-income students can stay on track; uneven accommodation implementation signals weak institutional commitment
key_sources: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5

article_title: The Distorting Influence of Primacy Effects on Reporting Cognitive Load in Learning Materials of Varying Complexity
citation: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Wesenberg, L., Rey, G. D., & Schneider, S. (2025). The Distorting Influence of Primacy Effects on Reporting Cognitive Load in Learning Materials of Varying Complexity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09980-0
title: When measuring cognitive load in learning materials of varying complexity, measure during learning rather than relying solely on a single post-learning self-report
description: The article shows that a single delayed self-report of cognitive load can be biased: in learning contexts the first impression of complexity is the strongest predictor of the overall assessment, and when complexity decreases the delayed rating significantly exceeds the during-learning average. The authors argue that "measuring cognitive load multiple times during problem-solving (i.e., after each individual problem-solving task) is more accurate than a single measurement after all problem-solving tasks have been completed" and extend this concern to explicit learning contexts.
requirements: Learning materials must contain varying levels of complexity for the bias to arise; the delayed assessment must be a retrospective self-report.
constraints: The bias toward the first impression appeared in learning contexts; delayed group-level assessments did not differ between increasing and decreasing complexity sequences.
target_learners: university students studying multimedia learning units
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of experienced cognitive load during learning
examples: In the main study, learners studied three learning units in increasing or decreasing complexity sequences and rated ICL, ECL, and GCL after each unit and once after learning; the delayed ICL assessment anchored on the first impression.
key_sources: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Wesenberg, L., Rey, G. D., & Schneider, S. (2025). The Distorting Influence of Primacy Effects on Reporting Cognitive Load in Learning Materials of Varying Complexity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09980-0

article_title: Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses and Self- and Socially- Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations
citation: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses, Self- and Socially-Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations. Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: Simulation video coding scheme for behaviors and SRL/SSRL strategies
description: The research team developed a coding scheme for (1) behaviors (posture and gestures, facial expressions, and vocalics) and (2) regulation strategies including SRL codes (C.2.1–C.2.6) and SSRL codes (C.3.1–C.3.2), plus social climate and participation codes (C.3.3–C.3.6), adapted from prior literature to fit a medical context. Each code was structured as "a superordinate code, a definition to that code, followed by an example of the code in a medical context," with nested subordinate codes. Four raters were trained; inter-rater agreement after the first negotiation ranged from 0.62 to 0.83 Cohen's kappa, described as "substantial" agreement, with perfect agreement reached after deliberation.
requirements: Rater training with expert evaluation and negotiation of coded events; codes made explicit to minimize rater inferences
constraints: Coding emotion regulation from video is difficult unless the learner verbalizes, which may require non-replicable rater inferences
target_learning_goals: observable indicators of SRL and SSRL during clinical simulation

article_title: A meta-analysis on the effectiveness of phonics instruction for teaching decoding skills to students with intellectual disability
citation: Sermier Dessemontet, Rachel; Martinet, Catherine; de Chambrier, Anne-Françoise; Martini-Willemin, Britt-Marie; Audrin, Catherine. (2019). A meta-analysis on the effectiveness of phonics instruction for teaching decoding skills to students with intellectual disability. Educational research review, no. 26, p. 52-70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2019.01.001
title: Meta-analytic evidence base of 14 studies (eight single-case, six group) on phonics instruction for students with intellectual disability
description: The evidence base synthesized by this meta-analysis consists of "Eight single-case experimental studies and six experimental or quasi-experimental group studies" that "met the inclusion criteria, encom- passing a total of 297 participants with intellectual disability". Effects were pooled with a random-effects model, and moderators including study design, outcome-measure type and interventionist type were examined.
requirements: Studies meeting the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for phonics instruction with students with intellectual disability
constraints: Limited to 14 studies and 297 participants; the abstract does not describe publication-date range or search strategy
examples: The random-effects synthesis pooled effects from the eight single-case and six group studies to estimate the overall effect of phonics instruction.

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Messick's unified validity framework applied to AI evaluation, with six sources of construct-validity evidence
description: The article anchors its validity discussion in Messick's unified theory of validity, which holds that validity is a property of inferences and decisions based on scores, not of instruments. It enumerates six interlocking evidence sources (content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external, and consequential) and gives each an AI analogue, such as item-level factor analysis for structural evidence and out-of-distribution testing for generalizability evidence.
requirements: Validity questions must be asked about the inferences drawn from benchmark scores for an intended use and context, not merely about whether a score is produced
constraints: The consequential strand becomes central when a benchmark is itself a training target, because optimizing against it changes what it measures
target_learners: educational psychologists assessing AI capability claims
target_learning_goals: Judging whether benchmark scores warrant inferences about capability, safety, or alignment
examples: The article reads specification gaming, shortcut learning, dataset contamination, and reward hacking as concrete forms of validity failure in LLM evaluation
key_sources: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8

article_title: Meta-Bias: A Practical Theory of Motivated Thinking
citation: Gehlbach, H., & Vriesema, C. C. (2018). Meta‐bias: A practical theory of motivated thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9454-6
title: Meta-bias theory: two competing motives derail the default goal of accurate person perception
description: The article proposes an organizing theory in which perceivers default to accurately reading themselves and others, but two meta-biases regularly trump this accuracy motive: a desire for cognitive efficiency and a need to protect or enhance one's sense of self. The authors state that "two competing motives—meta‐biases—often derail this default goal: a desire for cognitive efficiency and a need to protect or enhance one's sense of self." The theory distills large families of person-perception biases into these two motives to make them usable by educators and researchers.
requirements: Perceivers must have a default goal of accurately understanding others and themselves that the two motives can override
constraints: The authors make no claims as to when and where one meta-bias might override the other, and Figure 1 is not necessarily drawn to scale
Generalizability across cultures is flagged as an important area for future research
target_learning_goals: recognizing and mitigating bias in person perception
examples: The article maps a sample of biases (anchoring and adjusting, stereotyping, fundamental attribution error, availability heuristic, self-serving biases, spotlight effect, naïve realism, confirmation bias, in-group/out-group bias) onto the two motives in Figure 1
key_sources: Gehlbach, H., & Vriesema, C. C. (2018). Meta‐bias: A practical theory of motivated thinking. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9454-6

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Measurement local optima: canonical executive function tasks may reflect measurement inertia rather than genuine invariance
description: The article argues that operationalizations of psychological constructs settle into "local optima": "definitions that are reliable, interpretable, and widely accepted, yet not necessarily epistemically optimal for addressing all theoretical questions." Canonical tasks like the Flanker and Stroop are optimized for reliability, comparability, and stable individual differences, which can reduce sensitivity to transient, state-based perturbations. Apparent stability under perturbation may therefore reflect properties of the measurement instrument rather than genuine invariance of the underlying process.
requirements: Detecting measurement inertia requires deploying canonical tasks alongside alternative, context-aligned operationalizations within the same study
constraints: The article notes the observed sensitivity of the domain-aligned measure could reflect idiosyncratic task-specific measurement properties rather than construct-level differences
target_learning_goals: refining construct definitions and measurement of executive function in learning contexts
examples: The mathematics-specific negative priming task in Zhang et al. (2026) is presented as an alternative operationalization that prioritizes alignment with instructional content over generality.
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: Developing the Mental Effort and Load–Translingual Scale (MEL-TS) as a Foundation for Translingual Research in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Tino Endres, Lisa Bender, Stoo Sepp, Shirong Zhang, Louise David, Melanie Trypke, et al. (2025). Developing the Mental Effort and Load–Translingual Scale (MEL‑TS) as a Foundation for Translingual Research in Self‑Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09978-8
title: Mental effort versus mental load as the appropriate distinction of cognitive demand in self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes that in self-regulated learning, cognitive demand is best captured by two constructs: mental load, passively experienced, and mental effort, actively invested. It argues the classical CLT distinction (ICL/ECL/GCL) fits instructor-regulated settings but has less predictive value when learners self-regulate, since learners monitor an aggregation of demands rather than their source. The paper notes the mental load construct "is also referred to as data-driven demand (Koriat, 1997) and task-centered dimension of load", while the active component is also called goal-driven demand or goal-driven appraisals of cognitive load.
requirements: Assessment items must be interpretable across a broad range of learning situations, including learner-regulated contexts where learners cannot choose the design of materials
constraints: The distinction is argued to suit SRL contexts; classical CLT load types remain the focus in structured, instructor-regulated instructional design settings
target_learners: self-regulating learners across school and higher education
target_learning_goals: monitoring and regulating cognitive demand during self-regulated learning
examples: The authors use the terminology of mental load and mental effort (Klepsch & Seufert, 2021) because these terms were most idiomatic to participants in their qualitative interviews
