citation: Tino Endres, Lisa Bender, Stoo Sepp, Shirong Zhang, Louise David, Melanie Trypke, et al. (2025). Developing the Mental Effort and Load–Translingual Scale (MEL‑TS) as a Foundation for Translingual Research in Self‑Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09978-8
title: MEL-TS: a translingual set of mental effort and mental load self-rating items in six languages
description: The MEL-TS is a set of self-rating items assessing mental effort and mental load during self-regulated learning, developed in English, Dutch, Spanish, German, Mandarin Chinese, and French. The initial pool comprised ten items — "five for mental effort and five for mental load" — inspired by established measures (Paas, 1992; Klepsch & Seufert, 2021; Krell, 2017; Leppink et al., 2013), with reversed items to mitigate response bias. The final quantitative version used four items per construct plus a 'heart and soul' intensity item and a difficulty item, with all items available on the Open Science Framework.
requirements: Items must be rated with attention to cultural context, as translations are not expected to be literal matches across languages
constraints: The 'lifeblood' (heart and soul) item proved suitable only in Mandarin Chinese and Spanish contexts; item intensity differences across languages may produce floor or ceiling effects
target_learners: first-language speakers of English, Dutch, Spanish, German, Mandarin Chinese, and French in learning contexts
target_learning_goals: assessing invested mental effort and perceived mental load during self-regulated learning
examples: Table 2 presents the final items in all six languages, developed to ensure content validity within each language rather than literal matching translations

article_title: Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm
citation: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3
title: Metarepresentation as the generative mechanism of consciousness and cognitive change
description: The review defines metarepresentation as the generative aspect of consciousness: an ideoplastic process that looks for, encodes, and typifies similarities between mental experiences and representations. Through it, new mental operations, higher-order rules, and representations standing for them are created. Metarepresentation also builds self-evaluated maps of mental functions that guide problem solving, and links mind and personality through a personal constant moderating self-evaluations.
requirements: Consciousness mechanisms of monitoring, evaluation, and control operating on information from all other systems
constraints: There are large individual differences in the accuracy of self-generated maps of mental functions
key_sources: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3

article_title: Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl, Fred Paas. (2010). Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9132-9
title: Generalized knowledge structures of medium generality as a sensible compromise between generality and power for flexible expertise
description: The paper argues that knowledge structures neither narrowly task-specific nor fully general occupy a medium level of generality and are essential for flexible expertise. Such structures, like the FPS schema, act as deep explanatory principles that transfer across task classes. The authors state that knowledge structures of medium generality are important for flexible expertise as a "sensible compromise between generality and power" and allow adapting not-yet-fully-developed expertise to new demands.
requirements: Domain-specific knowledge base within which the generalized structures are developed; generalized structures are applicable within relevant domains only
constraints: Classical CLT formulations considering only routine low-level domain-specific knowledge are described as unnecessarily limited
target_learners: advanced learners in specific subject domains
target_learning_goals: flexible problem solving and transfer to novel situations within a domain
examples: The Function-Process-Structure schema in technical domains is given as an example of a medium-generality generalized knowledge structure
key_sources: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl, Fred Paas. (2010). Facilitating Flexible Problem Solving: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9132-9

article_title: Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children
citation: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4
title: Mental simulation training program: eight 30-min lessons alternating group instruction and individual computer-based practice
description: A 4-week reading strategy training in which "Mental simulation was taught in a 4-week training program containing eight 30-min lessons (two lessons per week)", alternating group instruction lessons with individual computer-based lessons. The lessons used "a balanced approach of direct instruction, modeling, guided practice, and individual practice", covered multisensory, visual, and motor simulation, and replaced the school's regular reading comprehension lessons during the training period.
requirements: Trained research assistants following standardized instructions delivered the lessons, with each computer-based lesson preceded by an instruction lesson
constraints: The eight lessons replaced the school's regular reading comprehension lessons for the 4-week training period
target_learners: third and fourth graders in regular primary schools
target_learning_goals: connecting sensorimotor experiences to text to build an embodied situation model and improve reading comprehension
examples: Instruction lessons had children describe what they saw, heard, smelled, tasted and felt for a described situation; computer-based lessons used cloze and movement-direction matching exercises
key_sources: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval?
citation: Higham, P. A., Fastrich, G. M., Potts, R., Murayama, K., Pickering, J. S., & Hadwin, J. A. (2023). Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09809-2
title: Reactivity of memory judgments as an explanatory framework for the restudy-versus-retrieval reversal
description: The article explains its unexpected restudy advantage through theories of reactivity of memory judgments, analogous to Judgment of Learning (JOL) reactivity. The authors hypothesized that the post-feedback rating "may have interfered with retrieval (negative reactivity) and/or boosted restudy performance (positive reactivity)". They note JOL reactivity is sometimes positive, sometimes negative, and sometimes absent, and that positive reactivity is seldom observed with unrelated word pairs, making the translation-pair setting novel. Experiment 2 tested this by manipulating the rating requirement.
requirements: A post-feedback memory rating prompt (e.g., "Was your answer correct?" or "Would you have remembered the correct translation?") must be administered during practice for reactivity to occur.
constraints: The article notes positive JOL reactivity is seldom observed with unrelated word pairs, and the detailed reactivity mechanisms for translation pairs had not previously been investigated.
target_learners: Adult online learners studying foreign-language vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of paired-associate material (e.g., Swahili–English translations)
examples: Experiment 2 manipulated whether the memory rating was required after feedback; with ratings, restudy exceeded retrieval, replicating Experiment 1, and without ratings the pattern was descriptively reversed.
key_sources: Higham, P. A., Fastrich, G. M., Potts, R., Murayama, K., Pickering, J. S., & Hadwin, J. A. (2023). Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09809-2

article_title: Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility
citation: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1
title: Methods Reproducibility framework for meta-analysis: four levels from Computational Reproducibility to Outcome Reproducibility
description: The article introduces a framework targeted at facilitating the reproducibility of meta-analysis, organized in four levels building on the TOP-guidelines, the Reproducibility Enhancement Principles, and Lakens et al.'s recommendations. It addresses "numerical accuracy (Computational Reproducibility: Level 1) and numerical validity (Computational Verification: Level 2)", then Analysis Reproducibility (Level 3) and Outcome Reproducibility (Level 4), which target researchers' degrees of freedom in analytical choices and database creation. The framework specifies what original authors must provide and what independent researchers or reviewers check at each level, and is demonstrated on the TRANSFER outcome of the Xie et al. meta-analysis.
requirements: Original authors provide original data including raw data used to estimate effect sizes, understandable analysis code, and description of used analysis tools; higher levels additionally require a codebook, workflow log of subjective decisions, and computational formulas
constraints: Level 1 and Level 2 are positioned prior to publication; the framework's logic moves from reliability to include validity aspects, per the article's own footnote
target_learning_goals: improving the credibility and reproducibility of meta-analytical evidence about learning interventions
examples: The appendices and supplemental materials demonstrate the approach on TRANSFER performance of Xie et al. (2018), with OSF-hosted check files for Levels 1–4
key_sources: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: MeDOL framework for reviewing learning-to-argue (LTA) instructional approaches
description: The MeDOL framework is the review's organizing scheme, adapting Morrison et al.'s instructional effectiveness model to the diversity of LTA research. It codes each study on four components: Methods (how dialogue is framed and fostered), Dialogue goals (epistemic goals participants pursue), Outcomes (LTA gains), and Learners (age/grade, learning structure, disciplinary field). The authors state: "Our MeDOL framework adapts Morrison et al.'s( 2019) effectiveness components as follows: Methods refer to the authors ' approach of framing educationally effective dialogue, and to the fostering methods used to increase LTA outcomes". Eleven coding categories emerged from applying it to 143 studies.
requirements: Studies must describe framing of dialogue, dialogue goals, LTA outcomes, and learner characteristics to be codable within the framework
constraints: The authors state applying Morrison et al.'s generic instructional effectiveness model directly to the LTA literature was not possible due to the great variety of approaches, so the framework is a transformed adaptation
target_learners: K-16 students across primary, middle, secondary, and university levels
target_learning_goals: Learning to argue through argumentative dialogue
examples: All 143 reviewed studies were coded on the framework's eleven categories, with inter-rater reliabilities of κ = .776, κ = .727, and κ = .702 for three high-inference variables
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement
citation: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712
title: Measurement battery: Adaptability Scale – Short, ICAR Letter and Number Series, and MES-UC motivation/engagement items
description: The study's instruments operationalize the JD-R constructs for university students: lockdown status as a dichotomous item, adaptability via the 3-item Adaptability Scale – Short, fluid reasoning via the 9-item ICAR Letter and Number Series sub-test (30 s per item, formed into three item parcels), and self-efficacy, participation, aspirations, enjoyment, and disengagement via MES-UC items rated 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree). Reliabilities (coefficient omega) ranged from .64 (fluid reasoning) to .87 (participation).
requirements: Administered via online questionnaire with screening and quality checks (straight-lining and speeder exclusion, IP cross-referencing)
constraints: The authors note the fluid reasoning measure was brief and restricted to 30 s per item, truncating variance so the effect of fluid reasoning may have been under-estimated
target_learning_goals: measuring adaptability, fluid reasoning, self-efficacy, engagement, and disengagement
examples: Fluid reasoning items ask participants to identify the next element in short digit or letter sequences, e.g. "C, F, I, L, O, …"
key_sources: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712

article_title: Bilingualism and symbolic abstraction: Implications for algebra learning
citation: Mielicki, M. K., Kacinik, N. A., & Wiley, J. (2017). Bilingualism and symbolic abstraction: Implications for algebra learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.002
title: Metalinguistic awareness account of the bilingual advantage in symbolic abstraction
description: The article proposes that prolonged bilingual experience may improve the ability to separate symbols from their referents, a form of metalinguistic awareness that supports symbolic abstraction in algebra. Building on Vygotsky's suggestion that expressing a thought in different languages lets one "separate labels from their referents", the authors argue bilinguals may be "better able to attend tothemeaningofthesymbolsthanmonolinguals". The account is offered as an interpretation of the hard-item advantage, alongside the alternative that bilinguals adapt faster to novel tasks.
requirements: The account presumes early bilingual experience with multiple languages, as only early bilinguals were tested
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation consistent with its results, not a directly tested mechanism
examples: The authors link MacGregor and Price's finding that metalinguistic awareness correlated with algebraic problem solving to their Symbol Math results
key_sources: Mielicki, M. K., Kacinik, N. A., & Wiley, J. (2017). Bilingualism and symbolic abstraction: Implications for algebra learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.002

article_title: Training children’s spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding
citation: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191
title: Mental number line account of the spatial language–numerical magnitude link
description: The article frames its intervention within the notion that "numerical magnitudes are represented spatially along a mental number line" (citing Dehaene, 1992; Siegler, 2016). Mastery of spatial language terms is expected to facilitate early numerical skills by helping children grasp spatial relations between numerical magnitudes on this line. The training effect on number words comparison is interpreted as consistent with spatial language facilitating associations of numerical magnitudes with physical space.
requirements: Mastery of spatial terms such as in front of, behind, to the left, and to the right within the egocentric frame of reference
constraints: The design cannot decide whether the effect reflects spatial mapping of serial order in working memory or of magnitude representations in long-term memory; both may apply
examples: Six small-group training sessions of about 20 min using a treasure hunt cover story in which children named and placed a wooden cube relative to a wooden half-sphere
key_sources: Nadja Lindner, Korbinian Moeller, Frauke Hildebrandt, Marcus Hasselhorn, Jan Lonnemann. (2025). Training children's spatial language skills improves their numerical magnitude understanding. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102191. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102191

article_title: Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning - Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1911). Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning.—Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mental+adaptation+during+the+school+day%22+Winch+1911
title: Mental adaptation as the cognate of mental fatigue, identifying the best times for school functions
description: The article frames mental adaptation as a school-day phenomenon parallel to mental fatigue: where fatigue knowledge shows the "worst times" for functions, adaptation knowledge shows the "best times". It complains that educationists have attended to fatigue but paid little attention to "the cognate phenomena of mental adaptation", and treats adaptation as the reason the same arithmetical tests yield better improvement at some morning hours than others, peaking at different times for different children.
requirements: Detecting adaptation effects requires dividing a class into equal groups on preliminary tests and comparing improvement when the same work is done at different times of day.
constraints: The article's evidence concerns problematic arithmetic in elementary school classes during the morning session; the general summary notes conclusions contradict current English pedagogical practice.
target_learning_goals: scheduling rational mental work such as problematic arithmetic at the time of day favoring improvement
examples: The experiments compared groups working identical test sets at 9.40 A.M. versus 11.25 A.M. (boys) and 9.40 A.M. versus 11.15 A.M. (girls).

article_title: Factors associated with children’s understanding of mathematical equivalence: An investigation across six countries.
citation: Şimşek, E., Xenidou-Dervou, I., Hunter, J., Gillon Dowens, M., Pang, J., Lee, Y., McNeil, N., Kirkland, P., & Jones, I. (2021). Factors Associated with Children's Understanding of Mathematical Equivalence: An Investigation across Six Countries. https://figshare.com/s/78625a6b0061200db6b7
title: Mathematical Equivalence Assessment (MEA), 15-item adapted instrument
description: The Mathematical Equivalence Assessment is a 15-item instrument adapted from Matthews et al. (2012) and Rittle-Johnson et al. (2011), including "open-ended equation solving, equation structure, and definition items". It was adapted to use two-digit numbers, shortened, and had algebraic items with letters removed for the age-nine sample. Items were scored dichotomously; after omitting four items, Cronbach's α was .80 for 11 items. Understanding of equivalence was treated as a latent variable with two student-level factors (equation-solving, definition) and one class-level factor (overall equivalence).
requirements: Translated and back-translated instruments with piloting in each target-language country
constraints: Adapted for students around age nine; algebraic items with letter variables excluded

article_title: A Survey of the Three First Grades of the Horace Mann School by Means of Psychological Tests and Teachers' Estimates, and a Statistical Evaluation of the Methods Employed.
citation: Chassell, C. F., & Chassell, L. M. (1921). A survey of the three first grades of the Horace Mann School by means of psychological tests and teachers' estimates, and a statistical evaluation of the methods employed. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(5), 243-252.
title: Statistical procedures for converting varied measures into mental ages
description: The article details procedures for reducing heterogeneous survey data to the common basis of mental age. For the Stanford Revision, mental ages at a common date were obtained "by using the intelligence quotients already determined as multipliers". For the group tests, tables of norms by months were constructed, since "it was necessary to build up a table of norms by months". Teachers' rankings were transmuted into mental ages by three methods: assuming a normal distribution, treating the distribution as rectangular, and treating ranks as gross scores.
requirements: Requires a common basis (mental age) to combine varied measures; for the Meyer Tests, norms had to be estimated by comparison with Stanford Revision records
constraints: The IQ-multiplier method is based on the assumption of the constancy of the I. Q., which the authors note is not thoroughly established
target_learning_goals: conversion of test scores and teacher rankings into comparable mental ages for reclassification
examples: For the Meyer Tests, norms were estimated by comparing scores of twenty-nine children on the Meyer tests with their Stanford Revision records, computing median intelligence quotients for each half year of chronological age

A survey of the three first grades of the Horace Mann School by means of psychological tests and teachers' estimates, and a statistical evaluation of the methods employed. Part II. article_title: The contribution of psychology to education.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074512
title: Decide competing teaching methods with controlled comparative trials and measurement, rather than from unaided classroom experience.
description: The article argues that psychology, by its methods of measuring knowledge and skill, can test and verify or refute the claims of any teaching method. Its worked example is whether to teach the spelling of a pair of homonyms together or apart in time, a question teachers had failed to decide from classroom experience. The prescribed recipe is a controlled comparison with measurement of errors afterwards.
requirements: Enough teachers using both methods with enough different classes
keeping everything else except the method constant
measuring the errors in spelling the words thereafter in the two cases
examples: The homonym-spelling comparison: the article states teachers could not decide the question from classroom experience, but measuring errors in the two cases would decide it for any given pair.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070113

article_title: Tests for Mental Alertness.
citation: L. W. Sackett. (1917). Tests for Mental Alertness. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Tests+for+Mental+Alertness%22
title: Sackett's mental alertness tests (story recall plus story exercises) with Alertness Quotient scoring
description: A two-part paper-and-pencil battery: Test 1 is a short story the pupil reads and reproduces from memory in his own words, and Test 2 is a set of fifteen questions and exercises based on the story. Scoring divides accomplishment by time: "In each case the 'score' forms the numerator and the 'time' the denominator of a fraction while the resulting quotient is the index of ability in the test," designated the Alertness Quotient. Test 2's parts have printed differential weights (1, 4, 2, 5, 5, 8, 8, 6, 9, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 12), though these were not used in the reported study.
requirements: Administered by teachers furnished with full instructions, cautions, grading directions, A.Q. calculation blanks, and original papers inspected before scores were accepted
Future use should employ the weighted values in scoring Test 2
constraints: Reading difficulties preclude extensive use below the fourth grade
Test 2 parts are not of equal difficulty, and the seventh grade showed technical difficulties with the second test
target_learners: Elementary school pupils in grades four to seven, with suggested extension to high school and university
target_learning_goals: Measuring speed and accuracy of simple school-like reading, recall, and direction-following tasks (mental alertness)
examples: One large city tested 4961 pupils in grades four to seven after the writer briefed principals and demonstrated the administration; smaller cities were run by cooperating principals and superintendents
key_sources: L. W. Sackett. (1917). Tests for Mental Alertness. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Tests+for+Mental+Alertness%22

article_title: Communications and discussions. The conference on mental hygiene at Boston.
citation: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Mental hygiene extending beyond the pathological to normal mental processes and school practice
description: The report highlights as noteworthy that "considerable attention was given at this conference to normal mental processes," in contrast to recent mental-hygiene writing that concerned the pathological. This framing extends mental hygiene into education: Dr. Burnham spoke on "Mental Hygiene in the School," Professor Yerkes on "Hygiene and Mental Development," and Dr. Cabot on "Four Laws for Mental Hygiene." The account treats mental health as something cultivated through schooling and child training, with prevention rather than treatment as the guiding aim.
requirements: Educational settings must attend to normal mental processes and child development, not only pathology
constraints: The report frames this as a notable shift of emphasis at one 1913 conference; it presents no data on outcomes in schools
examples: Talks at the conference on mental hygiene in the school and on hygiene and mental development exemplify the extension to normal processes.
key_sources: Wm. H. Burnham. (1913). The Conference on Mental Hygiene at Boston. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: The dynamics of motivation.
citation: Bell, J. C. (1919). The dynamics of motivation. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(5-6). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology+volume+X
title: The mechanism-drive framework: every mechanism requires a drive, and any mechanism may act as a drive for another
description: The editorial proposes an explanatory account of motivation built on Woodworth's Dynamic Psychology, in which behavior rests on the sensory-motor arc and its modifications. It states the fundamental distinction between "mechanism" and "drive": a mechanism is the neural structure that acts, while a drive is the impetus that sets it going. The article asserts that "any mechanism may act as a 'drive' to bring about a reaction of any other 'mechanism,'" so that complex behavior such as reflective action involves elaborately combined drives and mechanisms rather than a single stimulus-response link.
requirements: An adequate psychology of motivation to develop the account further, which the article says is yet to be written
constraints: The framework is presented as a theoretical account, not a tested result; the article says much current discussion of motivation is superficial or mystical
target_learning_goals: sustained motivation and effort in school learning
examples: The article applies the framework to explain how simple reflex arcs obtain drive from sensory stimulation while complex reflective behavior involves drives that reinforce or inhibit each other through memory and habit formation
key_sources: Bell, J. C. (1919). The dynamics of motivation. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(5-6). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology+volume+X

article_title: The Binet-Simon measuring scale for intelligence: An annotated bibliography. Part II.
citation: Kohs, S. C. (1914). The Binet-Simon Measuring Scale for Intelligence: An Annotated Bibliography. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Binet-Simon+Measuring+Scale+for+Intelligence%22+Kohs+annotated+bibliography
title: Mental-age-based classification of mental defectives
description: The bibliography records the proposal, attributed to Goddard, of 'a classification of mental defectives according to mental age' — ranking individuals by the age level their Binet performance attains rather than by chronological age alone. This organizing idea underlies the diagnostic and institutional applications the bibliography documents, including grading of institutional populations. Kuhlmann's entry criticizes the underlying quantity, arguing the difference between mental and chronological age 'does not represent the true degree of deficiency' and choosing rate of mental progress as more representative.
requirements: A normed scale yielding a mental-age estimate, such as the Binet-Simon scale with its age-graded tests.
constraints: Kuhlmann's annotated entry argues that the mental-age/chronological-age difference does not represent the true degree of deficiency; Kulpe's entry doubts the comparative value of mental age.
examples: Goddard's prognostical classification of mental defectives in institutional settings
Kuhlmann's grading of thirteen hundred feeble-minded children with the tests
key_sources: Kohs, S. C. (1914). The Binet-Simon Measuring Scale for Intelligence: An Annotated Bibliography. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Binet-Simon+Measuring+Scale+for+Intelligence%22+Kohs+annotated+bibliography

article_title: The teaching of elementary physics.
citation: Abstracts and Reviews. (1910). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: A memory research compilation gathering about 575 citations from over 200 contributors
description: A reviewed compilation on memory containing "some 575 citations from over 200 different contributors", with an appended bibliography of about 100 titles. The reviewer judges that little in it is actually new but that readers need not consult original sources for most purposes, since the facts are gathered there, and notes a wish for more discussion of the physiology of memory.
requirements: an appended bibliography of roughly one hundred titles supplements the compilation
constraints: the reviewer finds very little that is actually new and notes the physiological discussion of memory is thin
target_learning_goals: accessing the research literature on memory without going to original sources
examples: Since so many others are available, there is no attempt to make the appended bibliography complete
key_sources: Abstracts and Reviews. (1910). The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: Department for discussion of research problems. A problem for careful research: How does the ability to make rapid mental adjustments affect test scores and pupil achievements?
citation: Zirbes, L. (1919). A Problem for Careful Research: How Does the Ability to Make Rapid Mental Adjustments Affect Test Scores and Pupil Achievements? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22How+Does+the+Ability+to+Make+Rapid+Mental+Adjustments+Affect+Test+Scores+and+Pupil+Achievements%22+Zirbes
title: Mental set and rapid mental adjustment as a skill factor in achievement
description: The article proposes that many achievement errors arise not from lack of mathematical or reading ability but from 'a failure on the part of the child to set his mind for the particular reading task in hand, or to the persistence of one mental set through different types of reading'. Rapid mental adjustment — the ability to shift set quickly and to see the necessity of change — is framed as a general skill factor contributing to test scores across subjects, trainable in principle. The framework generates six stated research problems on its influence on standard tests, Binet scores, training and transfer.
requirements: Training and testing situations must make the need for change in mental set inhere in the material, since pupils may not see the need themselves
constraints: The ability is not distinctly characterized as mathematical ability, and the article states it is unknown to what extent training of this ability must be special rather than transferring
target_learners: elementary grade pupils (grades IV-VI in the illustrations)
target_learning_goals: accurate and flexible performance across mixed tasks
recall of learned material under varied conditions
examples: The Courtis arithmetic error analysis and the four-part timed reading test are the article's own illustrations of set effects and adjustment
key_sources: Zirbes, L. (1919). A Problem for Careful Research: How Does the Ability to Make Rapid Mental Adjustments Affect Test Scores and Pupil Achievements? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22How+Does+the+Ability+to+Make+Rapid+Mental+Adjustments+Affect+Test+Scores+and+Pupil+Achievements%22+Zirbes

article_title: Mental fatigue in day school children as measured by immediate memory. Part II.
citation: W. H. Winch. (1911). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Mechanical mental work of a memorizing kind may be scheduled late in the afternoon session with fair satisfaction for most children
description: The article's third summarized conclusion states that "The ordinarily accepted pedagogical maxim that, with most children, mental work of a mechanical kind may be done, with fair satisfaction, late in an afternoon session, appears to receive some corroboration." This rests on the finding that the average afternoon deficit was only about 2 per cent, though a minority of afternoon workers deteriorated markedly.
requirements: Applies to mechanical mental work of the memorizing kind, as measured by immediate memory tests
constraints: About one-third of the afternoon group showed deterioration, for whom the author advises a cessation of work or a longer interval between successive exercises
target_learners: Day school children of around 11 years of age
target_learning_goals: Scheduling mechanical memorizing work across the school day
examples: In the experiment, the afternoon group's average final-test mark (16.1) fell only 0.4 marks below the morning group's (16.5), despite the afternoon session ending at 4.15 P.M.
key_sources: W. H. Winch. (1911). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Extracurricular music and visual arts activities are related to academic performance improvement in school-aged children
citation: Chiaki Ishiguro, Toru Ishihara and Noriteru Morita. (2023). Extracurricular music and visual arts activities are related to academic performance improvement in school-aged children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00155-0
title: Mediated transfer of arts education to academic performance (Winner et al.'s second transfer hypothesis)
description: This framework holds that arts education affects general academic performance not directly but through artistic skills as mediating factors. The article quotes the hypothesis: "artistic skills are mediating factors in the transfer such that arts instruction can lead to the improvement of artistic skills and result in achieving certain academic outcomes". The study's structural equation models operationalized it by testing indirect effects of extracurricular music and visual arts on academic GP via art subject grades, and the authors report the mediated pattern "supported the second hypothesis of Winner et al.".
requirements: Longitudinal data capturing both art subject scores and general academic performance at two time points, plus baseline art scores and SES controls, to separate direct from mediated effects
constraints: The article states the current study shows correlational relationships and could not specify which activities within each club type drive the effect
The article notes the transfer effect size is quite small
target_learners: school-aged children in junior high school (seventh to ninth grade)
target_learning_goals: general academic performance in five major subjects (Japanese, mathematics, social studies, science, English) via music and visual arts skills
examples: The study measured music GP, visual arts GP, and ACGP of Japanese junior high students at the end of seventh and ninth grades and modeled indirect effects through art subject grades.
key_sources: Chiaki Ishiguro, Toru Ishihara and Noriteru Morita. (2023). Extracurricular music and visual arts activities are related to academic performance improvement in school-aged children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00155-0

article_title: Common health conditions in childhood and adolescence, school absence, and educational attainment: Mendelian randomization study
citation: Hughes, A., Wade, K. H., Dickson, M., Rice, F., Davies, A., Davies, N. M. & Howe, L. D. (2021). Common health conditions in childhood and adolescence, school absence, and educational attainment: Mendelian randomization study. npj Science of Learning 6:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00080-6
title: Mendelian randomization with polygenic scores for triangulating causal effects of health on educational outcomes
description: The article applies genetic causal inference to educational outcomes. Polygenic scores (PGSs) combine multiple SNPs associated with a condition into "a PGS representing genetic liability for a condition", improving statistical power relative to single SNPs. "In one-sample Mendelian randomization, causal influence of an exposure is estimated using the PGS as an instrumental variable for the exposure in a two-stage least-squares model." Two-sample MR instead compares SNP associations with exposure and outcome across independent GWAS samples. The article stresses triangulation across phenotypic, one-sample and two-sample MR approaches.
requirements: A polygenic score sufficiently strong to serve as an instrument (the article used first-stage F-statistics > 10 and found only the BMI PGS qualified)
constraints: Genetic results are conditional on MR assumptions; the article reports pleiotropy evidence for BMI–absenteeism and possible family-level (parental-genotype, assortative-mating) bias
Low PGS predictive power (<1% variance for ADHD, migraine, asthma; <0.1% for ASD, depression) limited genetic methods for those conditions, so nulls there should not be read as evidence of no effect
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents in an English birth cohort
target_learning_goals: educational attainment at age 16 (GCSE) and school attendance
examples: Only the BMI PGS passed instrument-strength tests in ALSPAC, so IV estimates were reported only for BMI; the study triangulated phenotypic, one-sample and two-sample MR results for the same conditions.
key_sources: Hughes, A., Wade, K. H., Dickson, M., Rice, F., Davies, A., Davies, N. M. & Howe, L. D. (2021). Common health conditions in childhood and adolescence, school absence, and educational attainment: Mendelian randomization study. npj Science of Learning 6:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00080-6

article_title: No guts, no glory: underestimating the benefits of providing children with mechanistic details
citation: Chuey, A., McCarthy, A., Lockhart, K., Trouche, E., Sheskin, M. & Keil, F. (2021). No guts, no glory: underestimating the benefits of providing children with mechanistic details. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00108-5
title: Expose young children to detailed causal mechanisms rather than omitting them, because exposure yields concrete memory plus abstract system-level knowledge that supports epistemic evaluation
description: The article argues educators should not strip mechanistic details from instruction for young children. A seven-minute adult-level video on a combustion engine gave 6–9-year-olds concrete memory for parts and, from around age 8, abstract causal patterns supporting expert detection: children "not only learned a surprising amount, but were notably engaged". Mechanistic exposure may also support relearning, generalization, categorization and induction.
requirements: Access to mechanistically rich material (e.g., a video of how a complex system works) rather than isolated facts alone
constraints: Findings come from a single mechanical system and a small subset of causal patterns; they may not generalize to biology or economics mechanisms
Classrooms should assess more than memory for details, since detail-only assessment can make complex mechanisms seem out of learners' reach
target_learning_goals: abstract causal understanding of complex systems
examples: 180 children were shown a seven-minute adult-level video about an internal combustion engine and tested immediately or one week later against a no-video control
key_sources: Chuey, A., McCarthy, A., Lockhart, K., Trouche, E., Sheskin, M. & Keil, F. (2021). No guts, no glory: underestimating the benefits of providing children with mechanistic details. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00108-5

article_title: Relation of life sciences students’ metacognitive monitoring to neural activity during biology error detection
citation: Mei Grace Behrendt, Carrie Clark, McKenna Elliott & Joseph Dauer. (2024). Relation of life sciences students' metacognitive monitoring to neural activity during biology error detection. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00231-z
title: Metacognitive calibration as a foundation for error detection, self-regulated learning, and conceptual change
description: The article frames metacognitive calibration—the match between objective performance and subjective self-assessment—as "fundamental to self-regulated learning because it forms the basis for performance monitoring". Well-calibrated learners should show high confidence when accurate and low confidence when not. Calibration is theorized as "a critical initial step in the process of conceptual change": students aware of their misconceptions detect and remedy them, while unaware students become overly secure and miss opportunities for knowledge revision. The study tests this account neurally during an authentic biology model evaluation task.
requirements: Confidence ratings must be collected so calibration can be scored against actual accuracy, ideally with bias-free signal detection metrics such as meta-d' and metacognitive efficiency
constraints: The relationship between brain activity and metacognitive calibration is described as complex and multifaceted; different metacognitive aspects may involve distinct regions, and it remains debated whether calibration is task-specific or trait-like
examples: The study operationalized calibration via phi coefficients, meta-d', and metacognitive efficiency computed from confidence ratings in the fMRI task
key_sources: Mei Grace Behrendt, Carrie Clark, McKenna Elliott & Joseph Dauer. (2024). Relation of life sciences students' metacognitive monitoring to neural activity during biology error detection. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00231-z

article_title: Does anxiety explain why math-anxious people underperform in math?
citation: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Necka, E.A., Green, A.E. & Lyons, I.M. (2023). Does anxiety explain why math-anxious people underperform in math? npj Science of Learning, 8:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00156-z
title: Mechanistic heterogeneity framework for math-anxious underperformance as a function of emotion regulation capacity (HF-HRV)
description: This framework holds that the mechanisms by which trait math anxiety leads to poor math performance differ across individuals as a function of physiological emotion regulation capacity, indexed by resting HF-HRV. As the article states, "there is substantial heterogeneity in the mechanisms by which math anxiety and math performance are associated, and this heterogeneity occurs as a function of HF-HRV." For low-HF-HRV individuals, the in-the-moment anxiety account is largely correct (the indirect effect is 94% of the total effect); for high-HF-HRV individuals it is largely incomplete (14%); for average levels it is in-between (about half). The article presents this as a corrective to the dominant single-mechanism account in which state anxiety is the primary cause of math-anxious underperformance.
requirements: Measuring both trait math anxiety and an index of emotion regulation capacity (baseline HF-HRV) alongside performance, so that the realized mechanism can differ across individuals
constraints: The article notes the current design is not well-suited for state-level analyses of HF-HRV, since anticipatory/task HF-HRV was collected after the state anxiety rating it is meant to moderate
The college-aged population and the particular difficult mental math task may limit generalizability; the authors state future work is needed for younger populations and other math task forms
target_learners: college-aged students high in math anxiety
target_learning_goals: improving math performance in math-anxious learners
key_sources: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Necka, E.A., Green, A.E. & Lyons, I.M. (2023). Does anxiety explain why math-anxious people underperform in math? npj Science of Learning, 8:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00156-z

article_title: Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training
citation: Yufeng Ke, Shuang Liu, Long Chen, Xiashuang Wang and Dong Ming. (2023). Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training. npj Science of Learning 8:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00200-y
title: Metaplasticity account of lasting tDCS-enhanced working memory training effects
description: The article offers a metaplasticity explanation for the lasting neurobehavioral improvements observed when anodal tDCS is paired with multi-session working memory training. It defines metaplasticity as "a higher-order form of plasticity that can enable or inhibit plasticity induction, stabilize synapses, and homeostatically regulate cellular activity". When stimulation is paired with repeated cognitive training that induces synaptic plasticity, metaplasticity modulates plasticity and extends the time window for associative plasticity, increasing stimulation-induced aftereffects on cortical excitability or learning. The authors propose that anodal tDCS over the left dlPFC modulated synaptic plasticity of WM-related neural substrates this way.
requirements: Pairing brain stimulation with repeated cognitive training capable of inducing synaptic plasticity
constraints: The authors present this as a possible interpretation rather than a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: healthy young adults undergoing working memory training
examples: The study applied anodal HD-tDCS over the left dlPFC simultaneously with ten consecutive days of adaptive verbal N-back training and measured lasting EEG and behavioral aftereffects three weeks later.
key_sources: Yufeng Ke, Shuang Liu, Long Chen, Xiashuang Wang and Dong Ming. (2023). Lasting enhancements in neural efficiency by multi-session transcranial direct current stimulation during working memory training. npj Science of Learning 8:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00200-y

article_title: How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y
title: Memory formation proceeds through successive phases of encoding, consolidation, retrieval and reconsolidation
description: The review organizes declarative memory formation as a cycle of phases: encoding by the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe, offline consolidation (especially during sleep) that semanticizes memories, retrieval that reconstructs memories depending on present cues, and reconsolidation whereby retrieved memories are updated and integrated into existing schemas. "Memories are then suggested to become reconsolidated into existing schemas, presumably altering their features again", so schemas are continuously adjusted to optimize understanding and prediction.
requirements: Memory content moves between episodic detail and semantic organization across phases, so interventions must be matched to the relevant phase
constraints: The review chose to focus on the adult brain and acknowledges not all discussed processes might translate directly to the developing brain
target_learning_goals: understanding how long-term knowledge is built
balancing episodic detail and semantic generalization
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y

article_title: Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function
citation: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1
title: Adaptive learning systems need memory models that are accurate both within and between learning sessions to make useful scheduling recommendations
description: The article argues that adaptive scheduling of practice should rest on a memory model that predicts retention correctly on both short (seconds to minutes) and long (hours to weeks) timescales. A model calibrated within a single session "will already systematically underestimate retention" after an hour or more, "hampering its ability to make useful scheduling recommendations in a subsequent learning session." A time-variant forgetting function is the proposed remedy, enabling a single model to tailor predictions to a wide range of intervals.
requirements: A theoretically grounded model with meaningful parameters (not a purely measurement-oriented model) so counterfactual scheduling scenarios can be simulated
Parameter estimates that remain valid across the interval range encountered in deployment, e.g., via time-variant parameters
constraints: A single fixed parameter value for the interference scaling factor h may work in settings with a limited range of intervals but is suboptimal for more general educational applications
target_learners: learners using adaptive practice systems across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: optimising the timing of retrieval practice within and across sessions to improve retention
examples: Using a within-session-fitted ACT-R model to schedule a second study session would systematically underestimate retention after an hour or more, per the article's analysis of the naturalistic dataset
key_sources: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1

article_title: Longitudinal associations between sedentary behavior types and mathematics ability mediated by externalizing and internalizing problems
citation: Guan, K., Zhang, Z., Liu, Z. et al. (2026). Longitudinal associations between sedentary behavior types and mathematics ability mediated by externalizing and internalizing problems. npj Sci. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00424-8
title: Mentally active versus mentally passive sedentary behavior classification
description: The study adopts a framework that classifies sedentary behavior by level of cognitive engagement rather than treating it as a uniform construct. The article notes that "research classified SB into passive and active categories based on the level of cognitive engagement, offering a framework to clarify their effects on psychological health and cognitive functions". In this study, "listening to music was considered mentally passive SB, whereas playing e-games and reading for leisure were classified as mentally active SB", while Internet use was left unclassified "due to ongoing debate about its categorization". The framework motivates the study's differentiation of SB types.
requirements: Classification of individual sedentary behavior types by cognitive engagement level, which the authors note requires finer-grained approaches (e.g., differentiating leisure- from learning-oriented Internet use)
constraints: Internet use for leisure "was not classified as either type of SB due to ongoing debate about its categorization"
examples: In the study, listening to music was mentally passive; playing e-games and reading for leisure were mentally active; TV viewing and homework durations were reported by caregivers
key_sources: Guan, K., Zhang, Z., Liu, Z. et al. (2026). Longitudinal associations between sedentary behavior types and mathematics ability mediated by externalizing and internalizing problems. npj Sci. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00424-8

article_title: Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits
citation: Vyshedskiy, A., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E. & Satik, D. (2024). Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00284-0
title: Refinement of the Merge hypothesis: a split into simple Merge (PFM-mediated) and complex Merge (PFS-mediated)
description: The article engages the linguistics hypothesis that unbounded Merge — a cognitive operation taking two linguistic units (e.g., 'blue' and 'cat') and forming a set — is the uniquely human generative engine of infinite expression. It argues the clustering data refine this hypothesis by distinguishing two subcomponents. The article reports that "25% of participants in our study acquired the modi ﬁer mechanism without developing the syntactic mechanism", which suggests "a division within the Merge operation": "simple Merge", underling comprehension of color, size, and number modifiers and mediated by PFM, and "complex Merge", underling syntactic structures and mediated by PFS. The finding of a large command-limited cluster also supports Merge by confirming command abilities are mediated by a separate mechanism.
requirements: Interpretation rests on the empirical dissociation of modifier from syntactic abilities in the phenotype data, which requires the PFM/PFS neurological account
constraints: Merge is positioned as a separator between modifier and syntactic abilities on one hand and command abilities on the other; command structures are limited by definition to comprehension of single words
target_learners: children and adolescents with language comprehension deficits
target_learning_goals: comprehension of modifiers and syntactic linguistic structures
examples: The modifier phenotype's possession of modifier abilities without syntactic abilities was taken as evidence for the simple-Merge/complex-Merge division
key_sources: Vyshedskiy, A., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E. & Satik, D. (2024). Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00284-0

article_title: Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER)
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7
title: Embrace methodological plurality when evaluating EdTech evidence rather than positioning RCTs as best for all
description: The authors argue that EdTech evaluation should recognise the value of all types of research. They state it is important "to embrace methodological plurality that recognises the value of all types of research, without positioning RCT evidence as the best evidence for all EdTech", because different designs and methods answer different research questions and there is no universally applicable hierarchy of research methods.
requirements: A match between the method and the question being asked
target_learners: All learners served by EdTech products
target_learning_goals: Sound evaluation of EdTech impact on learning
examples: EVER rates conceptual, qualitative, quantitative and validation approaches side by side rather than ranking them
key_sources: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7

article_title: Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups
citation: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5
title: MentorChat: a domain-independent architecture for conversational-agent-supported group learning
description: Tegos et al.'s MentorChat is described as "a domain-independent system architecture for building group learning applications that are supported by conversational agents." A focus is "the development of tools that allow educators to customize and control agent behaviour based on their own expert knowledge." In the article it is customized for a language learning application used by small groups of 2 to 3 students, exploring "directed prompts to elicit a higher degree of pedagogically beneficial responses from the learners."
requirements: Tools must allow educators to customize and control agent behaviour based on their own expert knowledge
constraints: Customized in the article for a language learning application used by small groups of 2 to 3 students
target_learners: small groups of 2 to 3 students in language learning
target_learning_goals: productive dialogue in group language learning
examples: Used for a language learning application where directed prompts elicit pedagogically beneficial responses
key_sources: Rohit Kumar & Jihie Kim. (2013). Special Issue on Intelligent Support for Learning in Groups. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0013-5

article_title: Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs
citation: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w
title: Four expert-derived case-based question templates for medical MCQ generation
description: Elsevier medical experts identified four question templates representative of board-examination preparation questions: What is the most likely diagnosis?, What is the drug of choice?, What is the most likely clinical finding?, and What is the differential diagnosis?. "Four medical question templates have been implemented in the current implementation of E MCQG." Each template specifies stem entities (patient demographic, history, symptoms), option-entity rules over ranked relations, and validity rules ensuring distractors are weaker than or unrelated to the key.
requirements: Templates require clinical semantic relations (hCF, hRF, hD, hDDx) with rankings, and POC attributes for patient demographics
constraints: Each template is structurally different, so each has its own difficulty calculator and explanation generator
target_learners: medical residents preparing for board examinations
examples: Template rules require that for any distractor, the sum of its relations' ranks to all stem entities is strictly less than the key's sum
key_sources: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w

article_title: A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students’ Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain
citation: Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S., & Tsiatsos, T. (2013). A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students' Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0007-3
title: MentorChat configurable domain-independent conversational agent architecture
description: MentorChat is a cloud-based dialogue-based ITS whose architecture consists of three core modules: student, conversational agent, and teacher. The agent module rests on three models — peer interaction, domain, and intervention — where the "peer interaction model analyses and stores the most important aspects of students' interactions" and the domain model comes from teacher-authored concept maps or rules. The design deliberately avoids hardwiring an explicit domain model, instead enabling teacher-led configuration of agent behavior, which the authors argue lowers development cost and increases reusability and teacher acceptance.
requirements: Teacher-led domain modeling via concept maps or event-condition-intervention rules
System dictionaries for stemming, synonyms and antonyms to support pattern matching
constraints: The system does not enable identification of multiple dialogue acts in a single student's utterance
The automatic concept-mapping modeling method is a work in progress not yet assessed
examples: In the pilot, the teacher configured agent behavior via rules consisting of a key word or phrase and a relevant reflective-question intervention
key_sources: Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S., & Tsiatsos, T. (2013). A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students' Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0007-3

article_title: A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students’ Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain
citation: Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S., & Tsiatsos, T. (2013). A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students' Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0007-3
title: MentorChat system
description: MentorChat is a cloud-based, web-technology application (MySQL, PHP, AJAX, HTML5, CSS3) available in English and Greek for synchronous text-based collaborative activities. Students discuss open-ended domain questions in phases and submit joint answers, while an animated two-dimensional avatar agent with Text-To-Speech tracks dialogue and delivers teacher-defined prompts. Teacher panels cover user management, activity structure, domain modeling, and real-time monitoring with interaction analysis indicators.
requirements: Teacher configuration of domain model, rules, groups, and roles before deployment
constraints: Requires teacher-defined key words/phrases to trigger interventions
target_learning_goals: collaborative discussion of open-ended domain questions
examples: Pilot installation used in a third-year English language course at Taurida National University of Ukraine
key_sources: Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S., & Tsiatsos, T. (2013). A Configurable Conversational Agent to Trigger Students' Productive Dialogue: A Pilot Study in the CALL Domain. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0007-3

article_title: MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks
citation: Tom Murray. (2003). MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.199-233. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197317
title: MetaLinks: an authoring tool and web server for adaptive hyperbooks
description: MetaLinks is an authoring tool and web server for producing adaptive hyperbooks that provide textbook-like content in a flexible manner. The abstract describes it as supporting "opportunistic processes of active reading and learning", so that "a single on-line artifact can address the diverse needs of a variety of user goals and backgrounds" through adaptive methods.
requirements: Requires an authoring tool and web server infrastructure as described in the article
target_learners: learners using adaptive hyperbooks with diverse goals and backgrounds
target_learning_goals: inquiry, exploratory, or curiosity-driven learning in richly interconnected material
examples: The system is designed to support inquiry, exploratory, or curiosity-driven learning in richly interconnected material.

article_title: MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks

title: Interface features of narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links address discontinuous flow in open-ended hyperbook learning
description: The article reports that its goals are addressed through interface features and adaptive methods "including narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links". These respond to the usability problem that flexible, idiosyncratic navigation through hyperbook content risks discontinuous conceptual and narrative flow for learners exploring open-ended material.

constraints: Targets usability issues arising in open-ended learning environments where users navigate flexibly and idiosyncratically

target_learning_goals: maintaining conceptual and narrative coherence during self-directed reading
examples: MetaLinks implements narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links as adaptive methods in its hyperbooks.

article_title: Neural Networks or Linguistic Features? - Comparing Different Machine-Learning Approaches for Automated Assessment of Text Quality Traits Among L1- and L2-Learners’ Argumentative Essays
citation: Lohmann, J. F., Junge, F., Möller, J., Fleckenstein, J., Trüb, R., Keller, S., Jansen, T., & Horbach, A. (2025). Neural Networks or Linguistic Features? - Comparing Different Machine-Learning Approaches for Automated Assessment of Text Quality Traits Among L1- and L2-Learners' Argumentative Essays. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 1178–1217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00426-w

description: The MEWS corpus (Measuring Writing Skills in English as a Second Language) contains "argumentative essays written by German and Swiss L2 upper secondary school students". The study uses two MEWS prompts (AD and TE, N3 = 1179; N4 = 1112) with analytic labels for content, organization, and language quality on a 0–6 scale, produced in the TrACE project and corrected for rater severity with an IRT-based rater model. The dataset is available on OSF.

constraints: Only rater severity effects were modeled, not rater centrality/extremity or consistency

target_learning_goals: Assessment of argumentative writing quality traits (content, organization, language quality) in English as a second language

article_title: Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments
citation: HaeJin Lee · Nigel Bosch. (2025). Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00514-5
title: Metacognitive experience as a distinct element in models of metacognition (Flavell, Pintrich, Efklides)
description: The article reviews models of metacognition and highlights that "metacognitive experience is identified as a separate and distinct element" in the frameworks of Flavell, Pintrich, and Efklides. In Efklides's model, metacognitive experiences manifest as "metacognitive judgments/estimates, feelings, and task-specific knowledge in real-time", serving as a bridge between cognitive and emotional regulation, and are distinguished from metacognitive knowledge and from metacognitive skills (intentional application of strategies for cognitive control).
requirements: Distinguishing momentary judgments and feelings from relatively static metacognitive knowledge when measuring metacognition
constraints: Brown's (1987) and Schraw and Dennison's (1994) models do not identify metacognitive experience as a separate main component, treating it instead as a skill within monitoring
target_learners: All learners, as framed in the article's general theoretical review
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring, judgment accuracy, and self-regulated learning
examples: In this study, students' pretest and posttest retrospective judgments (estimated scores 0–100%) operationalize metacognitive judgments as instances of metacognitive experience.
key_sources: HaeJin Lee · Nigel Bosch. (2025). Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00514-5

article_title: ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem
citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: Meta-adaptation transfers learners between systems (or to humans) based on needs and performance, via distributed or brokered adaptation
description: Meta-adaptation is described as "transferring the learner between different systems based on their needs and performance," the maximum possible grain size of adaptation, allowing learners to benefit from complementary strengths of multiple systems and potentially mitigating wheel spinning. It can also mean referring a learner to a human instructor, tutor, or peer. The article distinguishes distributed adaptation, where individual systems decide referrals, from brokered adaptation, which "would require a new type of service whose purpose is to monitor student learning across all systems (i.e., a student model integrator)" consulted as part of each system's outer loop.
requirements: Gains from system transitions must exceed the overhead costs of introducing learners to a new system, activity, or interface
constraints: Handoffs raise technical and societal issues: what data to share, which stakeholders (systems, teachers, students) control handoffs, and privacy/data-ownership concerns
target_learners: learners moving between multiple adaptive learning systems, individually or in cohorts
target_learning_goals: routing learners to the system, activity, or human support best suited to their current needs and performance
examples: First steps toward meta-adaptation cited include ONR STEM Grand Challenge integrations of Wayang Outpost with ASSISTments and AutoTutor with ALEKS, and integration of a version of AutoTutor with the ARL GIFT architecture.
key_sources: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8

article_title: How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System?
citation: Taub, M., & Azevedo, R. (2019). How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System? Int J Artif Intell Educ (2019) 29:1-28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0165-4
title: MetaTutor: hypermedia-based ITS with four SRL-specialized pedagogical agents and an SRL palette
description: MetaTutor is "a hypermedia-based intelligent tutoring system that teaches participants about the human circulatory system", containing 47 pages of text and static diagrams with a 90-minute learning session. It was "designed specifically to foster SRL processes during learning": a timer, table of contents, learning goal and sub-goals, an SRL palette for self-initiating cognitive and metacognitive processes, and "four pedagogical agents where each agent is responsible for a different aspect of SRL" (Gavin the Guide, Pam the Planner, Sam the Strategizer, Mary the Monitor). In this study it was used with prompt-and-feedback and control conditions.
requirements: A sub-goal setting phase prior to the 90-minute session, in which participants set two sub-goals with Pam the Planner
constraints: In the control condition the agents did not prompt or provide feedback, acting only as minimal external regulation
target_learning_goals: learning about the human circulatory system
planning, cognitive strategy use, and metacognitive monitoring
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to a prompt-and-feedback condition (n = 95) or a control condition (n = 99) during the 90-minute learning session.

article_title: MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions
citation: Patricia Azevedo Tedesco. (2003). MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, 117-155. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197314
title: Design collaborative environments so that conflicts inherent to group problem solving are mediated rather than suppressed, because well-employed conflicts refine solutions
description: The article motivates its framework by noting that the emphasis on building co-operative/collaborative environments has highlighted "the issue of conflicts, inherent to group problem solving." Rather than treating conflict as a failure to eliminate, it treats well-employed conflict as a resource: mediation should trigger articulation and reflection so the group's solution is refined. Designers of collaborative learning systems should therefore build in conflict detection and mediation.
requirements: Ability to analyse the ongoing interaction and diagnose changes to the group plan before intervening
constraints: Conflicts must be well employed; the article does not claim unmediated or poorly handled conflict is beneficial
target_learners: Learners working in co-operative or collaborative group settings
target_learning_goals: Cognitive change leading to more refined group solutions
examples: The MArCo prototype embeds the artificial conflict mediator to support group planning interactions
