article_title: Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry
citation: Martin, P. P., Kranz, D., & Graulich, N. (2025). Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 1465–1503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00440-y
title: Research-informed rubric of mechanistic reasoning comprising multivariate, comparative, and electronic reasoning categories
description: The research-informed rubric evaluates whether a student reasons in a multivariate, comparative, and electronic way. Multivariate reasoning identifies multiple chemical properties and explains how their interactions impact reaction plausibility (coded present if at least two chemical properties were outlined for at least one reaction). Comparative reasoning contrasts molecules or their reactivity to focus on similarities and differences. Electronic reasoning considers the movement and distribution of electrons, incorporating effects such as resonance, hyperconjugation, or inductive effects. Author DK binary-coded all responses; inter-rater reliability on a 20% subset reached Cohen's κ of 0.84 (95% CI [0.78, 0.91]) after discussion, described as almost perfect agreement.
requirements: Coders with domain expertise; the article reports binary coding of each category with inter-rater reliability checking on a randomly selected 20% subset
constraints: The productive code evaluating correctness rather than complexity was removed; the rubric captures complexity of reasoning, not correctness
target_learning_goals: multivariate, comparative, and electronic mechanistic reasoning
examples: Applied to student responses to two SN1 case comparisons prompting students to explain which of two contrasted reactions occurs at a higher rate
key_sources: Martin, P. P., Kranz, D., & Graulich, N. (2025). Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry. article_title: An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments
citation: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7
title: Meta-level MDP framework for modeling planning under uncertainty
description: The article formalizes human planning in partially observable environments as a meta-level Markov Decision Process that separates "an object-level component, which models the interaction with the real world, and a meta-level component, which models the (often internal) planning operations." Belief states are multivariate Normal distributions updated via Bayesian conjugate priors when noisy observations arrive. Computations can be repeated arbitrarily many times, iteratively increasing belief accuracy. This extends prior fully observable meta-level MDP models by incorporating observation noise, making the belief state reflect uncertainty rather than precise knowledge.
requirements: A model of the planning task as a directed acyclic graph with ground-truth rewards drawn from known distributions
Specification of observation precision and planning cost parameters
constraints: Assumes rewards are drawn from multivariate Normal distributions
Assumes computations produce Gaussian-noisy samples rather than deterministic revelations
examples: The framework was applied to a flight-planning task where learners route an airplane over a network of airports with uncertain profitability
key_sources: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7

title: Mental Hygiene Film Series (Feelings of Depression, Overdependency, Feelings of Hostility, Feelings of Rejection)

article_title: Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics
citation: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8
title: Probabilistic student model (MEBN) translating E-portfolio data into personalized feedback
description: The article's student model is a probabilistic representation of a learner's state and context: "A student model is a statistical model that translates the existing E-portfolio performance scores into the progress state of the learner" to predict future performance on workplace tasks. It is built on multi-entity Bayesian networks (MEBN), fed with numerical data (entrustment scores) and narrative data (sentiment analysis of written comments), and must support prediction of entrustability, selection of feedback, and selection of the topic of interest. One knowledge fragment implements a frustration alert based on portfolio consistency, score drops and feedback-seeking strategy.
requirements: The student model database must contain data about the learner's actual internal state, the learning context, and pedagogical knowledge in knowledge fragments to translate state and context into just-in-time messages and visualizations
Building the MEBN knowledge fragments requires that pedagogical knowledge about learning at the workplace is made explicit and translated into probabilistic terms
constraints: Probabilistic student models often require a lot of data points to generate reliable feedback messages, so programs of different duration gather different amounts and types of data
Combining numerical and narrative data requires text mining and natural language processing techniques whose usefulness the article says is still scarce
target_learners: students in professional education (medical, veterinary, teacher education)
target_learning_goals: development of professional competencies and entrustment for workplace tasks
examples: A level-1 (below level) assessment for EPA 1 is processed through assessment outcome, narratives, EPA level, domain competency level, interest selector and feedback decision blocks to generate improvement feedback and a timeline update

article_title: Multimedia learning
citation: Lohr, L., Gall, J.E. (2004). Multimedia learning. ETR&D 52, 87–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504677
title: The review situates multimedia learning within the debate over whether media influence learning
description: The reference list of this review on multimedia learning includes the two canonical positions of the media-methods debate: Clark's article titled "Media will never influence learning" and Kozma's article titled "Will media influence learning? Reframing the debate", both in Educational Technology Research and Development. Including both indicates the review treats multimedia learning as a field defined by this controversy over whether the medium itself or the instructional method carries the learning effect. The review's own text is not available, so this framing is inferred from its cited works.
requirements: The review must engage both sides of the debate, as its reference list includes both Clark's and Kozma's articles on the question
target_learners: educational technology researchers and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: understanding the theoretical foundations of multimedia learning
examples: The reference list pairs Clark (1994), "Media will never influence learning", with Kozma (1994), "Will media influence learning? Reframing the debate", both from ETR&D volume 42.

article_title: An international perspective for ‘Improving teacher professional development for online and blended learning: a systematic meta-aggregative review’
citation: Portillo, J., Lopez de la Serna, A. (2021). An international perspective for ‘Improving teacher professional development for online and blended learning: a systematic meta-aggregative review’. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09851-9
title: Meta-aggregative review methodology as an extensible synthesis allowing new evidence to be added without reinterpreting original findings
description: The article characterises the systematic meta-aggregative review approach adopted by Philipsen et al. (2019) as an accumulating synthesis structure: "As far as the authors adopted the approach of a systematic meta-aggregative review, new data supported by unequivocal or credible evidence can be conveniently incorporated without reinterpreting the original findings." This makes the review's TPD findings extendable to new contexts, such as frugal-technology use in international remote education.
requirements: New evidence must be supported by unequivocal or credible evidence to be incorporated
constraints: The original findings are not reinterpreted when new data are added
target_learners: Education researchers and policy-makers designing TPD programs
target_learning_goals: Synthesising and updating evidence on teacher professional development for online and blended learning
examples: The authors propose incorporating recent discoveries in frugal-technology use into the existing meta-aggregation as new aggregated components.

article_title: Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment
citation: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y
title: Metacognition Design Framework: a blended learning design placing the student learning journey centrally, aligned with learning outcomes
description: The Metacognition Design Framework is a learning design framework that scaffolds metacognitive skill development in blended higher-education settings. "The student's learning journey, comprising activities and tasks, is centrally placed within the Metacognition Design Framework (Fig. 2), constructively aligned with the learning outcomes." Core student activities are an authentic, complex project or assignment and a critical reflection on learning, with learning resources and supports arranged around this pathway; delivery mode (online/face-to-face, synchronous/asynchronous) is indicated by spatial arrangement. It builds on and adapts Oliver and Herrington's task, resources and supports classification and targets knowledge, regulation and social components of metacognition.
requirements: Requires integration of metacognitive approaches with subject-specific teaching in authentic contexts
Requires VLE tools and blended delivery with linkage between online and face-to-face components
constraints: Developed and trialed within one university's context and its VLE transition
examples: Design sequences were created for a veterinary clinical neurology module, a fully online social sciences module, and a sports science module
key_sources: O'Neill, E. J., Fulton, C., Matthews, J., & Hensey, C. (2026). Metacognition design framework to aid metacognitive skill development in university students supported by the virtual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10574-y

article_title: Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students
citation: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0
title: MeoGeo: marker-less AR app for area measurement with resizable virtual units on a regular grid
description: MeoGeo is an iOS AR app, built with Swift, ARKit and RealityKit using LiDAR sensors, that lets students tap the screen to place virtual unit squares superimposed on the camera feed and resize them by dragging a side length. It "employs real-time marker-less AR technology", and it "discretizes the physical space of the user into a regular grid, enforcing placement of virtual units", eliminating the gaps and overlaps common with physical manipulatives. Virtual objects stay anchored to physical locations and computational occlusion hides parts behind physical objects.
requirements: an iPad with ARKit-capable sensors (students used a 6th-generation iPad Pro)
constraints: the app enforces grid placement, so free-form unit placement is not possible
target_learning_goals: area measurement reasoning for basic and composite shapes
spatial structuring with units of varying sizes
examples: Activity 1 had students measure a 600 cm2 rectangle using 10 cm × 10 cm and 10 cm × 20 cm unit sizes

article_title: Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation
citation: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655
title: Network visualisations as metacognitive mirrors supporting cognitive offloading and reflection
description: The article conceptualises social and epistemic network visualisations as metacognitive mirrors that externalise learners' interaction and knowledge construction to support awareness and reflection on collaboration. Functioning as external cognitive representations, they serve "as visual anchors that cue recall of concrete communicative episodes and participation patterns", supporting cognitive offloading by reducing reliance on memory prone to decay and bias and freeing cognitive resources for higher-order reflective processes. This mechanism underpins the system's use in educator-guided debriefing.
requirements: Comprehensibility: if the networks are difficult to comprehend, they risk increasing extrinsic cognitive load, thereby obstructing effective debriefing
constraints: Comprehensibility does not guarantee pedagogical utility; the networks may be easy to comprehend yet fail to trigger deeper reflection
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing learners in team-based simulation
target_learning_goals: Recall and reflection on team communication experiences
examples: Educators displayed the networks on a projector during debriefing to help learners recall their experiences
key_sources: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. article_title: A Meta-Analysis: Improvement of Students' Algebraic Reasoning through Metacognitive Training
citation: Yujin Lee, Mary M. Capraro, Robert M. Capraro & Ali Bicer. (2018). A Meta-Analysis: Improvement of Students’ Algebraic Reasoning through Metacognitive Training. International Education Studies, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n10p42
title: Metacognitive training as small-group self-questioning built on metacognitive regulation
description: Metacognitive training is a practical teaching method that adopts the concept of metacognition — students' thought processes and beliefs that regulate learning. The article describes that "Metacognitive training provides small group activities for students to ask and answer questions by themselves", using self-addressed metacognitive questions about connections between prior and new knowledge and appropriate problem-solving strategies. In this meta-analysis it is the intervention whose pooled effect on algebraic reasoning is estimated, appearing in varied forms across the included studies.
requirements: Requires students to exert initial extra effort and prolonged training to guarantee smooth and maintained application of metacognitive activity, as the article quotes Veenman, Van Hout-Wolters, and Afflerbach
constraints: The degree of improvement might vary depending on the type of metacognitive training methods employed, per the article's discussion
examples: Included interventions ranged from metacognitive strategy instruction and IMPROVE method to computer-assisted interventions and self-explanation with game-reward strategies, across grades K through high school
key_sources: Yujin Lee, Mary M. Capraro, Robert M. Capraro & Ali Bicer. (2018). A Meta-Analysis: Improvement of Students’ Algebraic Reasoning through Metacognitive Training. International Education Studies, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n10p42

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Teachers' Provision of Structure in the Classroom and Students' Academic Competence Beliefs, Engagement, and Achievement
citation: Patall, E. A., Yates, N., Lee, J., Chen, S., Bhat, P., Lee, K., Beretvas, S. N., Guan, S., Cohen, M., Zhai, F., Brecht-Heitz, S., DeLorenzo, D., & Gonzales, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist.
title: Use research methods that center teachers' and students' experiences and align with the nature of the focal outcome when studying structure
description: The methodological moderator analyses highlighted "the importance of using methods that center teachers’ and students’ experiences and align with the nature of the focal outcome". Because personal perception is central to psychological experiences of motivation and engagement, survey measures and student respondents may yield stronger correlations for engagement and competence beliefs, while observation and teacher reports may align better with achievement outcomes. Researchers designing studies of classroom structure should match the measurement approach to the outcome's perceptual nature.
requirements: Studies must carefully consider whether structure is measured by survey or observation and who provides the report about structure or outcomes
constraints: The pattern may differ for achievement outcomes, which do not reflect personal perception, so student-report methods may not strengthen achievement correlations
target_learning_goals: Academic engagement, competence beliefs, and achievement
key_sources: Patall, E. A., Yates, N., Lee, J., Chen, S., Bhat, P., Lee, K., Beretvas, S. N., Guan, S., Cohen, M., Zhai, F., Brecht-Heitz, S., DeLorenzo, D., & Gonzales, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED631356

article_title: The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data
citation: Kaitlyn G. Fitzgerald and Elizabeth Tipton. (2022). The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2022.2031366
title: Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud (MARC) Plot
description: The MARC Plot is a visualization for clearinghouse meta-analytic evidence in which study weights are "encoded directly — as y-axis position, as dot size, and with a label for the actual study weight," with the summary effect placed at the top with weight 1.0. Individual studies appear as dots without confidence intervals to avoid encouraging vote-counting, while the summary effect's precision is shown as a cloud of values "created by generating random values from a normal distribution with mean and standard deviation equal to the mean and standard error of the summary effect." Annotations such as red/blue shading of negative/positive values and a 'More certain → Less certain' legend guide interpretation. R code and the 16 experimental visualizations were released in supplementary material.
requirements: Underlying meta-analytic data with per-study effect estimates, sampling variances, and an inverse-variance weighted summary effect
Uses the metaviz and ggplot2 packages in R (adapted source code) to render plots
constraints: Effect sizes were displayed as standardized mean differences; the article states that empirically determining which metric (e.g., Improvement Index, months of learning) best communicates to lay audiences is outside the scope of the present study
target_learners: education practitioners and policy-makers using clearinghouse evidence
target_learning_goals: correctly identifying study weights, certainty, summary effect magnitude, and uncertainty in meta-analytic evidence
examples: In the experiment, 16 visualizations (4 data sets × 4 plot types) with randomized study order were shown to participants randomized to blocks of four visualizations each

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Educator Training to Improve Implementation of Interventions for Students with Disabilities
citation: Matthew E. Brock and Erik W. Carter. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of Educator Training to Improve Implementation of Interventions for Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932516653477
title: Measure professional development reach by observable change in educator behavior, not training hours
description: The article recommends that administrators and training programs evaluate professional development by observing classroom implementation rather than counting hours, because increased training time alone showed no relation to fidelity. They state "the reach of professional development programs should be measured not in terms of the number of training hours, but in terms of observable change in educator behavior," suggesting existing observation tools to identify educators needing further support.
requirements: Classroom observation tools for documenting implementation of evidence-based practices must be available to program evaluators.
constraints: Recommendation is made cautiously given the small number of studies and identified threats to internal validity; increased training time alone did little to change educator behavior.
target_learning_goals: Implementation fidelity of evidence-based interventions for students with disabilities
examples: The article suggests practical observation tools (e.g., Neitzel & Wolery, 2009) could be used to measure training success and identify educators who would benefit from further training and support.

article_title: Objective technical skills assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a systematic review of manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools.
citation: Mainwaring Elizabeth M. A., Guidozzi Nadia, James Jonnie P., Pantling Jai, Menon Nainika, Salem Riadh, Markar Sheraz R. (2026). Objective technical skills assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a systematic review of manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-13309-z
title: Messick's unified construct-validity framework as a six-domain framework for appraising surgical assessment tools
description: Messick's unified theory of validity, as applied in this review, appraises assessment quality across six domains: "content, response process, internal structure, generalisability, relations to other variables, and consequences". The review graded each domain as reported-limited, reported-partial, reported-strong, or not reported, and used the framework to compare manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools within a common structure. It was chosen to enable multidimensional evaluation beyond isolated performance metrics, which the authors argue is particularly important for AI systems where internal accuracy may be robust while educational and safety implications remain untested.
requirements: Application requires study-level reporting on each validity domain; the review supplemented it with MERSQI for methodological quality and COSMIN/QUADAS-2 for risk of bias.
constraints: The review states domain ratings aggregated at tool level may favour tools evaluated in single studies, whose performance has not been challenged across multiple cohorts or settings.
examples: The review applied the framework to 46 manual study-tool evaluations, 6 kinematic systems, and 13 AI systems, summarising tool-level ratings in Tables 2, 4, and 6.

Objective technical skills assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a systematic review of manual, kinematic, and AI-based tools. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-13309-z

article_title: Educational assessments in entry-level physical therapy education: a scoping review.
citation: Tappan Rachel S., Holland Elizabeth E., Roth Heidi R. (2026). Educational assessments in entry-level physical therapy education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08927-z
title: Messick's five sources of validity evidence as the charting framework for assessment validity
description: The review categorizes validity evidence using the five sources from Messick's framework and the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing: content, response process, internal structure, relations with other variables, and consequences. In contemporary frameworks, "validity is a characteristic of the proposed interpretation of scores" for a specific assessment use rather than a property of the assessment tool itself. Each study's evidence was rated on a four-point scale adapted from Ghaderi et al. and Beckman et al.
requirements: Specification of the assessment's intended interpretation and use before gathering validity evidence
constraints: The review notes a detailed discussion of contemporary validity theory is beyond the scope of the article

target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of assessment scores for progression and competency decisions

article_title: Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review.
citation: Zhang YuKun, Wang YuWei, Jiang ManYu, Sun XiHui, Tang LiYoong. (2026). Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-026-01574-9
title: Mediational pathway in which NTS training shapes team cognition, coordination, and observable behaviours that are plausibly upstream of safety and timeliness outcomes.
description: The review proposes a conceptual mechanism account in which NTS training exerts its effects "primarily by shaping team cognition, coordination, and observable behaviours, rather than acting directly on distal clinical endpoints". Simulation followed by structured debriefing strengthens shared mental models and role clarity, reducing coordination losses; situation displays and checklists operate as "cognitive scaffolds that lower working-memory load, increase cue salience, and facilitate global monitoring and timely updates". Brief refreshers and micro-debriefs promote retrieval practice and error-based learning that consolidate habits.
requirements: Debriefing quality must be sufficient for simulation to strengthen shared mental models and role clarity.
constraints: The pathway is indirect: patient-level outcomes were infrequently evaluated, and the review notes the difficulty of attributing downstream clinical outcomes to educational interventions.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals working in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: Team cognition, coordination, and observable team behaviours in resuscitation and emergency care

Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review. title: Measure what matters: track a small set of sensitive, mechanism-linked behavioural indicators using periodic video-based audits with reliability checks.
description: The review's third actionable principle is to "measure what matters", recommending that EDs "track a small set of sensitive, mechanism-linked indicators, including closed-loop exchanges, prioritisation errors, and time to critical actions, using periodic video-based audits with reliability checks". Integrating these indicators into quality dashboards supports accountability and continuous improvement. This follows from the review's finding that behavioural outcomes were more robust when assessed by blinded raters using validated instruments.
requirements: Periodic video-based audits with reliability checks
A small set of mechanism-linked indicators such as closed-loop exchanges, prioritisation errors, and time to critical actions

target_learning_goals: Closed-loop communication, prioritisation, and timely critical actions in resuscitation teams
examples: The review recommends integrating these indicators into quality dashboards to support accountability and continuous improvement.

article_title: Training and assessment for colorectal surgery and appendicectomy- a systematic review.
citation: Hertz P , Rattenborg S , Haug TR , Houlind K , Konge L , Bjerrum F . (2024). Training and assessment for colorectal surgery and appendicectomy– a systematic review. Colorectal Dis. https://doi.org/10.1111/codi.16905
title: Messick's five-source validity framework for surgical assessment tools
description: The review applies a scoring tool based on the five sources of validity originally described by Messick: content, response process, internal structure, relation to other variables, and consequences. Assessment tools should ideally be supported by validity evidence from each of the five sources, though not necessarily within the same paper. The review used Ghaderi's toolbox, with scores from 0 to 15 points, to assess the validity evidence reported for each of the 31 identified assessment tools.
requirements: Validity evidence should be assessed against all five sources of validity
constraints: The review notes most studies reported validity using outdated terms, and only a very few described validity data using a current and recommended framework
target_learners: surgical trainees and residents in colorectal surgery
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of technical competence in colorectal and appendicectomy surgery
examples: The review's Table 1 maps each identified assessment tool against the five validity sources

article_title: Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic-assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review.
citation: Tesfai FM, Nagi J, Morrison I, Boal M, Olaitan A, Chandrasekaran D, Stoyanov D, Lanceley A, Francis N. (2024). Objective assessment tools in laparoscopic or robotic‐assisted gynecological surgery: A systematic review. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14840
title: Contemporary five-aspect validity framework (adapted from Messick) for appraising surgical assessment tools
description: The review applies a contemporary framework of validity, adapted from Messick's validity framework, with five aspects: content, response process, internal structure, relationship to other variables, and consequences. Each aspect is scored 0–3, giving a maximum of 15, banded as limited (1–5), moderate (6–10) or substantial (11–15) validity. The scoring system was adapted from Beckman, Ghaderi, Haug and Grüter and modified for this review; separate scoring definitions are provided for manual tools and APMs, e.g. for APMs "Performance metrics were recorded by the simulator (i.e., eliminating rater bias)". The framework structures the review's per-tool validity tables.
requirements: Assessment of all five aspects requires data such as expert consensus or task analysis for content, rater training or blinding for response process, and reliability measures for internal structure
constraints: Scoring bands and definitions were modified by the authors for this review; the framework was applied only to technical-skills tools in laparoscopic or robotic-assisted gynecological surgery
target_learners: surgical trainees in minimally invasive gynecological surgery
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of technical surgical skills
examples: Each of the 37 tools was categorized along the five dimensions of the framework in Tables 3–7 and Table S2, producing the substantial/moderate/limited ranking in Table 8

article_title: Indigenous Cultural Safety Training for Applied Health, Social Work, and Education Professionals: A PRISMA Scoping Review.
citation: MacLean Tammy L., Qiang Jinfan Rose, Henderson Lynn, Bowra Andrea, Howard Lisa, Pringle Victoria, Butsang Tenzin, Rice Emma, Di Ruggiero Erica, Mashford-Pringle Angela. (2023). Indigenous Cultural Safety Training for Applied Health, Social Work, and Education Professionals: A PRISMA Scoping Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20065217
title: Engage Indigenous groups intentionally and meaningfully throughout the entire duration of cultural safety training research and practice
description: The review's central recommendation is that "relevant Indigenous groups must be intentionally and meaningfully engaged throughout the entire duration of research and practice" on Indigenous cultural safety. This follows its findings that Indigenous involvement in development was common but roles rarely specified, only a fifth of papers had a named Indigenous author, and about a tenth failed to specify the relevant Indigenous population. The authors tie this to the need for Indigenous voices to be central to identifying and prioritizing training content and approaches, and cite a 2021 Yellowhead Institute report concluding symbolic actions were prioritized over lasting structural changes.
requirements: Indigenous voices must be central to identifying and prioritizing the content and approaches included in cultural safety training
Greater commitment to meaningfully engage Indigenous communities on projects concerning them is needed from researchers and educators
constraints: The review found roles of Indigenous people in development and delivery were rarely specified in the source literature, so current practice often falls short of meaningful engagement
target_learners: health, social work, and education professionals and students
target_learning_goals: developing cultural safety practice that addresses anti-Indigenous racism
examples: The review team used preliminary findings to prioritize development of Oshki M'naadendimowin, a 36 h Indigenous cultural safety training program for faculty, staff, and students at the University of Toronto's Faculties of Medicine, Nursing, Social Work, and Public Health

article_title: Virtual reality simulation in robot-assisted surgery: meta-analysis of skill transfer and predictability of skill.
citation: Schmidt MW, Köppinger KF, Fan C, Kowalewski K-F, Schmidt LP, Vey J, Proctor T, Probst P, Bintintan VV, Müller-Stich B-P, Nickel F. (2021). Virtual reality simulation in robot-assisted surgery: meta-analysis of skill transfer and predictability of skill. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zraa066
title: Messick's unified construct validity framework for evaluating robotic VR simulators as assessment and selection tools
description: The article applies Messick's framework, which "conceptualizes all validity under one overarching framework of construct validity", to robotic VR simulators. Within it, concurrent validity asks how accurately simulator performances predict current intraoperative performance, informing credentialing, while predictive validity asks how accurately they predict future performance, informing selection of future robotic surgeons. The review uses this framework to organize its predictability studies and to argue that terminology around validity is often misunderstood and misused.
requirements: Evidence must distinguish concurrent from predictive validity questions when assessing simulator performance against operative performance
constraints: The review found that not a single study comprehensively evaluated the predictability of future operative performance
target_learners: surgical trainees and surgeons training in robot-assisted surgery
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill assessment and credentialing in robot-assisted surgery
examples: The review grouped three cross-sectional studies as predictability (validity evidence) studies and pooled their correlation coefficients in a random-effects meta-analysis

article_title: A Systematic Review of Simulation-Based Training in Vascular Surgery.
citation: Haiser Alexander, Aydin Abdullatif, Kunduzi Basir, Ahmed Kamran, Dasgupta Prokar. (2022). A Systematic Review of Simulation-Based Training in Vascular Surgery. The Journal of Surgical Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2022.05.009
title: Messick's modern validity framework with Beckman ratings and McGaghie-style translational outcomes (LoE 1-5) for evaluating surgical simulators
description: The review applies a two-part evaluation framework to vascular surgery simulators. Validity evidence is judged against Messick's five sources — content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables, and consequences — each rated 0-2 with Beckman's scale, where 2 means "Data strongly supports the source of validity". Effectiveness is scored with an adapted McGaghie translational outcomes hierarchy from LoE 1 (trainee satisfaction) to LoE 5 (collateral effects such as "Cost saving; skill retention"). The authors argue modern unitary validity definitions are "vital in the in-depth assessment of simulators" and recommend the framework as standard practice.
requirements: Studies must report data for each validity source rather than discussion alone, since Beckman's rating 0 applies when there is discussion but no data presented.
Assessment of potential author bias and selective outcome reporting at study level.
constraints: The review found the framework underused: only 1.3% of studies featured all five validity criteria, and 25% used outdated conventional definitions such as face validity.
target_learning_goals: validity evidence for surgical skill assessment
examples: The review rated the Inanimate OAR bench simulator 2/2 for content, response processes, internal structure, and consequences, and awarded LoE 2/5 for decreased simulated procedure time and supervisor interference.

article_title: Critical analysis of evidence about the impacts on surgical teams of 'mental practice' in systematic reviews: a systematic rapid evidence assessment (SREA).
citation: Snelgrove Huon; Gabbott Ben. (2020). Critical analysis of evidence about the impacts on surgical teams of ‘mental practice’ in systematic reviews: a systematic rapid evidence assessment (SREA). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02131-3
title: Mental practice as an umbrella concept spanning mental imagery, mental rehearsal and mental simulation, explained by neurophysiological, cognitive and motivational theories
description: The article construes mental practice as "the ‘symbolic’ mental rehearsal of a task in the absence of actual physical rehearsal", subsuming mental imagery, mental rehearsal and mental simulation, undertaken by surgeons prior to performing a task to improve knowledge, skills and behaviour. The six reviews explained MP through theories from functional neuroscience and the PETTLEP model to dual code theory, neuroplasticity, self-efficacy, cognitive load and goal-setting, with neurophysiological accounts proposing that imagining movements strengthens cortical representations or primes neuromuscular pathways. The authors argue MP is under-theorised and can extend beyond individual psychomotor skill to team-level information sharing.
requirements: Practitioners must already possess imaginative resources, which the article says need organisational support such as instantiation in pre-surgical routines
constraints: The article states there is still confusion about the boundaries of what constitutes simulation through mental practice and incomplete knowledge of the interplay between broader cognitive skills and psychomotor skills
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills including stress coping, confidence and teamwork
examples: The six reviews referenced explanatory frameworks including functional neuroscience, the Holmes and Collins PETTLEP model, dual code theory, neuroplasticity, self-efficacy and cognitive load theory (Table 7).

article_title: A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology.
citation: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1
title: Dual-framework evaluation model: Messick's five-source validity framework combined with adapted McGaghie translational outcome levels
description: The review organises its appraisal of every simulator around two complementary frameworks. Validity is judged against Messick's modern validity framework, whose five sources are content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables and consequences, each rated 0–2 on a validated scale. Effectiveness is judged against "an adaptation of McGaghie's proposed levels of simulation-based translational outcomes", ranging from internal acceptability (level 1) through contained, downstream and target effects to collateral effects (level 5).
requirements: Studies must report outcome data addressable to at least one validity source or translational level; studies without original data were excluded.
constraints: The review carried out qualitative analysis due to the heterogeneity of study designs, so no pooled quantitative estimates are produced.
target_learners: medical students completing their ophthalmology attachment
examples: Each row of the review's Tables 2–5 records per-study validity scores for the five Messick sources and a single effectiveness level for each simulator model.

title: Two reusable learning objects on meta-analysis (Introduction to Meta-analysis; Presenting and interpreting Meta-analysis)
description: Two interactive, multimedia web-based RLOs were developed on meta-analysis for healthcare students. The first "provided an introduction to meta-analysis, sections covered pooling results, improving precision and improving power"; the second "was more detailed covering effect measures, forest plots, heterogeneity and effect methods". Both incorporated activities and a self assessment activity to provide formative feedback, take about 15 minutes to complete, and are openly accessible under a Creative Commons licence.

article_title: Teaching meta-analysis using MetaLight.
citation: Thomas James, Graziosi Sergio, Higgins Steve, Coe Robert, Torgerson Carole, Newman Mark. (2012). Teaching meta-analysis using MetaLight. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/1756-0500-5-571
title: MetaLight: free software application for teaching and learning meta-analysis
description: MetaLight is a freely available software application that runs simple meta-analyses and contains specific functionality to facilitate the teaching and learning of meta-analysis. It is a lightweight application that aims to support the teaching of meta-analysis, designed primarily as a teaching aid for use in the classroom and for conducting student assignments. Its interface has been designed to develop understanding of the relationship between effect sizes and their appearance on the forest plot, the impact of selecting a fixed or random effects model, and how funnel plots are constructed.
requirements: Requires the Microsoft Silverlight browser plugin and internet access to run in a web browser, or can run 'out of browser' if needed
constraints: Intended primarily as a tool for teaching and learning rather than for advanced analyses such as meta-regression and Bayesian meta-analysis
target_learners: students learning meta-analysis in higher education
target_learning_goals: interpreting forest plots and funnel plots
understanding fixed and random effects models
examples: Developed to support a series of ESRC-funded workshops to develop capacity in meta-analysis in education in the UK, running from April 2008 to March 2009

article_title: Digital asthma self-management interventions: a systematic review.
citation: Morrison D, Wyke S, Agur K, Cameron EJ, Docking RI, MacKenzie AM, McConnachie A, Raghuvir V, Thomson NC, Mair FS. (2014). Digital Asthma Self-Management Interventions: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3958674/
title: Metareview method: systematic review of systematic reviews with AMSTAR quality filtering to map effectiveness evidence and identify research gaps
description: The article uses a review-of-reviews design: comprehensive multi-database searching identified 29 systematic reviews of digital asthma self-management interventions, which were then quality-appraised with AMSTAR so that only reviews meeting predetermined standards (at least 50% of quality indicators plus documented quality assessment of included studies) advanced to data extraction. This yielded 10 reviews describing 19 RCTs whose outcomes were synthesized narratively by outcome domain. The authors frame this as an approach that has "proven helpful in synthesizing a broad base of literature in order to identify research gaps and inform future intervention programs".
requirements: Included reviews must meet AMSTAR quality thresholds including documented quality assessment of their included studies
constraints: Meta-analysis was not possible due to heterogeneity and inadequate information provision within reviews
Data are an extra step away from original research, increasing possibility of reporting errors
target_learning_goals: self-care behaviors such as medication use and action plan use
examples: Searches of 14 databases identified 3810 unique citations; 29 reviews met inclusion criteria and 10 passed AMSTAR appraisal

article_title: Measuring the effectiveness of mentoring as a knowledge translation intervention for implementing empirical evidence: a systematic review.
citation: Abdullah, G., Rossy, D., Ploeg, J., Davies, B., Higuchi, K., Sikora, L., & Stacey, D. (2014). Measuring the Effectiveness of Mentoring as a Knowledge Translation Intervention for Implementing Empirical Evidence: A Systematic Review. Worldviews on Evidence-Based Nursing, 11(5), 284-300. https://doi.org/10.1111/wvn.12060
title: Mentoring as a knowledge translation intervention defined by three essential characteristics: mentor expertise, individualized support, and an interpersonal relationship
description: The review defines mentoring as a social-influence knowledge translation intervention with three essential characteristics drawn from business and health care literature: "(a) mentors are more experienced than mentees as related to a specific task; (b) mentors provide individualized support based on mentees’ learning needs; and (c) mentoring involves an interpersonal relationship as generally indicated by mutual benefit, engagement, and commitment." It distinguishes mentoring from champions, local opinion leaders, facilitation, and educational outreach visits, noting mentoring "focuses on mentees’ needs rather than on organizational or study program needs" and uniquely requires mentors more experienced at the specific task. The review further identifies three operational characteristics: regular meetings over time, flexible delivery approaches (individual or group meetings, telephone, e-mail), and a selection process matching mentees and mentors.
requirements: Mentors must be more experienced than mentees related to the specific task
Support must be individualized based on mentees' learning needs
The relationship must show mutual benefit, engagement, and commitment
constraints: The review found the act of mentoring was not consistently called mentoring in included studies, and the lack of a clear taxonomy for social influence roles made determining eligibility challenging
target_learners: Healthcare professionals responsible for patient care, including nurses and physicians
target_learning_goals: Uptake of empirical evidence and clinical practice guidelines into clinical practice
examples: Included studies delivered 3 to 12 mentoring sessions (Median = 7.5) of approximately 2 hours scheduled over 14 to 360 days (Median = 90), via individual meetings, group meetings, telephone, or e-mail

article_title: Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies
citation: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560
title: Mediator–moderator distinction in randomized intervention research
description: The article defines an organizing distinction for intervention research: a mediator explains how or why a treatment works, while a moderator reflects who benefits. As printed, "a mediator explains how or why an intervention works, whereas a moderator explains who the intervention benefits or what conditions must exist for the intervention to be effective." Mediators are intermediate outcomes measured after treatment onset; moderators typically predate the intervention. Fidelity of implementation is given as a mediator example and special education status as a moderator example.
requirements: The mediator must be a malleable factor that treatment changes, measured after the onset of the intervention in both treatment and control groups
constraints: The distinction is framed for between-groups randomized designs, not single-case or single-group pre/post designs
target_learners: students in school-based randomized intervention studies
target_learning_goals: understanding why an educational or behavioral intervention produces its effects on outcomes
examples: In a treatment provided in general education classrooms, researchers might investigate special education status as a moderator to determine if the treatment had a differential effect on students with disabilities
key_sources: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560
