citation: Sutiarso, S., Coesamin, M., & Nurhanurawati. (2018). The effect of various media scaffolding on increasing understanding of students' geometry concepts. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 95-102. https://ejournal.unsri.ac.id/index.php/jme
title: Three media scaffolding types: charts, props, and visual
description: The article describes three instructional media provided by the teacher as scaffolding for geometry learning: "charts, props and visual". Charts show geometry pictures, properties, and worked example problems; props are manipulable physical objects students try and modify (e.g., modifying a kite into a rectangle); visual is a third offered medium that students used least. The media served as learning aids for students with difficulty learning geometry.
requirements: provided by the teacher as learning aids for students who have difficulty learning geometry
constraints: visual was used least (10% of both male and female students) and students reported being confused using it
target_learning_goals: understanding geometry concepts such as shape properties and area of trapezoid and kite
examples: Students used a props kite, modified it into a rectangle, and concluded the area of a kite is half the area of a rectangle.
key_sources: Sutiarso, S., Coesamin, M., & Nurhanurawati. (2018). The effect of various media scaffolding on increasing understanding of students' geometry concepts. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 95-102. https://ejournal.unsri.ac.id/index.php/jme

article_title: Dynamic Assessment, Potential Giftedness and Mathematics Achievement in Elementary School
citation: Nicoleta Laura Popa, Ramona Loredana Păuc. (2015). Dynamic Assessment, Potential Giftedness and Mathematics Achievement in Elementary School. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN-2065-1430
title: Mediate classroom assessment sequences with prompts, error analysis, and transfer support rather than assessing without assistance
description: The article's intervention mediated all classroom assessment sequences over eight weeks: the teacher communicated types of errors collectively, had students re-solve failed items and argue for new approaches, and encouraged "the progressive transfer in new learning situations, based on pupils’ individual zone of proximal development". This contrasted with static assessment, which the article says provides late feedback that does not support real learning.
requirements: A teacher informed and trained in dynamic assessment procedures administering the assessment sequences
constraints: In this study collective prompts and feedback dominated the intervention plan, with individual procedures applied as often as possible
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and task-solving strategies in curriculum-based assessment
examples: The experimental class teacher mediated all assessment sequences for eight weeks, using guiding questions such as asking pupils how they should proceed and whether they had solved similar exercises before
key_sources: Nicoleta Laura Popa, Ramona Loredana Păuc. (2015). Dynamic Assessment, Potential Giftedness and Mathematics Achievement in Elementary School. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN-2065-1430

article_title: Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Elementary School
citation: Stephanie M. Jones, Sophie P. Barnes, Rebecca Bailey, and Emily J. Doolittle. (2017). Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Elementary School. The Future of Children, Vol. 27, No. 1, Spring 2017. https://www.futureofchildren.org
title: Measure teacher and classroom-level outcomes alongside student skills, because teachers' social-emotional competency and classroom quality shape student SEL
description: The article recommends that evaluations of elementary SEL programs attend to teachers and classrooms, not only students. Measuring student skills in isolation gives an incomplete picture; as the article argues, "Teacher- and classroom-level outcomes can give us a richer picture of classroom practices, processes, and relationships, which are likely to affect student-level SEL skills and other key outcomes." The principle operates by adding direct measures of adult outcomes and classroom environment features (such as the CLASS domains of emotional, instructional, and organizational support) to evaluation designs, so the mechanisms through which interventions affect students become visible.
requirements: Evaluations should include direct measures of adult outcomes and classroom-level outcomes, even for programs not strictly adult focused
constraints: Few studies currently measure classroom-level outcomes or features of the classroom environment, leaving current understandings of interventions largely devoid of context
target_learners: Elementary school students in middle childhood
examples: The three reviewed studies that used the CLASS observational measure identified statistically significant effects on at least some classroom-level variables, with effects ranging from moderate for emotional support to large for instructional support
key_sources: Stephanie M. Jones, Sophie P. Barnes, Rebecca Bailey, and Emily J. Doolittle. (2017). Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Elementary School. The Future of Children, Vol. 27, No. 1, Spring 2017. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1144815

article_title: The Effects of Metacognitive Strategy in Reading Expository Text
citation: Yahya Othman, Zamri Mahamud & Noradinah Jaidi. (2014). The Effects of Metacognitive Strategy in Reading Expository Text. International Education Studies, 7(13). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p102
title: Metacognitive reading lesson pattern combining prediction, question-building, difficult-word handling and summarising
description: The article's lesson pattern engages students actively at each reading phase: "Students will engage actively in guessing and constructing questions before the reading process begin", then examine difficult words, associate the text with existing knowledge and answer formulated questions while reading, and finally make a summary and overall assessment of key ideas after reading. The conclusion highlights strategies such as "guessing, building questions, highlighting difficult words and referring meanings in dictionaries and connecting meanings with sentences according to the context". The article notes even basic forms of these strategies suit primary students.
requirements: Teacher preparation sets that emphasise metacognitive strategy application rather than conventional question-answer teaching
constraints: Strategies used were "only in basic form"; the study applied them with moderate-achieving primary students on adapted Standard 5 Malay-language expository texts
target_learners: primary school students with moderate achievement
examples: Six lesson sessions with the experimental group using five adapted expository texts (e.g. Dragon Fruit Special Fruit, Hydroponic) with metacognitive strategy emphasis
key_sources: Yahya Othman, Zamri Mahamud & Noradinah Jaidi. (2014). The Effects of Metacognitive Strategy in Reading Expository Text. International Education Studies, 7(13). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p102

article_title: The Effects of Quality Books for Children and the Metacognitive Strategy on Students' Self-Esteem Levels
citation: Erkan Cer & Ertugrul Sahin. (2017). The Effects of Quality Books for Children and the Metacognitive Strategy on Students’ Self-Esteem Levels. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p72
title: Metacognitive reading strategy structured as pre-reading planning, during-reading self-monitoring, and post-reading self-assessment
description: The article operationalizes the metacognitive strategy as 28 enumerated procedures organized into three phases: "Pre-Reading Strategy: Planning", "During-Reading Strategy: Self-Monitoring", and "Post-Reading Strategy: Self-Assessment" (Table 1). Pre-reading items include setting a reading goal and anticipating content; during-reading items include becoming aware of problems within the text and rereading complicated parts; post-reading items include creating a cohesive summary and evaluating the text. The experimental group was taught these items one by one in small groups during the first week.
requirements: Students must be explicitly taught each strategy item in pre-, during-, and post-reading processes before independent use
constraints: The article notes it was difficult to implement this process on a class level, so students were divided into five groups for individual explanation
examples: Researchers divided students into five groups and tested each group daily during the first week to confirm understanding of the strategy items
key_sources: Erkan Cer & Ertugrul Sahin. (2017). The Effects of Quality Books for Children and the Metacognitive Strategy on Students’ Self-Esteem Levels. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p72

article_title: The Effects of Quality Books for Children and the Metacognitive Strategy on Students' Self-Esteem Levels
citation: Erkan Cer & Ertugrul Sahin. (2017). The Effects of Quality Books for Children and the Metacognitive Strategy on Students’ Self-Esteem Levels. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p72
title: Metacognitive strategy as controlling, monitoring, evaluating, and self-regulating during reading
description: The article defines metacognitive strategy as "controlling, monitoring, evaluating, and self-regulating in order to reach the subtext during the reading process", building on cognitive skills such as perception, grasping, synthesizing, analyzing, and evaluating before, during, and after reading. It purposefully restructures relationships between the reader and the book. The authors argue that the self-regulation processes involved lead students to make positive judgments about their self-worth, linking comprehension skill development to affective outcomes such as self-esteem.
requirements: Instruction must cover pre-reading, during-reading, and post-reading processes explicitly
examples: The experimental group was taught the strategy with books of literary quality in the first week, then applied it across 10 weeks of reading
key_sources: Erkan Cer & Ertugrul Sahin. (2017). The Effects of Quality Books for Children and the Metacognitive Strategy on Students’ Self-Esteem Levels. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p72

article_title: The Effect of Talking Drawings on Five-Year-Old Turkish Children's Mental Models of the Water Cycle
citation: Berat Ahi. (2017). The Effect of Talking Drawings on Five-Year-Old Turkish Children’s Mental Models of the Water Cycle. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 12(3), 349-367.
title: Mental models as internal cognitive structures explaining how children make sense of phenomena
description: The article frames learning through mental model theory: Johnson-Laird (1983) stated that individuals create internal structures related to concepts, which he called mental models. The article describes them as "continuously developing cognitive structures, reinforced and augmented by the experiences of daily life and newly learned information". Mental models are used in science education to understand how individuals make sense of a phenomenon and to determine the extent to which scientific knowledge has been acquired; the study operationalises them through children's water-cycle drawings.
requirements: New knowledge is needed for the construction of mental models, per Vosniadou and Brewer (1994) as cited
constraints: Mental models are affected by different disciplines and cultural lifestyles, per Judson (2010) as cited
target_learning_goals: constructing scientific understanding of natural phenomena such as the water cycle
examples: Children's drawings were classified into five levels (Çardak, 2009) as indicators of mental model level, with inter-rater Kappa of 0.91
key_sources: Berat Ahi. (2017). The Effect of Talking Drawings on Five-Year-Old Turkish Children’s Mental Models of the Water Cycle. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 12(3), 349-367. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1141375

article_title: The Efficacy of Phonics-Based Instruction of English as a Second Language in an Italian High School: A Randomised Controlled Trial
citation: Robert Alexander Graham Coates, Judith Gorham, and Richard Nicholas. (2017). The Efficacy of Phonics-Based Instruction of English as a Second Language in an Italian High School: A Randomised Controlled Trial. Gist Education and Learning Research Journal, No. 15, pp. 29-67. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1692-5777
title: Meta-cognitive phonics with prosodic ERP reinforcement as a mechanism for older L2 learners to overcome Critical Period Hypothesis barriers
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that older L2 learners can overcome Critical Period Hypothesis barriers by relying on cognitive reasoning rather than rote learning: meta-cognitive phonics techniques teach phonics patterns rather than sight words, so students can recognise or invent new lexis intuitively, while prosodic exercises using rhymes, songs or dictation create Event Related Potential events that, citing Nickels et al. (2013), open neurological circuits for efficient learning. The authors define prosody as "a series of exercises, which use the natural prosody of rhymes, songs or dictation to reinforce phonic patterns". The trial was designed to test these inter-disciplinary neurological findings in a TESOL classroom.
requirements: Instruction must concentrate on pattern recognition rather than memorised sight words
Prosodic ERP-inducing material must accompany the patterns
constraints: The authors state the theoretical base comes from neurological research (Hensch, Nickels et al., Goswami) that still needed empirical testing in a TESOL classroom, which this small trial only partially provides
target_learners: adolescent and young-adult L2 English learners beyond primary age
examples: The trial taught patterns meta-cognitively, allowing students to recognise patterns and then create prosodic exercises as ERPs to reinforce retention
key_sources: Robert Alexander Graham Coates, Judith Gorham, and Richard Nicholas. (2017). The Efficacy of Phonics-Based Instruction of English as a Second Language in an Italian High School: A Randomised Controlled Trial. Gist Education and Learning Research Journal, No. 15, pp. 29-67. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1692-5777

article_title: Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Bogale, Y. N. (2018). Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(2), 93–117. http://ijci.wcci-international.org
title: Metacognitive and socio-cultural accounts of reading comprehension underlying the intervention
description: The article frames reading comprehension instruction with Flavell's model of metacognition, in which one component is metacognitive knowledge and the second, occurring before, during and after reading, is "meta-cognitive experience". It adds Vygotsky's socio-cultural theory, under which "teachers can transfer higher order meta-cognitive reading strategies to t heir students by scaffolding, modeling and thinking aloud methods", and Smith's cognitive view of comprehension as constructing meaning in transaction with texts. The intervention's modeling-then-guided-then-independent practice sequence operationalizes these accounts.
requirements: Instruction must include explicit demonstration, modeling and explanation of when and why each strategy is used
constraints: The article notes teaching several metacognitive strategies at once in limited time may not be feasible, so only a few strands were selected
examples: The researcher modeled strategies, provided guided practice and independent work across four reading texts over 12 weeks
key_sources: Bogale, Y. N. (2018). Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(2), 93–117. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1207221

article_title: A Complete Review for Metacognitive, Cognitive, and Social/Affective Strategies as Essential Components of Learning Strategies and Their Relationships with EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Promotion
citation: Mahdiyeh Seyed Beheshti Nasab & Seyyed Fariborz Pishdadi Motlagh. (2015). A Complete Review for Metacognitive, Cognitive, and Social/Affective Strategies as Essential Components of Learning strategies and their relationships with EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Promotion. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.3p.166
title: Metacognition as knowledge of cognition plus regulation of cognition, with declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge
description: The article organizes metacognition as a two-component framework: knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition. Knowledge of cognition comprises "declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge" — knowing about things, how to do things, and when and why to use strategies. Regulation of cognition encompasses planning, information management strategies, comprehension monitoring, debugging strategies, and evaluation. The study draws on this framework, citing Pintrich, Wolters, and Baxter's three main aspects of metacognition, to design its metacognitive reading-strategy training around planning, monitoring, and evaluation.
requirements: Learners must become aware of their own learning tendencies and be willing to be introspective for metacognition to enhance learning
examples: The study's metacognitive training asked learners to think about the passage's topic, monitor comprehension through thinking aloud, and self-evaluate how well they understood
key_sources: Mahdiyeh Seyed Beheshti Nasab & Seyyed Fariborz Pishdadi Motlagh. (2015). A Complete Review for Metacognitive, Cognitive, and Social/Affective Strategies as Essential Components of Learning strategies and their relationships with EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Promotion. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.3p.166

article_title: The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the Symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates
citation: Batdal Karaduman, G. (2019). The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates. Acta Didactica Napocensia, 12(1), 107-116. https://doi.org/10.24193/adn.12.1.7
title: Metaconceptual activities in concept learning comprise metaconceptual awareness, monitoring, and evaluation
description: Because metacognition is broad, the article adopts the term metaconceptual activities for concept learning, analyzed "under three main headings: metaconceptual awareness, metaconceptual monitoring and metaconceptual evaluation" (attributed to Yürük, 2005). Awareness activities involve noticing the concepts, ontological assumptions, models and experiences in one's mind; monitoring gathers knowledge about mental processes and current cognitive status; evaluation involves interpreting the rationality or efficiency of ideas and choosing among alternatives. The experimental texts operationalize all three, e.g. asking candidates to choose among different opinions.
requirements: Learners engage with texts or activities that explicitly prompt awareness of their own concepts, monitoring of their cognitive status, and evaluation among alternative ideas
constraints: The article presents this taxonomy as attributed to Yürük (2005) rather than developing it anew
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of abstract mathematics concepts such as symmetry
examples: The appendix texts ask candidates to draw concept maps, agree or disagree with fictional peers' ideas about symmetry axes, summarize the text in their own words, and compare first and second answers
key_sources: Batdal Karaduman, G. (2019). The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates. Acta Didactica Napocensia, 12(1), 107-116. https://doi.org/10.24193/adn.12.1.7

article_title: The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level
citation: Fatemeh Abdollahizadeh Masouleh, Masoumeh Arjmandi, Fereydoon Vahdany. (2014). The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(7): 504-511. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020702
title: Ten-session explicit metapragmatic treatment program with six instructional elements
description: The treatment consisted of ten classroom sessions of 30 minutes each, developed from deviations found in learners' questionnaire answers. The article states "These materials consist of six different elements": explicit explanation of request behaviors, information sheets, role-play activities, pair-work discussions of appropriateness, listening to native-speaker dialogues, and classroom discussions of how requests are realized in English. Sessions began with teacher-fronted discussion of how one utterance conveys different meanings in context.
requirements: Learners work with researcher-prepared informative papers and materials based on available literature on request speech acts
Sessions include role plays, pair work, listening to native-speaker dialogues, and classroom discussion
constraints: Studied only with intermediate-level, above-18, Persian-speaking learners at institute level over ten 30-minute sessions
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners at institute level
target_learning_goals: awareness and appropriate use of the request speech act in English
examples: The experimental group received teaching materials covering ten classroom sessions of 30 minutes; the control group was taught only according to the institute's syllabus
key_sources: Fatemeh Abdollahizadeh Masouleh, Masoumeh Arjmandi, Fereydoon Vahdany. (2014). The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(7): 504-511. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020702

article_title: Using a Digital Planetarium for Teaching Seasons to Undergraduates
citation: Ka Chun Yu, Kamran Sahami, Victoria Sahami, Larry C. Sessions. (2015). Using A Digital Planetarium For Teaching Seasons To Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 2(1). https://www.cluteinstitute.com
title: Constructivist mental-model account of seasonal-conception change
description: The article adopts a constructivist framework in which a learner holds a privately held mental model built from prior information and experience, which may contain alternative conceptions at odds with accepted science. New scientific information combines with existing alternative conceptions into synthetic models that evolve toward scientific correctness as learning continues. The article applies this to seasons misconceptions, noting that "an alternative conception that has taken hold in the mind of a learner can be difficult to dislodge", and that introducing conflicting evidence can promote conceptual change.
requirements: Instruction must introduce conflicting or discrepant evidence to start conceptual change, since anomalous data alone may not dislodge a deeply held incorrect conception
constraints: Transformation of mental models to scientific form can be very gradual, per the article
target_learning_goals: understanding the cause of Earth's seasons
examples: The ALIVE seasons lecture introduces discrepant information, such as Earth's slightly eccentric orbit, to counter the Sun-Earth distance misconception
key_sources: Ka Chun Yu, Kamran Sahami, Victoria Sahami, Larry C. Sessions. (2015). Using A Digital Planetarium For Teaching Seasons To Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 2(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101071

article_title: Investigating the Effects of Blended Learning Approach on Vocabulary Enhancement from EFL Learners' Perspectives
citation: Saman Ebadi, Khadijeh Davood Ghuchi. (2018). Investigating the Effects of Blended Learning Approach on Vocabulary Enhancement from EFL Learners' Perspectives. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2, April - June 2018.
title: Memrise mobile application used as the asynchronous online component of a supplemental blended course
description: Memrise is a free web-based and mobile application with community-created courses, used here to teach the first 400 TOEFL words. It "teaches words by first showing students meanings, concepts, pronunciations", followed by timed speed-review quizzes with immediate feedback marking right answers in green and wrong answers in red. The researchers created a course whose content ran parallel with classroom teaching, and learners accessed it via Telegram invitations and submitted screenshots as proof of study.
requirements: A course can be created on Memrise by uploading content; the app is free to use and allows simple account creation
constraints: Participants needed internet-connected devices; interviews mention internet connection and technical problems
examples: Experimental-group learners used the Memrise course asynchronously outside scheduled class time for 4 weeks, studying about 260 of the first 400 word items
key_sources: Saman Ebadi, Khadijeh Davood Ghuchi. (2018). Investigating the Effects of Blended Learning Approach on Vocabulary Enhancement from EFL Learners' Perspectives. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2, April - June 2018. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1185411

article_title: Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future
citation: Elena V. Soboleva, Nikita L. Karavaev, Nadezhda V. Shalaginova, Marina S. Perevozchikova. (2018). Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.845
title: Clarified content of key cross-professional competences for the profession of the future Medical robot designer
description: The article specifies what four cross-professional competences concretely include for training specialists for the future profession of Medical robot designer, drawing on the Atlas of new professions, which lists skills only generically. As printed, "The content of a set of key competences for such a profession of the future as “Medical robot designer” includes systems thinking, cross -industry communication, project management and programming (artificial intelligence)." Each competence is then unpacked: systems thinking combines treating an object as a system with organising activity systemically; cross-industry communication means understanding technologies and processes across related and non-related fields; project management covers leadership, prioritising and team selection; programming is required at least at a basic level.
requirements: Competence content must be particularised for definite industries and professions, since the Atlas lists the skills without such particularisation
constraints: The clarification is given for the example profession Medical robot designer, professionals designing biocompatible robotic complexes and cyberdevices for medicine and biotechnology
target_learners: students in robotics and engineering training across school and university levels
target_learning_goals: cross-professional (soft) skills for professions of the future
examples: For systems thinking, the article distinguishes principles of mutual determination, structure's hierarchy, the object's integrity, purposefulness and historicity, plus system-challenge problem, system analysis and synthesis of results
key_sources: Elena V. Soboleva, Nikita L. Karavaev, Nadezhda V. Shalaginova, Marina S. Perevozchikova. (2018). Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.845

article_title: The Effect of Metadiscourse Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability
citation: Touran Ahour & Saeideh Entezari Maleki. (2014). The Effect of Metadiscourse Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability. English Language Teaching, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p69
title: Metadiscourse taxonomy of textual and interpersonal categories with seven textual subcategories
description: The article adopts, citing Kong and Xin (2009), a taxonomy in which "the taxonomies of metadiscourse generally fall into two main categories of textual and interpersonal". Textual metadiscourse is classified into seven categories: logical connectives, interpretative markers, attributors, validity markers, attitudinal markers, commentaries, and clarifying connectives. Logical connectives are further subcategorized by occurrence and function; four logical subcategories (additional, contrastive, sequencers, summative connectives) were chosen for instruction in this study. Metadiscourse itself is framed as language that brackets discourse organization and expresses the speaker's stance while building a relationship with an audience.
requirements: Instruction should sensitize students to rhetorical effects and features within a given genre and community
constraints: Uses of metadiscourse display different characteristics in various genres and styles, per Kong and Xin (2009) as cited by the article
target_learners: EFL learners, particularly non-native speakers in L2 instructional contexts
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing factual content from commentary; structuring oral and written discourse; grasping a writer's or speaker's stance
examples: The study operationalized the taxonomy by teaching additional connectives (e.g. "also", "moreover"), contrastive connectives (e.g. "on the contrary"), sequencers (e.g. "firstly", "then"), and summative connectives (e.g. "in conclusion", "to sum up").
key_sources: Touran Ahour & Saeideh Entezari Maleki. (2014). The Effect of Metadiscourse Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability. English Language Teaching, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p69

article_title: The Effect of Metadiscourse Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability
citation: Touran Ahour & Saeideh Entezari Maleki. (2014). The Effect of Metadiscourse Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability. English Language Teaching, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p69
title: Teachers can use metadiscourse instruction to enhance students' speaking ability, attending to learner needs, attitudes, and proficiency
description: Based on their findings, the authors recommend that "teachers can benefit from metadiscourse instruction to enhance the speaking ability of their students." They add that metadiscourse instruction can extend turns in pair discussions and serve as a strategy to give lower-fluency students time to think, but that successful integration into EFL classrooms is dependent on the teacher's method, and that learner's needs, attitudes, and proficiency levels must be considered.
requirements: Instruction delivered with a method suited to successful integration into EFL classrooms
Attention to learners' needs, attitudes, and proficiency levels
constraints: The recommendation rests on one small quasi-experiment (34 participants); the authors state further research is needed on the relationship between learner styles and variables and frequency of metadiscourse instruction
target_learning_goals: Speaking ability and fluency in pair discussion and oral production
examples: The study's experimental group received four sessions of explicit metadiscourse instruction while the control group received a placebo of story narration and news discussion only.
key_sources: Touran Ahour & Saeideh Entezari Maleki. (2014). The Effect of Metadiscourse Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability. English Language Teaching, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n10p69

article_title: The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance
citation: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71
title: The training pamphlet 'The Metafunctions and Their Applications'
description: The experimental group's instructional material was a pamphlet titled "The Metafunctions and Their Applications", composed of three chapters of up to 60 pages each. Chapter one introduced metafunction and the theoretician; chapter two explained the three metafunctions, of which only the textual metafunction section was taught, divided into subsections on Textual Metafunction and Components, and Cohesion and Coherence; chapter three taught how to write a standard three-paragraph essay in English. Exercises at the end of each chapter and section let participants check their understanding. The control group received a one-chapter pamphlet on writing a three-paragraph essay, similar to the experimental group's third chapter.
requirements: Sessions were held two sessions per week for a ten-week term, with exercises at the end of each chapter and section
constraints: Only the textual metafunction section of chapter two was taught, since the study focused on its application
target_learners: adult female intermediate EFL learners aged twenty to thirty-five
target_learning_goals: writing a standard three-paragraph essay with improved cohesion and coherence
examples: At the end of chapter 2, section 3, participants were asked to underline the Theme and Rheme in each sentence
key_sources: Mandana Eftekhar Paziraie. (2013). The Effect of Textual Metafunction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Performance. English Language Teaching; Vol. 6, No. 2; 2013. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p71

article_title: Effects of Extensive Engagement with Computer-Based Reading and Language Arts Instructional Software on Reading Achievement for Sixth Graders
citation: Securro, S., Jr., Jones, J. D., & Cantrell, D. R. (2010). Effects of Extensive Engagement with Computer-Based Reading and Language Arts Instructional Software on Reading Achievement for Sixth Graders. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology, 6(1). https://www.jimanager.com
title: Merit Software Solutions for middle school reading and language arts
description: An integrated computer-based learning system with tutorial and content modules delivering individualized reading and language arts instruction for grades 5-8. The article describes it as "an integrated computer-based learning system with tutorial and content modules arranged to deliver, on demand, basic and intermediate individualized reading and language arts instruction for grades 5-8." Modules cover reading comprehension skill sets (main idea, sequence, inference, fact-opinion, vocabulary), critical thinking within content areas, and interactive grammar exercises, with a management component giving performance feedback to students and teachers.
requirements: Password access in a computer lab; software content aligned to local course content and expected assessments, as the article states achievement gains assume "software content is aligned to local course content and to the expected assessments"
constraints: Validity of vocabulary lists rests on cited research word lists; content validity established by correlating West Virginia standards with the modules
examples: In the study, treatment students used the software 90 minutes weekly in two 45-minute periods for 24 weeks in addition to four 90-minute blocks of conventional in-class instruction
key_sources: Securro, S., Jr., Jones, J. D., & Cantrell, D. R. (2010). Effects of Extensive Engagement with Computer-Based Reading and Language Arts Instructional Software on Reading Achievement for Sixth Graders. i-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102789

article_title: The Effect of a Metacognition-Based Instructional Practice on the Metacognitive Awareness of the Prospective Teachers
citation: Burcu Duman, Çetin Semerci. (2019). The Effect of a Metacognition-based Instructional Practice on the Metacognitive Awareness of the Prospective Teachers. Universal Journal of Educational Research 7(3): 720-728. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2019.070311
title: Metacognition-based instructional practice combining reflective tasks, self-reflection and concept mapping
description: A ten-week instructional pattern implemented in a Testing and Evaluation in Education course, built on the notion of cognition embedded with metacognition, with in-class and out-of-class activities and tasks. It includes "tasks towards learning the learning and thinking about the thinking", reflective questions about prospective teachers' own performances, and "a conceptual mapping , which is suggested as a metacognitive skill by Daley [33] has also been included in the process". Planning, observing and evaluating stages of metacognitive regulation were observed during the activities.
requirements: Participants share experiences prior to, during, and following the tasks; activities target defining, explaining, giving examples, interpreting, guessing, applying, summarizing, arguing, contacting and inquiring
constraints: Was implemented over ten weeks in a single course; the authors note improving adults' metacognitive skills takes time and metacognition should be planned together with the teaching program and extended over a long period
target_learners: 3rd-year prospective teachers at a department of Turkish language education
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness, planning, questioning, awareness of learning strategies
examples: In-class and out-of-class activities and tasks with self-reflection and reflective questions about participants' own teaching performances
key_sources: Burcu Duman, Çetin Semerci. (2019). The Effect of a Metacognition-based Instructional Practice on the Metacognitive Awareness of the Prospective Teachers. Universal Journal of Educational Research 7(3): 720-728. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2019.070311

article_title: The Effectiveness of Inquiry Learning Model in Improving Prospective Teachers' Metacognition Knowledge and Metacognition Awareness
citation: Asy’ari, M., Ikhsan, M., & Muhali. (2019). The Effectiveness of Inquiry Learning Model in Improving Prospective Teachers’ Metacognition Knowledge and Metacognition Awareness. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 455-470. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12229a
title: Metacognition knowledge and metacognition awareness as distinct, measurable components of metacognition
description: The article treats metacognition as two measurable constructs. Metacognition knowledge comprises declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge, while metacognition awareness is measured with the Metacognition Awareness Inventory (MAI) of Schraw and Dennison (1994), which "contains 8 aspects, i.e. (1) declarative knowledge (DK), (2) procedural knowledge (PK), (3) conditional knowledge (CK), (4) planning (P), (5) information management (IMS), (6) monitoring (M), (7) debugging (D), and (8) evaluating (E)". The study operationalizes both constructs with tests and questionnaire indicators drawn from these frameworks and uses them as outcome measures for the inquiry intervention.
requirements: Instruments validated for content and construct: the knowledge test was declared valid and reliable (Cronbach's alpha = 0.944) and the MAI was stated as generally consistent (α Cronbach = 0.96)
constraints: The authors state students generally could not make generalization of statements towards MAI items to be suitable with the actual awareness
target_learners: prospective physics teacher-students in higher education
target_learning_goals: metacognition awareness (planning, information management, monitoring, debugging, evaluation)
examples: The study measured both constructs before and after inquiry-based learning about fluid in three experimental classes of 30 students each
key_sources: Asy’ari, M., Ikhsan, M., & Muhali. (2019). The Effectiveness of Inquiry Learning Model in Improving Prospective Teachers’ Metacognition Knowledge and Metacognition Awareness. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 455-470. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12229a

article_title: An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Concept Mapping on Turkish Students' Academic Success
citation: Yavuz Erdoğan. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Concept Mapping on Turkish Students' Academic Success. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(6). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i6.1380
title: Concept mapping rests on Ausubel's meaningful learning theory, in which new concepts are accommodated with existing cognitive structure
description: The article frames concept mapping theoretically in Ausubel's meaningful learning theory: "students accommodate new concepts and ideas with existing those already ones in their cognitive structure". Novak and Gowin built an instruction theory integrating concept maps to produce meaningful connections between concepts. A concept map is a graphical tool comprising concepts in boxes or circles connected by lines showing hierarchical relationships.
requirements: Instruction must relate new knowledge to the learner's prior knowledge to foster meaningful learning
constraints: The article's empirical synthesis covers only academic success outcomes in Turkish primary, secondary and higher education studies
target_learners: primary, secondary and higher education students in Turkey
key_sources: Yavuz Erdoğan. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Concept Mapping on Turkish Students' Academic Success. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(6). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i6.1380

article_title: Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools
citation: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581
title: Multimedia educational and methodical complex (MEMC) 'Multimedia in education'
description: The MEMC "Multimedia tools in teaching" supported the specialized course "Non-traditional methods of teaching Informatics". The article states the developed MEMC "combined the properties of an ordinary textbook, reference book, laboratory manual and an expert of the acquired information". It was used both in classrooms and for students' independent study, with emphasis on independent study, team work, mini-research, and activation of cognitive activity.
requirements: Used alongside teachers' supervision and the credit education system's SIS and TSIS formats
constraints: Developed specifically for Informatics teacher training courses
target_learning_goals: Professional knowledge of multimedia tools and independent application in teaching
examples: The MEMC supported acquisition of professional knowledge both under teachers' supervision and independently
key_sources: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581

article_title: The Effectiveness of CBL Model to Improve Analytical Thinking Skills the Students of Sport Science
citation: Elok Sudibyo, Budi Jatmiko & Wahono Widodo. (2016). The Effectiveness of CBL Model to Improve Analytical Thinking Skills the Students of Sport Science. International Education Studies, 9(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n4p195
title: Meaningful contextual learning theory grounding: CBL as learning for transfer supported by schema and constructivist theory
description: The article grounds the CBL model in the claim that higher-order outcomes require "learning for transfer" attentive to meaningful learning, which occurs "when a new information into the mind associated with prior knowledge" (citing Slavin, 2009). It argues sport activities are the proper context for sport science students, aligning with schema theory's account that a person reconstructing information adapts it to existing prior knowledge, and with constructivist theory, under which lecturers act as facilitators and students actively construct their own knowledge and implement their own learning strategies.
requirements: Meaningful learning requires a proper context for learners; for sport science students the article identifies sport activities as that context.
constraints: The article presents this as a rational theoretical foundation for the observed outcomes, not as a separately tested mechanism.
examples: The discussion cites Raub et al. (2015) finding that contextual learning implementation can increase higher order thinking skills, and Ng and Nguyen (2006) on context developing critical thinking and problem solving.
key_sources: Elok Sudibyo, Budi Jatmiko & Wahono Widodo. (2016). The Effectiveness of CBL Model to Improve Analytical Thinking Skills the Students of Sport Science. International Education Studies, 9(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n4p195

article_title: The Effect of Mesnevî Supported Values Education on the Attitudes of 4th Grade Students in Primary School = Mesnevî destekli degerler egitiminin ilkokul 4. sinif ögrencilerinin tutumlarina etkisi
citation: Taş, H. & Kıroğlu, K. (2019). The effect of Mesnevî supported values education on the attitudes of 4th grade students in primary school. Pegem Eğitim ve Öğretim Dergisi, 9(1), 209-254. http://dx.doi.org/10.14527/pegegog.2019.008
title: Mesnevî Supported Values Education programme
description: A 10-week values education application for 4th graders built on stories from Mevlâna's Mesnevî, delivered within the social studies course to an experimental group while the control group was taught "on the basis of the normal curriculum". It targeted five values selected from the 4th grade social studies programme: hospitality, philanthropy, patriotism, giving importance to family unity, and tolerance. The article reports that "Experimental application was carried out for a total of 10 weeks and 20 sessions. Two sessions were held per week and one session was planned as 80 minutes."
requirements: Stories from the Mesnevî matched to each target value, with activities developed by the researchers
Delivery within the 4th grade social studies course
constraints: Evaluated in one primary school in Ordu province with 31 students per group
examples: Hospitality events used the stories "The Guest Remained on Our Neck", "Big Guest" and "Peasant and City-dweller"; tolerance events used "Hz. Musa and the Shepherd", "Scholar and Boatman", "Mouse and Camel" and "The Elephant in the Dark".
key_sources: Taş, H. & Kıroğlu, K. (2019). The effect of Mesnevî supported values education on the attitudes of 4th grade students in primary school. Pegem Eğitim ve Öğretim Dergisi, 9(1), 209-254. http://dx.doi.org/10.14527/pegegog.2019.008

article_title: Helping Students Understand Media: Examining the Efficacy of Interdisciplinary Media Training at the University Level
citation: Hans Schmidt. (2014). Helping Students Understand Media: Examining the Efficacy of Interdisciplinary Media Training at the University Level. Journal of Media Literacy Education 7(2), 50-68. https://www.jmle.org
title: Media literacy as a set of access, analysis, evaluation, and communication competencies
description: The article organizes media literacy as a set of competencies associated with accessing, analyzing, evaluating, and communicating media messages, following the definition adopted by the National Association for Media Literacy Education and UNESCO. Media access involves finding and selecting media for specific purposes; mediated message communication involves creating and sharing original media; analysis and evaluation involve identifying media text and context. The study operationalizes these dimensions in its measures and treats development of one dimension as potentially supporting the others.
requirements: When developed together, this mix of competencies leads to technical proficiency and awareness of media authors and audiences, meanings and messages, and representation and reality
target_learning_goals: media literacy competencies of accessing, analyzing, evaluating, and communicating media messages
examples: The study's pretest and posttest measured self-assessed competency in locating and accessing media, creating original media, sharing original media, and analyzing or evaluating media content
key_sources: Hans Schmidt. (2014). Helping Students Understand Media: Examining the Efficacy of Interdisciplinary Media Training at the University Level. Journal of Media Literacy Education 7(2), 50-68. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1074678

article_title: Metaphorical Thinking Learning and Junior High School Teachers' Mathematical Questioning Ability
citation: Hendriana, H., Rohaeti, E.E., & Hidayat, W. (2017). Metaphorical Thinking Learning and Junior High School Teachers’ Mathematical Questioning Ability. Journal on Mathematics Education, 8(1), 55-64. https://jme.ejournal.unsri.ac.id/index.php/jme
title: Metaphorical thinking in mathematics learning via conceptual metaphors
description: The article presents metaphorical thinking as a way of organising abstract mathematical concepts through concrete structures: "Abstract concepts that are organized through metaphorical thinking are expressed in concrete things based on structures and ways of reasoning based sensory -motor system called conceptual metaphor." It names three metaphorical conceptual forms — grounding, linking, and re-definitional metaphors — and links the approach to questioning by having students connect statements to questions, find conjectures, create ideas, and apply thinking to posed questions.
requirements: Learning must teach students to connect given statements to posed questions, find conjectures, create ideas, and apply results of thinking to questions
target_learners: mathematics students from elementary to secondary education
examples: The experimental class received learning that teaches metaphorical thinking while the control class received conventional learning
key_sources: Hendriana, H., Rohaeti, E.E., & Hidayat, W. (2017). Metaphorical Thinking Learning and Junior High School Teachers’ Mathematical Questioning Ability. Journal on Mathematics Education, 8(1), 55-64. https://jme.ejournal.unsri.ac.id/index.php/jme

article_title: Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps
citation: Nadezhda M. Andreeva, Ivan P. Artyukhov, Elena G. Myagkova, Nikolay I. Pak, Zhamilya K. Akkasynova. (2018). Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 47-64. http://www.jsser.org
title: Methodological system of blended learning in computer science with four components
description: The article develops a methodological system of blended learning in computer science whose components are "the target one, the content-related one, the procedural component and the assessment and performance one". The target component reflects educational demands and state standards; the content-related component develops information-activity skills and ICT modelling; the procedural component includes the schedule and roadmap activity elements and determines check points; the assessment and performance component uses a module and rating system correlating scores to information and communication competency development level. The system is built on six transformed general didactic principles and realised through learning roadmaps in a subject information environment.
requirements: A specially designed subject information environment has to be created to provide the multitude of conditions for drawing up learning roadmaps
constraints: The system was developed and trialled for computer science courses at higher education institutions in Russia and Kazakhstan
target_learners: first-year university students of economics and related directions
senior pedagogical-university students of physics and mathematics profile
target_learning_goals: information and communication competency in computer science
examples: At SFU the system was implemented for first-year Economics direction students, with a 101-person diagnostic group using roadmaps and a 23-person control group taught by cooperative learning methods
key_sources: Nadezhda M. Andreeva, Ivan P. Artyukhov, Elena G. Myagkova, Nikolay I. Pak, Zhamilya K. Akkasynova. (2018). Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 47-64. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1181973

article_title: Student Academic Performance Outcomes of a Classroom Physical Activity Intervention: A Pilot Study
citation: Heather Erwin, Alicia Fedewa, Soyeon Ahn. (2012). Student Academic Performance Outcomes of a Classroom Physical Activity Intervention: A Pilot Study. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 4(3), 473-487. https://www.iejee.com
title: Mediating-processes account of physical activity effects on children's cognition
description: The article frames PA's cognitive benefits through "a number of mediating processes", attributing to Trudeau and Shephard (2010) physiological influences such as greater arousal and enhanced neurotrophins stimulating neural connections in the hippocampus, plus psychosocial influences including increased self-esteem and school connectedness. The article uses this account to motivate why classroom PA might enhance learning, while noting the specific causal pathways have yet to be identified.
requirements: Research designs capable of identifying mediating relationships between children's PA levels and cognitive outcomes
constraints: The article states the specific causal pathways between PA and children's cognitions have yet to be identified and that existing methodology is limited
key_sources: Heather Erwin, Alicia Fedewa, Soyeon Ahn. (2012). Student Academic Performance Outcomes of a Classroom Physical Activity Intervention: A Pilot Study. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 4(3), 473-487. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068595

article_title: The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes
citation: Liya F. Shangaraeva, Alfiya A. Yarkhamova, Zubayda A. Biktagirova, Dorice Agol. (2016). The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1267-1274.
title: Methodic recommendations on English-language material for forming creative independence
description: The authors developed a course and methodic recommendations on material of English for forming students' creative independence, including "test tasks, speech situations, creative tasks for knowledge of lexical, grammatical material". Procedures suggested include analysis, heuristic methods, vision of structure of object, alternative decisions, creation of essentially new ways of solving a problem, and use of elements of game activity, with question-answer work as a form of control. Formation was estimated by performance of creative tasks such as making up dialogues, writing compositions and letters, and translating texts and verses.
requirements: Requires creative tasks and exercises expecting individual student work and use of language material for expressing thoughts in dialogues and monologues
constraints: Developed and tried out on first- and second-year students at Kazan (Volga region) Federal University
target_learners: first- and second-year university students of English
examples: Students were involved in finding synonyms and antonyms, translating from one language into another, completing sentences, and expressing opinions on a subject
key_sources: Liya F. Shangaraeva, Alfiya A. Yarkhamova, Zubayda A. Biktagirova, Dorice Agol. (2016). The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1267-1274. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114326

article_title: The Impact of Metacognitive Strategies and Self-Regulating Processes of Solving Math Word Problems
citation: Eda Vula, Rrezarta Avdyli, Valbona Berisha, Blerim Saqipi, Shpetim Elezi. (2017). The impact of metacognitive strategies and self-regulating processes of solving math word problems. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017131886
title: Metacognitive question sequence for solving math word problems: comprehension, connections, strategies, calculations, reflection
description: The article's intervention organized solving around a sequence of metacognitive question steps adapted from Mevarech & Kramarski (1997) and Montague, Wagner & Morgan (2000). Learners first describe the problem in their own words, then identify keywords and connect them to operations (using an underlining routine and a classroom "wall of words" classified by operation), then select strategies via schemes or drawings, calculate, and finally reflect on whether the solution makes sense. Each step carries an explicit check question, such as "Is the problem understood?" and "Is my answer correct?".
requirements: Learners work in small heterogeneous groups and pairs, answering metacognitive questions during collaborative work, followed by whole-class question-answer discussion led by the instructor.
constraints: The modified program was implemented within a period of a month, which the authors judged insufficient for third graders.
target_learners: third-grade and fifth-grade elementary learners in heterogeneous classes
target_learning_goals: connecting mathematical vocabulary to arithmetical operations
examples: Instructors of the four experimental classes met regularly with researchers to plan instruction and the word problems to be solved; learners underlined words and completed a wall of words divided into four columns by operation.
key_sources: Eda Vula, Rrezarta Avdyli, Valbona Berisha, Blerim Saqipi, Shpetim Elezi. (2017). The impact of metacognitive strategies and self-regulating processes of solving math word problems. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017131886

article_title: Teaching the English Active and Passive Voice with the Help of Cognitive Grammar: An Empirical Study
citation: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak, Anna Mystkowska-Wiertelak. (2013). Teaching the English active and passive voice with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching 3 (4). http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: Use meaning-oriented grammatical descriptions to elucidate semantic differences between competing structures
description: The article argues that functionally-oriented theories offer valuable descriptions for teaching because they focus on "their meaningfulness and its conceptual motivation," incorporating linguistic and extralinguistic context and speaker perspective. This is particularly valuable for elucidating nuances of meaning and semantic differences between competing grammatical structures suitable for a given situation. The study tested this potential empirically for the English voice.
requirements: Descriptions must be simplified and modified for pedagogic purposes given the theory's complexity
constraints: The practical efficacy of such descriptions has been tested much less frequently than it has been endorsed
target_learners: language teachers attending to grammatical issues
target_learning_goals: developing explicit knowledge of grammatical form-meaning mappings
strengthening form-meaning connections for target structures
examples: The study exposed participants to detailed semantic descriptions of the English active and passive voice grounded in cognitive grammar

article_title: A Study of Developing Multicultural Awareness in Teacher Education: Watch, Write and Talk a Movie
citation: Karadeniz, O., & İncirci, A. (2016). A Study of Developing Multicultural Awareness in Teacher Education: Watch, Write and Talk a Movie. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(34), 81-89. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1119119
title: Movie Evaluation Scale (MES)
description: A two-part instrument prepared by the researcher and a panel of five experts (three curriculum instructors and two media literacy teachers). The first part records the movie's name, date, and origin; the second asks trainee teachers to write the possible reflections of the movie on their personal and professional life. Experts agreed 100% on the scale. The MES served as the data source for qualitative content analysis of positive and negative sentences.
requirements: Completed individually after each movie viewing
Expert panel validation for content
constraints: Content analysis performed by only one researcher
target_learning_goals: Reflecting on multicultural themes in movies
examples: Filled after each of three movies, yielding 623, 698, and 732 sentences respectively
key_sources: Karadeniz, O., & İncirci, A. (2016). A Study of Developing Multicultural Awareness in Teacher Education: Watch, Write and Talk a Movie. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(34), 81-89. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1126694

article_title: Effects of Intervention to Improve At-Risk Fourth Graders' Understanding, Calculations, and Word Problems with Fractions
citation: Lynn S. Fuchs, Robin F. Schumacher, Jessica Long, Jessica Namkung, Amelia S. Malone, Amber Wang, Carol L. Hamlett, Nancy C. Jordan, Robert S. Siegler, and Paul Changas. (2016). Effects of Intervention to Improve At-Risk Fourth Graders' Understanding, Calculations, and Word Problems with Fractions. Elementary School Journal.
title: Teach fractions primarily through the measurement interpretation (number lines) rather than mainly part-whole representations
description: The article's intervention allocated roughly 70% of representational emphasis to number lines reflecting the measurement interpretation, whereas typical classroom instruction emphasized part-whole representations (74.71% of teacher emphasis). Both intervention variants built on this measurement focus outperformed business-as-usual control on number line, calculations, and NAEP outcomes, and improvement in measurement understanding mediated the NAEP effect. The principle is to make the measurement interpretation of fractions the central instructional focus, using number lines, while still building on students' prior part-whole knowledge.
requirements: Formal instruction that explicates the conventions of symbolic notation, the inversion property of fractions, and the infinite density of fractions on the number line
constraints: The mediation analysis is correlational, so causation should not be inferred, as the article itself reminds readers
examples: In the intervention program, number lines reflected 70% of the emphasis, with only 30% allocated to part-whole representations, and number lines, fraction tiles, and fraction circles were used throughout the 36 lessons.
key_sources: Lynn S. Fuchs, Robin F. Schumacher, Jessica Long, Jessica Namkung, Amelia S. Malone, Amber Wang, Carol L. Hamlett, Nancy C. Jordan, Robert S. Siegler, and Paul Changas. (2016). Effects of Intervention to Improve At-Risk Fourth Graders' Understanding, Calculations, and Word Problems with Fractions. Elementary School Journal. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566704

article_title: Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education.
citation: İnan Onur; Akyüz Ali. (2026). Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09952-8
title: Mechanism-based technical troubleshooting as target competence
description: The article defines mechanism-based technical troubleshooting as the intended competence: learners "observe device outputs, recognize abnormal waveforms or alarm patterns, relate these observations to possible technical or physical mechanisms, and decide which verification step would be appropriate." It contrasts this with output-oriented reasoning that stops at alarms or abnormal values, and structures all scenarios around an observation–hypothesis–verification–interpretation sequence.
requirements: Learners need prior theoretical instruction on device operating principles and a safe, repeatable environment for fault practice
constraints: The simulator is limited to interpreting simulated device behavior and does not replace workplace-based learning
target_learning_goals: relating device outputs to underlying mechanisms
key_sources: İnan Onur; Akyüz Ali. (2026). Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09952-8

article_title: Enhancing objective structured clinical examination performance through an artificial intelligence virtual patient: a proof-of-concept study.
citation: Chan Betty S., Marjot Jack, Dodds Timothy, Jo Lucy S. R., Yang Hyun, Xiang Jen, Dyer Paul, Kannan Bhavani, Hannah Graham, Torda Adrienne. (2026). Enhancing objective structured clinical examination performance through an artificial intelligence virtual patient: a proof-of-concept study. Proceedings (Baylor University. Medical Center). https://doi.org/10.1080/08998280.2026.2699604
title: MEET AIVP platform: nine emergency medicine scenarios with AI-driven dialogue, speech recognition, and immediate feedback
description: The MEET AIVP platform is a Unity-based virtual patient system containing "nine emergency medicine scenarios authored by senior emergency physicians." It uses OpenAI Whisper speech-to-text, ChatGPT-4 for adaptive dialogue, text-to-speech synthesis, and 3D avatars with distinct personalities. An AI tutor module provides immediate feedback mapped to OSCE criteria, and students can repeat cases and trial different questioning strategies in a low-stakes environment.
requirements: Built in Unity, the platform used OpenAI Whisper speech-to-text for spoken input, ChatGPT-4 for adaptive dialogue, and text-to-speech synthesis for natural responses.
constraints: Technical limitations constrained realism in this iteration.
examples: Cases replicated authentic emergency department encounters and required both technical and interpersonal skills.

Medical Center). https://doi.org/10.1080/08998280.2026.2699604

article_title: The myth that slow test-takers are worse students: Implications for time-limited testing.
citation: Weiner Saul J., Park Yoon Soo, Gernsbacher Morton Ann, Petersen Kristina H. (2026). The myth that slow test-takers are worse students: Implications for time-limited testing. Medical education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70215
title: Messick's unified validity framework grounds the critique of speededness as construct-irrelevant variance
description: The commentary grounds its critique in Messick's unified validity framework, which "conceptualizes validity as integrated sources of evidence encompassing construct representation, sources of construct-irrelevant variance and the social consequences of score use." Within this framework, speededness represents a systematic source of construct-irrelevant variance targeting response process and consequential validity, undermining equity without enhancing inference about clinical competence. The framework is used to argue that time limits reduce assessment validity while adding inequity.
requirements: Assessment validity must be evaluated as integrated evidence including construct representation, construct-irrelevant variance, and social consequences of score use
constraints: The commentary applies the framework specifically to time-limited written assessments in medical education, not to practical tests where time is part of the construct
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of medical knowledge, problem solving and clinical reasoning
key_sources: Weiner Saul J., Park Yoon Soo, Gernsbacher Morton Ann, Petersen Kristina H. (2026). The myth that slow test-takers are worse students: Implications for time-limited testing. Medical education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70215

article_title: The digital transformation of clinical teaching: a review of AI and data-driven quality assurance systems in medical education.
citation: Zhao Kexin, Wang Ningning, Xie Zhicai. (2026). The digital transformation of clinical teaching: a review of AI and data-driven quality assurance systems in medical education. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1915158
title: METRIC framework emphasizing bias detection, transparency, interpretability, and completeness for trustworthy AI in medical education
description: The review cites the METRIC model as a framework emphasizing "bias detection, transparency, interpretability, and completeness" as essential elements of trustworthy AI products. These components support confident incorporation of AI into medical education. The framework complements explainable AI (XAI) methodology, which helps educators understand how decisions were reached, increasing trust and willingness to adopt.
requirements: High-quality, representative data; technological robustness combined with appropriate ethics
constraints: Poor-quality data (missing, incomplete, inconsistent, biased) produces inaccurate predictions and poor decisions
key_sources: Zhao Kexin, Wang Ningning, Xie Zhicai. (2026). The digital transformation of clinical teaching: a review of AI and data-driven quality assurance systems in medical education. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1915158

article_title: Metaverse-based virtual reality and spatial learning in cervicofacial anatomy: A curriculum-embedded comparative study in undergraduate medical students.
citation: Ito T, Kawasaki H, Yamazaki A, Mizoguchi Y, Yamaguchi K, Kaneko E, Tsutsumi T. (2026). Metaverse‐based virtual reality and spatial learning in cervicofacial anatomy: A curriculum‐embedded comparative study in undergraduate medical students. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70277
title: Metaverse-based VR anatomy practicum using Meta Quest 2 on the Spatial platform
description: A curriculum-embedded VR session in which "students and instructors entered a shared virtual space as avatars and collaboratively explored detailed 3D anatomical models" using Meta Quest 2 head-mounted displays on the Spatial platform. Delivered in small groups of 2–3 learners per session due to device availability, each comprising approximately 20 min of guided exploration followed by brief open discussion. Models could be scaled, rotated, and dissected virtually to reveal internal structures.

description: The article proposes that medication safety competence is not a fixed individual attribute but a context-dependent capacity. description: The article operationalises clinical performance determinants through a longitudinal measurement burst design combining short-intensive weekly surveys with long-term tracking across placements. Each case carried three expert-assigned MeSH terms "pre-assigned to each case by subject experts" to identify key diagnostic concepts and drive structured feedback generation. article_title: Impact of a WeChat-based intervention on nurses knowledge and practice in peripheral venous catheter insertion.
citation: Hu Ai-zhen, Yin Xiao-ying, Luo Chen, Lu Liang-ai, Lai Hong-li, Liu Lin. (2025). Impact of a WeChat-based intervention on nurses knowledge and practice in peripheral venous catheter insertion. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-03430-9
title: Media richness and cognitive load accounts of mobile micro-learning effectiveness in nursing education
description: The article explains its intervention's effectiveness through two theoretical lenses. Consistent with cognitive load theory, the message design kept content concise, and the authors state that "multimodal delivery systems incorporating video demonstrations facilitate more effective skill acquisition than text-only formats", citing media richness theory to explain their superior practice gains versus an SMS-based study. They also invoke the Technology Acceptance Model: WeChat's familiarity and user-friendly interface lowered technological resistance while clinically relevant content enhanced perceived usefulness, improving adherence.
requirements: Learners must already use and trust the delivery platform; the study notes > 2 h average daily WeChat usage lowered resistance
constraints: Accounts are the authors' interpretations of between-study comparisons, not tested mechanisms in this trial
target_learners: Hospital nurses using familiar mobile platforms for continuing education
examples: The authors contrast their 40.47% practice gain with a reported 24% improvement in an SMS-based intervention, attributing the difference to video-enhanced multimodal delivery

title: Meta-debriefing: a consensus definition as a facilitated learning conversation for debriefers to review and critically reflect on debriefing practices
description: The article negotiates a consensus definition of meta-debriefing, otherwise known as debriefing the debrief: "a facilitated learning conversation enabling debriefers to review and critically reflect upon their own or others' debriefing practices." It distinguishes meta-debriefing from peer coaching, which involves "2 or more people, usually with similar levels of experience, voluntarily assisting each other to improve teaching practice," noting meta-debriefing focuses on concrete debriefing experiences and is often facilitated by experienced faculty. The definition is offered to provide shared language for practitioners and researchers.
requirements: A facilitator (meta-debriefer), typically faculty with extensive debriefing experience and training, to conduct the conversation
constraints: The article notes the earlier ASPiH definition is open to interpretation, which may inhibit constructive discourse; practice should be tailored to local professional, cultural, and environmental contexts and the debriefer's learning needs and preexisting experience
target_learners: Simulation faculty debriefers, from novice to expert
target_learning_goals: Reflective review and critical analysis of debriefing practice
examples: An international group of simulation practitioners negotiated the consensus definition to provide a common language enabling shared understanding of the concept

description: The article argues that while group discussion and debate deepen cognitive processing, they "may also increase cognitive load, particularly for trainees with less experience", and that excess demand can overwhelm working memory. description: This principle holds that school-based efforts to improve academic performance through high-quality teaching should consider students' mental health, because elevated symptoms appear to weaken the association between perceived teaching quality and grades. title: The megastudy paradigm: a large field experiment simultaneously testing many interventions in the same sample with the same preregistered outcome
description: A megastudy is defined by the article as "a large field experiment that simultaneously tests a variety of interventions developed by different scientific teams targeting theoretically distinct mechanisms, providing an apples-to-apples comparison of efficacy by doing so in the same sample and with the same preregistered outcome". In this article, 156 behavioral scientists submitted nudge ideas that were screened, developed collaboratively, and tested in 16 randomized conditions. The paradigm had previously been applied to vaccination, physical exercise, and democratic attitudes, and the authors argue it reduces the marginal cost of field research for individual teams.

target_learning_goals: improving students' math progress and achievement
examples: 15 theoretically distinct email interventions (e.g., planning prompts, empathy appeals, social comparisons, weekly dashboard reports) tested against a reminder-only control in one randomized megastudy

description: The article employs Messick's validity framework as the systematic structure for collecting validity evidence about peer assessment in PtBL. title: Framework for incorporating metaphors into trauma-informed ACEs inquiries across a clinical encounter
description: The article develops a general framework, displayed as a sample clinical encounter flow (Figure 4), based on integrating quantitative and qualitative results about when metaphor use promoted simulated patients' understanding of ACEs' long-term health impact. It positions metaphor use at multiple points of an encounter: introducing ACEs, illustrating ongoing impact, facilitating understanding of maladaptive behaviors, proposing interventions, and setting realistic expectations. The authors state that "clinical encounters should be individualized to patients' needs" and that the figure shows "a potential flow" rather than a prescription.
requirements: Metaphor use should be integrated into the flow of a typical primary care encounter and tailored to the patient's presentation and history
constraints: The framework was developed from simulated encounters and, per the authors, encounters should be individualized to patients' needs
target_learners: health care trainees (residents and students in medicine, nursing, social work, and allied health)
target_learning_goals: trauma-informed communication skills for discussing ACEs with adult patients
examples: The article illustrates the framework with trainee quotes using the backpack metaphor to explain chronic pain-related substance use and to propose 'taking those rocks out' as a possible solution
key_sources: Ha Monica MD, Rowe Allyson MD, Hendrix Katlynn, Anwar Summer BS, Mang Khup BS, Wen Frances PhD, Coon Kim EdD, Bragg Jedediah MSW, PhD, Foulks Kristin MPH, Miller-Cribbs Julie MSW, PhD, Jelley Martina MD, MSPH.
