citation: niromand Elham, Mansoory Meysam Siyah, Ramezani Ghobad, Khazaei Mohammad Rasool. (2024). Design, implementation and evaluation of e-learning program for common diseases to smartphone-based medical students: at a developing university. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-05023-4
title: Android mobile application for teaching common diseases to medical interns (education, examinations and reporting)
description: The article describes an Android application developed in Java within Android Studio, with content served from an ASP.NET MVC server using C#, HTML and an MS SQL database, connected "through two-way encryption". Its education section was "organized into eight general chapters, encompassing topics like COVID, Cardiology, Pediatrics, Pulmonology, Psychiatry, Orthopedics, Obstetrics & Gynecology, and Diabetes" with text and video content, multiple-choice exams scored immediately, a Report section for historical results, and a web-based management panel for uploading or modifying content.
requirements: Android platform and a server delivering content through two-way encryption; instructor-validated educational videos
constraints: Content production was limited to 15 common diseases due to financial and time constraints
target_learners: medical interns and trainees at a medical university
target_learning_goals: diagnosis and management of common diseases across eight medical topic areas
examples: Educational videos were filmed, edited and approved by the Deputy of General Medicine, then shared via a virtual Telegram group and the app

article_title: Objective structured assessment ultrasound skill scale for hyomental distance competence - psychometric study.
citation: Gomes Sara Hora, Trindade Marta, Petrisor Cristina, Costa Dinis, Correia-Pinto Jorge, Costa Patrício S., Pêgo José M. (2023). Objective structured assessment ultrasound skill scale for hyomental distance competence – psychometric study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04146-y
title: Messick's validity framework (internal structure, relations to other variables, response process) as the organizing structure for assessing OSAUS-HMD
description: The study organizes its psychometric evaluation of the OSAUS scale for ultrasound HMD competence using Messick's category framework, analyzed "according to three domains (internal structure, relation to other variables and response process)". Internal structure covers internal consistency and inter-rater reliability; relations to other variables covers criterion-related comparisons with GRS and expertise groups; response process covers rater training, blinding and bias-reduction strategies. The content and consequences domains were not explored.
requirements: Assessment data from blinded raters of videorecorded performance, plus rater training and agreed scale use, to gather response-process evidence
constraints: The study did not explore the content nor the consequences domains of the validity framework from Messick
target_learners: medical trainees and clinicians learning airway ultrasound
target_learning_goals: competence in ultrasound hyomental distance measurement
examples: Response-process evidence was built via assessor training, anonymized videos encoded by acquisition time, and double blinding of raters and principal investigator

article_title: Residency training for minimally invasive surgery.
citation: Campos MEC, Monteiro MVC, Kakehasi FM. (2022). Residency training for minimally invasive surgery. Revista do Colégio Brasileiro de Cirurgiões. https://doi.org/10.1590/0100-6991e-20213040
title: Merrill's five first principles of instruction as the organizing framework of the training program
description: The article organizes its training program around Merrill's (2002) five instructional principles to promote learning, drawn from problem-centered competence development: "Learning is promoted when learners are engaged in solving real-world problems", when existing knowledge is activated, when new knowledge is demonstrated, applied by the learner, and integrated into the learner's world. The authors state that in a way all these principles were included in their program, with the online stage supporting motivation and the face-to-face stage enabling activation, demonstration, application, and integration.
requirements: Instruction must engage learners in solving real-world problems for learning to be promoted, per the framework
target_learners: surgical residents in specialty residency programs
examples: The program's online module provided motivation and fundamentals; the face-to-face modules provided activation via video discussion, demonstration, application in dry-lab practice, and encouragement to integrate skills into real operations.
key_sources: Campos MEC, Monteiro MVC, Kakehasi FM. (2022). Residency training for minimally invasive surgery. Revista do Colégio Brasileiro de Cirurgiões. https://doi.org/10.1590/0100-6991e-20213040

article_title: Robotic training for medical students: feasibility of a pilot simulation curriculum.
citation: Greenberg AL, Syed SM, Alseidi A, O'Sullivan PS, Chern H. (2022). Robotic training for medical students: feasibility of a pilot simulation curriculum. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-022-01508-4
title: Pilot medical student robotic course combining IS online module, IS-led robot overview, console skills practice, and bedside-assist simulation
description: A four-component course: a 1-h online module introducing "components of the da Vinci Xi platform, terminology, and basic features"; a 1.5-h IS-led robot overview with docking and instrument-exchange practice; 1.5 h of console skills practice (ring transfer, suturing, SimNow tasks); and a 1-h faculty-led bedside-assist simulation with instrument introduction around an obstacle, instrument exchange, and camera cleaning. Designed for senior students, capped at six per session.
requirements: Access to a da Vinci trainer robot and IS trainer
A surgical faculty member to design and facilitate the simulation exercise
constraints: The simulation exercise was added as a supplement to the standard IS curriculum
Access relied on limited loaner-robot availability
target_learning_goals: bedside assist competencies: safe instrument introduction, visuospatial targeting, instrument handling and exchange, communication with the console surgeon
examples: Total implementation resources were 33 h of staff time at an implied cost of $2,800

article_title: Using Virtual Reality Head-Mounted Displays to Assess Skills in Emergency Medicine: Validity Study.
citation: Marie Høxbro Knudsen, Niklas Breindahl, Tor-Salve Dalsgaard, Dan Isbye, Anne Grethe Mølbak, Gerhard Tiwald, Morten Bo Søndergaard Svendsen, Lars Konge, Joanna Bergström, Tobias Todsen. (2023). Using Virtual Reality Head-Mounted Displays to Assess Skills in Emergency Medicine: Validity Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/45210
title: Messick's five-source validity framework as the organizing structure for VR assessment validation
description: The study structures its validity investigation around Messick's framework, which "consists of 5 sources of validity evidence regarding content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables, and consequences." Each source is addressed with a dedicated analysis: expert-written curriculum-based scenarios for content, standardized instructions and equipment for response process, Cronbach α for internal structure, between-group score comparisons for relations to other variables, and contrasting-groups standard setting with false-positive/false-negative reporting for consequences. This framework serves as the article's organizing taxonomy for gathering validity evidence before implementing VR-based assessment.
requirements: Validity evidence must be gathered across all five sources before implementation of an assessment technology
constraints: The framework was applied here specifically to a 360-degree VR MCQ assessment for medical students in emergency medicine
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of emergency medicine skills
examples: The study addressed each Messick source in a dedicated Methods subsection: Content, Response Process, Internal Structure, Relations to Other Variables, and Consequences

article_title: Objective structured clinical examination in basic thoracic ultrasound: a European study of validity evidence.
citation: Pietersen Pia Iben, Bhatnagar Rahul, Andreasen Freja, Konge Lars, Laursen Christian Borbjerg, Rahman Najib, Nielsen Anders Bo. (2023). Objective structured clinical examination in basic thoracic ultrasound: a European study of validity evidence. BMC Pulmonary Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12890-022-02285-4
title: Messick's five-source validity framework applied to a clinical skills test
description: The article organises its validation around Messick's framework, which "gathers validity evidence from five sources": content validity, response process, internal structure, relationship to other variables, and consequences. Each source was operationalised for the OSCE — content via expert and ERS task-force review, response process via standardised examiner instructions, internal structure via Cronbach's alpha and item analysis, relationships via comparison across experience groups, and consequences via contrasting-groups standard setting with false-positive/false-negative analysis.
requirements: Evidence must be gathered from all five sources for a defensible validity argument
A predefined competency grouping of candidates for relationship-to-other-variables analysis
constraints: The framework is applied here to a simulation-based performance assessment of a specific clinical skill, not to general educational testing
target_learning_goals: Valid assessment of clinical procedural competence
examples: The contrasting groups' method was used on novice and experienced score distributions to set the 71-point pass/fail standard

article_title: A randomized controlled trial of simulation training in teaching coronary angiographic views.
citation: Lee Kwan S., Natarajan Balaji, Wong Wei X., Yousman Wina, Koester Stefan, Nyotowidjojo Iwan, Lee Justin Z., Kern Karl B., Acharya Deepak, Fortuin David, Hung Olivia, Voelker Wolfram, Indik Julia H. (2022). A randomized controlled trial of simulation training in teaching coronary angiographic views. BMC Medical Education 22:644. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03705-z
title: Mentice VIST-C endovascular simulator with 3D virtual coronary anatomy overlay
description: The Mentice VIST-C (Gothenburg, Sweden) is a portable, high-fidelity endovascular simulator used in this trial as the intervention platform. The article describes it as "a portable, high-fidelity endovascular simulator, with good construct and concurrent validity, used in catheter training", connected to a monitor, laptop running VIST-8 software, foot switches and a contrast syringe. Its distinctive studied feature is the ability to switch to 3D visualized virtual anatomy overlaying the coronary anatomy on the fluoroscopic image, alongside virtual manipulation of the patient table and C-arm.
requirements: Requires the simulator hardware with monitor and laptop running the simulation software, a trained operator, and a standardized instruction guide
constraints: A single standard case with normal coronary anatomy was selected and used uniformly throughout the study
Fellow-level benefit was not demonstrated in this trial
target_learning_goals: correct identification of coronary arteries and standard angiographic projections
examples: Trainees used it for one-on-one mentored practice of 10–40 min (median 20 min) manipulating the C-arm to acquire standard projections in 2D and 3D modes

article_title: Impact of mental imagery on enhancing surgical skills learning in novice's surgeons: a pilot study.
citation: Souiki Tarik, Benzagmout Mohammed, Alami Badreeddine, Ibn Majdoub Karim, Toughrai Imane, Mazaz Khalid, Boujraf Saïd. (2021). Impact of mental imagery on enhancing surgical skills learning in novice's surgeons: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02987-z
title: Use mental imagery as a complement to, not a substitute for, traditional supervised surgical learning for novices
description: The article concludes that mental imagery rehearsal immediately after a learning session improves selected gestural performance in novice surgeons but cannot replace hands-on training. It states that "mental imagery will not be able to substitute the traditional learning of surgery for novice surgeons; it is an important approach for improving the technical skills acquisition and shortening the physical learning." The principle positions MI as an inexpensive adjunct that shortens physical learning while supervised practice remains essential.
requirements: A well-defined, protocolized surgical procedure divided into explicit sequences so the gesture can be mentalized
constraints: Benefit was demonstrated only for some gestures (6 of 14 items) in a small pilot sample of novice surgeons
target_learners: Novice surgeons (first-semester surgical residents and interns)
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of technical surgical gestures such as hand-sewn intestinal anastomosis
examples: Participants in the MI arm completed a 45-min imagery session matched to the control arm's review time, then all performed a bovine-intestine anastomosis evaluated on 14 criteria.
key_sources: Souiki Tarik, Benzagmout Mohammed, Alami Badreeddine, Ibn Majdoub Karim, Toughrai Imane, Mazaz Khalid, Boujraf Saïd. (2021). Impact of mental imagery on enhancing surgical skills learning in novice's surgeons: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02987-z

article_title: Supporting Undergraduate Biology Students' Academic Success: Comparing Two Workshop Interventions.
citation: Hensley Lauren, Kulesza Amy, Peri Joshua, Brady Anna C., Wolters Christopher A., Sovic David, Breitenberger Caroline. (2021). Supporting Undergraduate Biology Students' Academic Success: Comparing Two Workshop Interventions. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-03-0068
title: Metacognition workshop structured around task-tool matching, metacognitive process, and Bloom's taxonomy
description: The hourlong Metacognition workshop titled "Strategies to Get the Grade You Want in Bio [Course Number]!" had three main sections: "1) matching the task with the tool, 2) applying the metacognitive process (planning, monitoring, and evaluating) as a way of purposefully learning, and 3) selecting learning strategies based on the depth of learning desired, following Bloom's taxonomy." Active-learning exercises and peer discussion maintained engagement throughout.
requirements: A worksheet for notes and major takeaways accompanies the workshop
constraints: Content was designed for introductory college biology following a first exam
target_learning_goals: Selecting strategies matched to learning-task depth
examples: Students brainstormed approaching a massive redwood tree with just a handsaw to introduce matching task with tool

article_title: Introductory patient communication training for medical physics graduate students: Pilot experience.
citation: Padilla L, Meleski WB, Dominick C, Athing C, Jones CL, Burns D, Cathers LA, Fields EC. (2022). Introductory patient communication training for medical physics graduate students: Pilot experience. Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics. https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.13449
title: Introductory patient communication training curriculum for medical physics graduate students
description: An introductory patient communication training curriculum for medical physics graduate students, developed by a medical physicist together with a radiation oncologist, social workers, and two experts in simulated patient interactions. Instruction centered on "a 1.5‐h lecture developed and led by the social workers", and encounters were scored with a rubric "based on the communication rubric developed through the Macy Initiative in Health Communications".
requirements: "Simulated patient encounters require knowledge of how to design the activity, train the actors, and obtain funding to pay for them."
Instructors with medical interpersonal communication expertise, such as the social workers who led the didactic content
constraints: Where funding is difficult, the authors note that "alternative formats such as role play between participants or other faculty, may be more viable and should be investigated"
target_learners: medical physics graduate students at certificate, Masters, and PhD levels
target_learning_goals: effective communication skills for interacting with patients
examples: Preparation included four YouTube videos recorded by a young breast cancer patient documenting her journey through radiotherapy, chosen for an unscripted first-hand description of the patient experience.

article_title: Linguistic metaconcepts can improve grammatical understanding in L1 education evidence from a Dutch quasi-experimental study.
citation: van Rijt, Jimmy; Myhill, Debra; De Maeyer, Sven; Coppen, Peter-Arno. (2022). Linguistic metaconcepts can improve grammatical understanding in L1 education: evidence from a Dutch quasi-experimental study. PLoS ONE 17(2): e0263123. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263123
title: Five design principles for metaconceptual grammar interventions
description: The intervention was underpinned by five design principles adopted from a previous study and printed in Table 1. The first principle holds that teachers should "first aim to establish an understanding of the metaconcept before moving on to specify that metaconcept with traditional concepts". The remaining principles are: use inductive exercises to introduce linguistic (meta)concepts; expose students to limited degrees of grammatical uncertainty (e.g., odd one-out tasks); stimulate various forms of talk; and support teachers' scaffolding strategies so they guide evaluation of possible solutions rather than give right answers.
requirements: Teachers guide students in evaluating solutions rather than simply giving right answers, attending to conceptual terminology
constraints: Clear-cut answers hardly exist in grammatical analysis, making grammar an ill-structured knowledge domain
examples: Students did inductive exercises, odd one-out tasks, and group work; teachers received an instruction manual explaining the design principles
key_sources: van Rijt, Jimmy; Myhill, Debra; De Maeyer, Sven; Coppen, Peter-Arno. (2022). Linguistic metaconcepts can improve grammatical understanding in L1 education: evidence from a Dutch quasi-experimental study. PLoS ONE 17(2): e0263123. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263123

article_title: Innovative digital tools for new trends in teaching and assessment methods in medical and dental education.
citation: Park Jung-Chul, Kwon Hyuk-Jae Edward, Chung Chul Woon. (2021). Innovative digital tools for new trends in teaching and assessment methods in medical and dental education. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2021.18.13
title: Taxonomy of new teaching trends in medical education: computer-aided instruction, virtual patients, augmented reality, and human patient simulation
description: The article organizes emerging teaching methods in medical education into four technology-based formats: computer-aided instruction, virtual patients, augmented reality, and human patient simulation. It states that "new trends of teaching and assessment methods are discussed" and that "new tools are presented." Each format is characterized by its advantages and obstacles: computer-aided instruction offers visualization and accessibility, virtual patients enable customized scenario-based learning, augmented reality overlays medical information on real patients, and simulation provides repetitive hands-on practice.
requirements: Institutional investment in content creation and equipment, with substantial early costs before maintenance costs drop
constraints: The authors note computer-aided instruction is "insufficient to replace practical practice" and that virtual patient systems are expensive to build and maintain
examples: The article cites a 2018 study in which Hololens images were controlled by voice for reconstructive surgery planning, and robotic manikin systems as the current common form of virtual patient education

article_title: The Smart Class Teaching Module for Rehabilitation Medicine English Education in China.
citation: Lin Qiang, Qiu Yaxian, Liang Junjie, Zheng Yuxin, Liao Yujun, Huang Huina, Hou Lingying, Lang Shijuan, Zhao Biyi, Yiming Zulipiya, Yan Qinghua, Ou Haining, Zhang Yanni. (2021). The Smart Class Teaching Module for Rehabilitation Medicine English Education in China. Medical Science Monitor. https://doi.org/10.12659/MSM.929834
title: Anonymous online student questionnaire for medical English course evaluation with reported reliability and validity statistics
description: An anonymous online questionnaire distributed by cell phone one week after the medical English course, collecting basic information (grade, age, gender, entrance exam scores, learning characteristics, objectives, weekly study time) and 14 five-point Likert multiple-choice questions grouped into five topics: course attractiveness, teaching effectiveness, workload, curriculum resources, and curriculum improvement. The article reports an external reliability coefficient of 0.814, Cronbach's alpha of 0.762, and a KMO value of 0.832.

target_learning_goals: Evaluating student-perceived course attractiveness, teaching effectiveness, workload, resources, and improvement needs
examples: Eleven Grade 2019 students completed the questionnaire twice with a 2-week interval for the test-retest reliability check.

article_title: Efficacy of Smart Speaker-Based Metamemory Training in Older Adults: Case-Control Cohort Study.
citation: Kim J, Shin EJ, Han KH, Park S, Youn JH, Jin G, Lee JY. (2021). Efficacy of Smart Speaker–Based Metamemory Training in Older Adults: Case-Control Cohort Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/20177
title: Metamemory training based on metaknowledge, meta-monitoring, and meta-judgment
description: Metamemory training (MMT) is a memory training program for older adults grounded in the metamemory concept, which "consists of metaknowledge, meta-monitoring, and meta-judgment." In the metaknowledge component, participants learn how cognitive aging affects memory and how the brain memorizes, along with efficient strategies for dealing with cognitive aging. The meta-monitoring and meta-judgment components develop the ability to monitor and judge one's own memory performance. Training uses multimnemonic strategies such as storytelling, imagination, and associations, and prior studies cited by the article report positive effects on everyday memory and executive abilities in healthy older adults and adults with mild cognitive impairment.
requirements: Delivery through structured sessions covering all three components; in the source offline program this meant 10 weekly 90-minute sessions
constraints: Traditional MMT is limited by accessibility and continuity: travel to centers, insufficient experts, and business-hours scheduling, which the smart speaker delivery was designed to overcome
target_learners: older adults, including those with subjective memory complaints or mild cognitive impairment
target_learning_goals: knowledge and awareness of one's own memory system, memory strategy use, and monitoring and judging of memory performance
examples: Brain Toktok translated this three-component framework into voice-delivered sessions emphasizing steady participation over correctness rate.
key_sources: Kim J, Shin EJ, Han KH, Park S, Youn JH, Jin G, Lee JY. (2021). Efficacy of Smart Speaker–Based Metamemory Training in Older Adults: Case-Control Cohort Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/20177

article_title: Comparison of 'Mental training' and physical practice in the mediation of a structured facial examination: a quasi randomized, blinded and controlled study.
citation: Nelskamp Arne, Schnurr Benedikt, Germanyuk Alexandra, Sterz Jasmina, Lorenz Jonas, Sader Robert, Rüsseler Miriam, Seifert Lukas B. (2021). Comparison of ‘Mental training’ and physical practice in the mediation of a structured facial examination: a quasi randomized, blinded and controlled study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02603-0
title: Mental simulation theory: mental training activates similar neural pathways as physical practice
description: The article frames Mental Training via Janerod's simulation theory, which hypothesizes that "the motor system is part of a bigger cognitive network which includes various psychological activities". During mental training, similar neural pathways are activated and similar brain changes occur as during actual motor performance, as functional MRI investigations have shown. This explains why mental training can directly improve motor skills and help close the gap between observing and executing a skill.
requirements: Students actively develop an individual detailed, stepwise sequence of the skill and visualize it subvocally, as in the study's protocol
constraints: The authors note the literature is heterogeneous: not all studies of Mental Training in surgical education found beneficial effects compared to physical practice
target_learners: undergraduate dentistry and medical students learning clinical psychomotor skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of structured physical examination and other clinical motor skills
examples: In this study, students built an individual 'mental map' of the examination on index cards and visualized each step subvocally for 30 minutes after 30 minutes of supervised practice
key_sources: Nelskamp Arne, Schnurr Benedikt, Germanyuk Alexandra, Sterz Jasmina, Lorenz Jonas, Sader Robert, Rüsseler Miriam, Seifert Lukas B. (2021). Comparison of ‘Mental training’ and physical practice in the mediation of a structured facial examination: a quasi randomized, blinded and controlled study. article_title: Cognitive training for the prevention of skill decay in temporarily non-performing orthopedic surgeons.
citation: Kelc Robi, Vogrin Matjaz, Kelc Janja. (2020). Cognitive training for the prevention of skill decay in temporarily non-performing orthopedic surgeons. Acta Orthopaedica 91(5). https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2020.1771520
title: Three competing theories of why mental practice improves motor skills
description: The article presents mental practice as "a symbolic rehearsal of a physical activity in the absence of any gross muscular movements" and offers three explanatory accounts: the psychoneuromuscular theory, "that mental training causes activation pattern of muscles similar to actual movements"; the symbolic learning theory, "that symbols are coding the sequence of movements" whose repetition "facilitates execution of an actual motor pattern"; and a functional-equivalence account that motor imagery and performance involve "the same underlying neural structures and mechanisms."
requirements: The article treats these as hypotheses about the mechanism linking imagery to motor execution; a theoretical grounding is needed to justify imagery-based training
constraints: The article presents these as theories without adjudicating among them
target_learning_goals: retention and improvement of surgical psychomotor skills during periods of non-performance
examples: The article grounds surgical mental practice in musicians' corticospinal activity shared between imagery and action
key_sources: Kelc Robi, Vogrin Matjaz, Kelc Janja. (2020). Cognitive training for the prevention of skill decay in temporarily non-performing orthopedic surgeons. Acta Orthopaedica 91(5). https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2020.1771520

article_title: Physicians' attitudes towards psycho-oncology, perceived barriers, and psychosocial competencies: Indicators of successful implementation of adjunctive psycho-oncological care?
citation: Senf B , Fettel J , Demmerle C , Maiwurm P . (2019). Physicians' attitudes towards psycho‐oncology, perceived barriers, and psychosocial competencies: Indicators of successful implementation of adjunctive psycho‐oncological care? Psycho‐Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1002/pon.4962
title: Medical training should incorporate an increased focus on psychosocial issues and psychosocial communication
description: The article's conclusion recommends shifting medical training towards psychosocial content: "An increased focus on psychosocial issues and psychosocial communication should be achieved through specific training." This rests on its finding that physicians rated their psychosocial education and knowledge as moderate while stronger competencies and commitment correlated with more frequent integration of psychosocial care. The authors argue sound psychosocial knowledge may result in increased integration of psycho‐oncological aspects into treatment and might enhance physicians' self‐efficacy.
requirements: Specific training on psychosocial issues and psychosocial communication must be provided within medical training.
constraints: Evidence is exploratory, monocentric, and correlational; the authors call for larger, multicentric samples and objective outcome data.
target_learning_goals: psychosocial knowledge and communication skills for assessing and referring cancer patients' psychosocial distress
examples: The survey found self-rated psychosocial education and knowledge moderate (M = 3.62) while skills and abilities were rated higher, and both correlated with integration frequency.

title: MetaCogmed metacognitive strategy workbook
description: A novel workbook developed from the education literature that trained three strategies — planning, monitoring and evaluating — while children completed Cogmed tasks, reading comprehension exercises and word-based maths problems. Questions prompted planning before tasks, monitoring during, and evaluation after, focusing on task goals, strategy generation, and motivation and focus strategies adopted from paediatric neurorehabilitation programmes. Children recorded strategies in a Personal Strategy Guide available throughout training.
requirements: Completed one 10–15 minute section after each computerized training session, checked by certified Cogmed coaches
Two age-appropriate versions: ages 9–11 and 11–14
constraints: Children were not instructed in any task-specific mnemonic, reading, mathematical or problem-solving strategies, only encouraged to generate their own

title: Strong mentorship is essential for successful capstone completion
description: The article concludes that strong mentorship is essential for successful capstone and program completion. Students are encouraged to pursue global health capstone projects with mentors they align with, and the authors anticipate that dedicated mentors can improve the quality of the capstone experience and help students create a stronger final scholarly product. Completion of quality global health capstones could be enhanced with strategic efforts to create more structured mentorship and recruit more global health faculty.
requirements: Dedicated project mentorship for every student

Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2019.1666537
title: Actor-training framework for empathetic medical communication (medical improv)
description: The article grounds medical improv in foundational actors training: deep listening, emotional understanding, connections, and authenticity. It draws parallels between acting and patient-centered care, arguing that just as effective actors treat their scene partner as the most important person in the room, clinicians see the patient as an equal partner, so both communicate with clarity, authenticity, and impact. As the article puts it, "Medical improv draws upon the actor's training with theater games in order to lower defenses, generate creativity and deep emotional connections when communicating." It also distinguishes having empathy from displaying it, with empathy plus action equaling compassion felt by others.
requirements: Improvisation-trained facilitators and theater-game activities integrated into communication coursework
constraints: The article notes that suggesting theater games improve medical communication may be a leap, since prior literature measured only learner perspectives
examples: RWJMS integrated approximately three hours of standard medical improv into the first-year Patient Centered Medicine course, with an optional six-hour enhanced elective

citation: Wadowski PP, Litschauer B, Seitz T, Ertl S, Löffler-Stastka H. (2019). Case-based blended eLearning scenarios—adequate for competence development or more? Neuropsychiatrie. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40211-019-00322-z

description: An interactive, interdisciplinary e-learning platform at the Medical University of Vienna into which anonymized real-life patient cases are transferred from hospital information management into a Moodle database. The framework consists of "A) case based textbook material, B) online e‑CBL with question driven learning scenarios and C) simulated patient (SP) contact seminars". "Over 100 different cases" across specialties from internal medicine to psychiatry are offered, with varying complexity and learning objectives, aligned with Dublin descriptors and the CanMED framework.

an e-learning platform database
alignment with competence frameworks such as Dublin descriptors and CanMED

examples: Since 2014, cases from General Hospital data have been anonymized and transferred into the Moodle e-learning database, spanning ordinary infections to complex interdisciplinary biopsychosocial cases

article_title: Mento's change model in teaching competency-based medical education.

title: Mento's 12-step change-management model as a framework for pedagogical change in CBME
description: Mento's model is a change-management framework blending Kotter's, Jick's and GE's change models, organized into 12 steps from defining the idea through integrating lessons learned. The article uses it to blueprint the introduction of flipped teaching in phase-1 structure-function courses, stating it "draws from the precepts of Kotter's model, but also incorporates axioms from two other model of change". Steps include preparing recipients, creating a Leader Team, creating small wins, measuring progress, and integrating lessons learned.
requirements: A Leader Team assembled to maximize appropriate skill-sets
A sponsor among academic leadership to legitimize the change effort
A faculty development plan to prepare recipients of change
constraints: The article presents it as a proof-of-concept framework; outcomes of the change process are not yet measured
examples: A guidance plan mapped each of the 12 steps to activities and timelines across a nine-week study duration at MBRU

article_title: Bachelor of Nursing students' HIV and AIDS knowledge in KwaZulu-Natal province: An evaluation study.
citation: Ngcobo, S.J. & Mchunu, G.G., 2019, 'Bachelor of Nursing students' HIV and AIDS knowledge in KwaZulu-Natal province: An evaluation study', Curationis 42(1), a1928. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v42i1.1928
title: HIV and AIDS education intervention programme (Medical Education Partnership Initiative) for undergraduate nursing students at a selected KwaZulu-Natal university
description: An innovative HIV and AIDS clinical education programme embedded in the undergraduate Bachelor of Nursing curriculum at a selected KwaZulu-Natal university, whose broader objective was to 'improve and strengthen the HIV and AIDS content in the existing curriculum'. Sessions lasted on average 45–60 minutes and the programme was first introduced amongst second-year students within the community nursing science course. It was delivered by a professional nurse with a postgraduate diploma in clinical management of HIV and AIDS, and was evaluated 3 years after implementation.
requirements: Inputs the article lists as needed before implementation: existing curriculum content, infrastructure, stakeholders, project goals, a budget managed by the principal investigators, and tutor training guidelines.
constraints: Only students in their second to fourth years of study were allocated to the programme; first-year students were excluded because of high attrition rates and insufficient exposure.
target_learners: Undergraduate Bachelor of Nursing students (second to fourth year) at a South African university
target_learning_goals: HIV and AIDS knowledge and clinical management competencies, including prevention, transmission, diagnosis, staging, counselling and antiretroviral treatment
examples: The programme included six processes: annually updated HIV and AIDS case studies per year of study, NIMART training for final-year students, 20 HIV and AIDS-orientated clinical competencies, clinical mentorship, twice-weekly HIV morning sessions with skills practice until mastery, and an HIV resource room accessible to students at all times.

citation: Haubruck P, Nickel F, Ober J, Walker T, Bergdolt C, Friedrich M, Müller-Stich BP, Forchheim F, Fischer C, Schmidmaier G, Tanner MC. (2018). title: Mental practice account of serious-game training effects on instrument handling
description: The authors propose mental practice as the mechanism behind the serious-game group's better instrument handling: "Mental practice utilizes the systemic use of mental imagery to rehearse an action before the actual performance without the need for physical movement". Because TS requires gesture-based controls and visualization of the correct instrument use before each task, the authors argue the app induces mental rehearsal, whereas the control group trained with a different instrument set and lacked this visualization. They link this to the stronger sport-performance correlation in the control group, since TS with relevant content might induce mental practice regardless of sports experience.
requirements: the trained module must visualize and require gesture-based use of the same instruments as the target procedure
constraints: the account is offered as an interpretation of observed group differences, not a tested mediation
examples: Mental practice has been validated as an efficient training method in teaching laparoscopic surgery and in learning basic surgical skills, according to the article's cited literature

title: Mentice VIST-Lab high-fidelity coronary angiography simulator session

In the trial, each SIM student received the same 30-min theoretical course as controls plus 15 min of individual simulator manipulation on a single case, in sessions of 8 to 10 students.

A trained cardiologist delivering content identical to the traditional course

examples: SIM students individually manipulated the simulator for 15 min to learn coronary anatomy in a real 3D environment

citation: Kobayashi L, Zhang XC, Collins SA, Karim N, Merck DL. (2018). Exploratory Application of Augmented Reality/Mixed Reality Devices for Acute Care Procedure Training. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2017.10.35026
title: Medical holoimaging pipeline infrastructure for generating modular AR/MR holoimages from clinical CT/MR imagesets
description: A pipeline infrastructure that identifies, retrieves, and manipulates real patients' de-identified CT and MR imagesets for "rendering, packaging, transfer, and display of modular holoimages onto AR/MR headset devices and connected displays." It comprises a PACS query mechanism, voxel intensity-based segmentation, marching-cubes mesh conversion, mesh smoothing with MeshLab, compositing in Maya, and transfer/retrieval mechanisms. In its current implementation the pipeline required approximately 30 minutes for a typical head or chest CT imageset from patient selection to holoimage display.
requirements: Requires authorized access to the institution's clinical diagnostic imaging systems and department-funded off-the-shelf HoloLens headsets at a hospital simulation center.
constraints: The manual overlay and registration process intermittently lost spatial alignment between the holoimage and the task trainer and required adjustments.
target_learners: emergency medicine fellows, residents, advanced practice providers, and medical students
target_learning_goals: invasive acute care procedure training (central venous line and tube thoracostomy insertion)
examples: Used to generate holoimages of cervical and thoracic anatomic structures and pathology overlaid onto task trainers for blind insertion procedural training.

title: Measure of Effective Attributes of Trainers (MEAT)
description: The MEAT is a 33-item measure of trainee-perceived trainer characteristics, developed through three steps: item generation from literature, expert and trainee input; evaluation of clarity and face validity with target users; and administration to a convenience sample viewing training videos. citation: Schiekirka S, Feufel MA, Herrmann-Lingen C, Raupach T. (2015). Evaluation in medical education: A topical review of target parameters, data collection tools and confounding factors. GMS German Medical Science. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/gms/2015-13/000219.shtml
title: Catalogue of evaluation instruments for medical education, including MedSEQ, Marburger questionnaire, DREEM, LEQ, MSLES, MedIQ, SETOC and SFDP-26
description: The review compiles a summary table of identified evaluation instruments targeting teaching quality in medical education. Structures-and-processes instruments include the MedSEQ (32 items), the Marburger questionnaire (12 items), DREEM (50 items, available in German), LEQ (65 items) and MSLES (50 items); the MedIQ (25 items) targets clinical teaching in outpatient settings. constraints: The review found no instruments covering the full range of teaching outcomes, and generalisability of non-medical instruments such as SEEQ and HILVE to medical education is questionable

examples: The SFDP-26 was originally developed at the Mayo Clinic and is described as well-grounded in theory

article_title: Teaching health science students foundation motivational interviewing skills: use of motivational interviewing treatment integrity and self-reflection to approach transformative learning.

Teaching health science students foundation motivational interviewing skills: use of motivational interviewing treatment integrity and self-reflection to approach transformative learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0512-1
title: Mezirow's Transformative Learning Theory with content, process and premise reflection as a taxonomy of reflective practice
description: The article applies Mezirow's Transformative Learning Theory to classify student reflection after MI self-assessment. It states that "Mezirow [58] refers to meaning schemes in his Transformative Learning Theory, describing the way individuals perceive events influences what they see and how they see it". Three reflection types are distinguished: content reflection (self-examining actions), process reflection (considering actions and influential factors) and premise reflection (achieving a broader perspective), with premise reflection taken as the deepest indicator of meaning transformation. The article uses this taxonomy to code what students wrote in their reflective assignments.
requirements: Students must complete a structured reflective task that asks what they could have done differently, so that reflection types can be elicited and classified
constraints: The taxonomy is used interpretively to classify written excerpts; the article states it did not quantify or validate students' performance against MI experts
target_learners: graduate-entry pre-registration health science students (occupational therapy and physiotherapy)
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills such as motivational interviewing
examples: Assignment excerpts in Table 1 include a content reflection on which principles came intuitively, process reflections on making questions more open-ended, and premise reflections on ambivalence and resistance in health behaviour change

article_title: Virtual patients on the semantic Web: a proof-of-application study.
citation: Dafli E, Antoniou P, Ioannidis L, Dombros N, Topps D, Bamidis PD. (2015). Virtual Patients on the Semantic Web: A Proof-of-Application Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3933
title: The mEducator metadata schema for describing and repurposing medical educational resources
description: The mEducator schema defines the metadata accompanying an educational resource such as a virtual patient case, and is designed to support specific functions including retrieval and repurposing. It is based on the established Health Care Learning Object Metadata standard, itself an extension of IEEE Learning Object Metadata, and "consists of 10 mandatory fields and a number of optional fields" covering identifier, title, creator, intellectual property rights license, language, dates, keywords, and description, with optional fields such as educational objectives and discipline. A widget for searching SNOMED and MeSH terms via the NCBO BioPortal platform supports coding consistency.
requirements: Metadata annotation is important for searching among a large set of learning resources; the schema is applied through the existing OpenLabyrinth metadata editor
constraints: Without semantic metadata, virtual patients lack capacity to expose or consume meaningful information with other data consumers or providers
examples: OLabX authors select subject values from an autocomplete list of terms from ontologies registered in the NCBO BioPortal platform

article_title: Computer-supported feedback message tailoring: theory-informed adaptation of clinical audit and feedback for learning and behavior change.
citation: Landis-Lewis Zach, Brehaut Jamie C, Hochheiser Harry, Douglas Gerald P, Jacobson Rebecca S. (2015). Computer-supported feedback message tailoring: theory-informed adaptation of clinical audit and feedback for learning and behavior change. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-014-0203-z
title: Menu-of-constructs approach: selecting theoretical constructs from the TDF and COM-B frameworks to map feedback messages to individual barriers to behavior change
description: The article proposes using a "menu of constructs" approach, which involves "the selection and evaluation of theoretical constructs from many relevant theories" to represent networks of causal mechanisms mediating behavior change interventions. It operationalizes this with the Theoretical Domains Framework, "a taxonomy of 13 behavior change theory categories," and the COM-B framework, which "models the determinants of behavior" as capability, opportunity, motivation, and behavior. Six example constructs spanning all three COM-B categories are preliminarily mapped to barriers to antibiotic prescribing, each with a hypothetical causal mechanism for how feedback might act.
requirements: Supervisors must have some awareness of individual recipients' barriers to behavior change
Performance data of adequate quality to convey meaningful feedback
constraints: No single theory encompasses all causal mechanisms for a specific setting
The six constructs are examples, not a definitive survey of the theoretical landscape
target_learners: health-care providers receiving audit and feedback
target_learning_goals: behavior change such as reducing unnecessary antibiotic prescribing
examples: The article maps six TDF constructs (knowledge, interpersonal skills, material resources, social pressure, self-efficacy, fear) to barriers to antibiotic prescribing in Table 1, and illustrates tailoring with a scenario of a supervisor preparing feedback for a low-performing physician.
key_sources: Landis-Lewis Zach, Brehaut Jamie C, Hochheiser Harry, Douglas Gerald P, Jacobson Rebecca S. (2015). Computer-supported feedback message tailoring: theory-informed adaptation of clinical audit and feedback for learning and behavior change. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-014-0203-z

article_title: Theory in practice instead of theory versus practice--curricular design for task-based learning within a competency oriented curriculum.
citation: Rotthoff T, Schneider M, Ritz-Timme S, Windolf J. (2015). Theory in Practice instead of Theory versus Practice – Curricular design for Task-based Learning within a competency oriented Curriculum. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4330634/
title: Medical Expertise assessment framework combining case documentation, tutorial presentations and Mini-CEX
description: A competency-oriented, workplace-based assessment framework in which students document every case (3–4 cases per week) using predetermined questions and present it to a doctor, assessed by checklist with individual feedback; present cases in twice-weekly tutorials of up to 15 students rated by medical tutors; and pass at least one Mini-CEX per practice block, predominantly performed on the patient. "All of the above listed assessments of point 3) to 5) have to be successfully passed, they sum up to the faculty internal transcript „Medical Expertise"." Students collect these assessments in a portfolio until the Second State Examination (M2).
requirements: Mini-CEX needs and expectations and rating criteria must be transparent and available for the students; about 80 Mini-CEX developed by the departments are available
constraints: A Mini-CEX should average about 20-30 minutes, including an oral feedback; some manual skills are performed on a model and complex communicative situations with simulated patients
target_learners: medical students in years 3–5 practice blocks
examples: The range of Mini-CEX topics includes physical examination techniques, change of postoperative bandaging, Prick testing, bedside tests on blood transfusions or communication skills in dealing with suicidality

article_title: We must teach more effectively: here are four ways to get started.
citation: Dolan Erin L.; Collins James P. (2015). We must teach more effectively: here are four ways to get started. Molecular Biology of the Cell. https://doi.org/10.1091/mbc.E13-11-0675
title: Posing messy, open-ended problems that demand more than simple factual answers helps students transfer classroom learning to the real world
description: The article's third tactic is posing messy problems, "also called open-ended, rich, ill-structured, or wicked problems," which "demand more than simple, factual answers." What distinguishes them is that "straightforward, algorithmic approaches are usually insufficient," so students must practice solving them to transfer classroom learning to the real world. They are also more interesting, making them more motivating to solve. The lesson/unit-level pattern is backed by case studies, problem-based learning, POGIL, CUREs, and project-based applied learning as starting resources.
requirements: Students need scaffolding—breaking the complex problem into manageable elements—and diagnosis of their knowledge and abilities before the problem is assigned.
constraints: Messy problems are challenging; without scaffolding, portions may be so challenging that students give up.
target_learners: junior-level undergraduate life sciences majors and similar students
target_learning_goals: applying biological knowledge to authentic scenarios and transferring classroom learning to real-world problems
examples: The first author presents real data sets and scenarios in a junior-level biochemistry course, such as a hospitalized patient case followed by questions about the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, the citric acid cycle, and vitamin B1 deficiency.
key_sources: Dolan Erin L.; Collins James P. (2015). We must teach more effectively: here are four ways to get started. Molecular Biology of the Cell. https://doi.org/10.1091/mbc.E13-11-0675

article_title: How to become an expert educator: a qualitative study on the view of health professionals with experience in patient education.
citation: Svavarsdóttir MH, Sigurðardóttir ÁK, Steinsbekk A. (2015). How to become an expert educator: a qualitative study on the view of health professionals with experience in patient education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0370-x
title: Mentoring and structured supervision pattern for developing expert patient educators
description: Participants mainly described becoming an expert educator through experience, support, and supervision, preferably a formal mentorship from an experienced educator. A structured mentoring program would let the mentor become aware of the novice's learning process, limits, and capabilities and individualize supervision, while guidance from various educators raises exposure to a variety of educational strategies and methods.
requirements: Access to an experienced mentor or educators
Constructive critical reflection and encouragement of novice questions
constraints: Informal guidance from different educators is less able to individualize supervision than formal mentorship, per participants' preference
target_learners: Novice and developing health professional patient educators
target_learning_goals: Development of expert-level patient education competency
examples: An experienced nurse explained the value of access to someone with more knowledge "not only to receive knowledge but also to discuss problems that arise in individual interviews and in patient education".
key_sources: Svavarsdóttir MH, Sigurðardóttir ÁK, Steinsbekk A. (2015). How to become an expert educator: a qualitative study on the view of health professionals with experience in patient education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0370-x

article_title: Differences in metacognitive regulation in introductory biology students: when prompts are not enough.
citation: Stanton, J. D., Neider, X. N., Gallegos, I. J., & Clark, N. C. (2015). Differences in Metacognitive Regulation in Introductory Biology Students: When Prompts Are Not Enough. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.14-08-0135
title: A working continuum of metacognitive-regulation development in introductory biology students with four categories: not engaging, struggling, emerging, and developing
description: The article proposes a working model of metacognitive-regulation development in introductory biology students. It states: "We suggest four possible metacognitive-regulation categories: 'not engaging,' 'struggling,' 'emerging,' and 'developing' (Table 3 and Figure 1), which we propose exist in a continuum." Most students in the study fell in the struggling-to-emerging range. The model is used to generate hypotheses about underlying causes (agency, self-efficacy, metacognitive knowledge) and to target instructor support to each category.
requirements: The model was built from postexam self-evaluation and follow-through assignment data in one introductory biology course; it is a working model meant to be refined through further study.
constraints: The article calls it a working model proposed from a single course population and states the aim "to more effectively target metacognitive development" through continued study.
target_learners: undergraduate introductory biology students, mostly freshmen and sophomores
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of study strategies: monitoring, evaluating, and planning learning
examples: The article assigns students from the E1-SE and E2-FT data to categories and hypothesizes that not-engaging students lack agency, struggling students lack metacognitive knowledge, and emerging students lack procedural knowledge.
key_sources: Stanton, J. D., Neider, X. N., Gallegos, I. J., & Clark, N. C. (2015). Differences in Metacognitive Regulation in Introductory Biology Students: When Prompts Are Not Enough. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.14-08-0135

article_title: Metacognition and evidence analysis instruction: an educational framework and practical experience.
citation: Parrott J. Scott, Rubinstein Matthew L. (2015). Metacognition and evidence analysis instruction: an educational framework and practical experience. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-015-0101-8
title: Three-type taxonomy of meta-strategic skills in evidence analysis: synchronic, diachronic, and iterative evaluation
description: The article names and substantively describes a conceptual framework locating meta-strategic skills within evidence analysis instruction. It states: "We identify three general types of meta-strategic skills implicated in the evidence analysis process". Synchronic evaluation is "strategies for weighing alternatives" among tools and approaches at each step; diachronic evaluation is "assessing current activities in light of downstream goals"; iterative evaluation is "evaluating current results based on previous activities". The framework is grounded in andragogical theory and metacognition as meta-level elements of critical thinking.
requirements: Instruction must make higher-order processes explicit within the context of instruction, per the article's grounding in critical-thinking research
constraints: The authors offer the framework as a point of departure for critique and future research, not as a prescriptive exemplar
target_learning_goals: integrating discrete evidence analysis skills into a coherent systematic review or meta-analysis process
examples: Used in a 15-week online health sciences graduate evidence analysis course at Rutgers University, mapped across steps in Table 1
key_sources: Parrott J. Scott, Rubinstein Matthew L. (2015). Metacognition and evidence analysis instruction: an educational framework and practical experience. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-015-0101-8

article_title: Comfort and experience with online learning: trends over nine years and associations with knowledge.
citation: Cook David A, Thompson Warren G. (2014). Comfort and experience with online learning: trends over nine years and associations with knowledge. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-128
title: Measure and maximize course satisfaction and usability in online learning because good experiences may beget subsequent learning success
description: The article recommends that even apparently low-level outcomes of online courses deserve attention. As the authors put it, "even “low level” outcomes like course satisfaction and usability are important to measure and maximize," because favorable prior experiences were associated with knowledge in a subsequent course. This rests on the observed experience–knowledge association, whose direction and causality the authors explicitly leave open.
requirements: Attitude and satisfaction data should be collected before the course (as in this study, where ratings were collected before the first module) so they reflect prior rather than current course experiences.
constraints: The association is modest and its direction and causal status could not be determined, as the article states.
target_learners: postgraduate medical trainees (internal medicine and family medicine residents)
examples: Across nine annual studies, residents rated prior online learning experiences before starting modules, and those ratings predicted end-of-course knowledge posttest scores.
key_sources: Cook David A, Thompson Warren G. (2014). Comfort and experience with online learning: trends over nine years and associations with knowledge. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-128

article_title: Should essays and other "open-ended"-type questions retain a place in written summative assessment in clinical medicine?
citation: Hift Richard J. (2014). Should essays and other “open-ended”-type questions retain a place in written summative assessment in clinical medicine? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-014-0249-2
title: Mental-models / cognitive-constructivist account of why multiple-choice items achieve high validity
description: The article proposes a cognitive-constructivist explanation, grounded in mental-models theory, for why the multiple-choice format matches or exceeds open-ended validity. It argues that "a well-constructed context-rich multiple-choice item represents a complex problem-solving exercise which activates a sequence of cognitive processes which closely parallel those required in clinical practice". On this account, constructing an answer is not inherently more valid than selecting one, because both formats can evoke the same analysis, application and evaluation processes; the account also explains why the intuitive appeal of open-ended questions persists despite the evidence.
requirements: Items must be well-constructed and context-rich, presenting information in raw format so candidates must analyse, interpret and evaluate it
constraints: The author offers this as a hypothesis with some empiric support, not as a tested result; the article notes much remains unknown about assessment for learning and the cognitive basis of recall and reasoning
target_learners: medical students in exit-level summative assessment
examples: The article's worked example of a context-rich internal-medicine MCQ on immune thrombocytopenic purpura, which the author argues requires analysis and evaluation before any option can be selected
key_sources: Hift Richard J. (2014). Should essays and other “open-ended”-type questions retain a place in written summative assessment in clinical medicine? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-014-0249-2

article_title: Heuristic model of teaching
citation: Stanisław D. Głażek. (2008). Heuristic model of teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.4796
title: The meta-dictionary of teaching: concepts beyond any subject matter needed to discuss the dynamics of teaching
description: The meta-dictionary is the article's proposed extension of the subject-matter dictionary: a complete MOT, the article argues, "must include an extended dictionary that by deﬁnition includes speciﬁc dictionaries for all disciplines and the additional words and concepts that pertain to the process of teaching irrespective of the discipline." It contains concepts such as success with students, wanting to learn, starting from where the student is, educating a citizen, safety, trust, and curiosity. The article motivates it with cited data showing declining mathematics proficiency across grades, which it interprets as evidence that teaching inadequate to students' interests cannot be described in the subject language alone.
requirements: The meta-dictionary is required to discuss the dynamics of teaching
Concepts in the meta-dictionary must be associated with concrete events, which for these concepts are internal events
constraints: The broader concept of starting from where S is goes beyond the subject-matter dictionary and requires assessing the variety of dictionaries already in the student's space of knowledge
examples: The article cites that the percentage of students scoring at or above proficiency levels in mathematics drops from about 80% in third grade to below 60% in eighth grade
key_sources: Stanisław D. Głażek. (2008). Heuristic model of teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.4796

article_title: Shaping Attitudes Toward Science in an Introductory Astronomy Class
citation: David Wittman. (2010). Shaping Attitudes Toward Science in an Introductory Astronomy Class. https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.3321
title: Design an attitude survey before instruction to clarify goals, and measure attitudes before and after instruction
description: If shaping student attitudes is an instructional goal, the article argues instructors should measure those attitudes before and after instruction and connect attitude changes to classroom activities. The author concludes that "the process of preparing the attitude survey was key to the entire venture, as it forced me to reﬂect on and organize my objectives with respect to student attitudes", and encourages other instructors to engage in this process. Existing field-tested instruments should be used when appropriate, but their absence should not prevent instructors from measuring attitudes.
requirements: An attitude survey designed before instruction begins, clarifying the instructor's objectives
Pre- and post-instruction administration with a mechanism for matching responses, such as student ID numbers
constraints: Without a control group the efficacy of the instructional approach cannot be rigorously established; results from a non-field-tested survey cannot be interpreted as rigorously
target_learners: non-science majors in general education science courses
examples: The author asked students to write their student identification numbers on the survey so pre- and post-instruction could be rigorously matched, and assured them their attitudes would not be studied individually
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: La Nube: La Manera Mas Emocionante De Experimentar Espejos Planos
citation: José J. Lunazzi. (2009). "LA NUBE": LA MANERA MÁS EMOCIONANTE DE EXPERIMENTAR ESPEJOS PLANOS. Caderno Brasileiro de Ensino de Física V26 N2. https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.5259
title: Teach with simple, familiar materials so students learn that new results can come from re-analyzing known experiments
description: The article's central pedagogical idea is 'mental independence': students should learn that new scientific results can emerge from analyzing experiments that need neither new elements nor sophisticated procedures. The plane-mirror activity, using household mirrors 'de esos que usamos en casa', exemplifies how a familiar setup can still surprise and provoke conceptual rethinking of virtual-image symmetry.
requirements: Teachers must be attentive to discoveries 'aún en los asuntos más simples y conocidos' and avoid limiting students to typical exercises
constraints: The article frames this as the author's conjecture and argument, not a tested intervention
target_learning_goals: conceptual depth in physics, rethinking foundations and conditions of established laws
examples: The author reports teachers who skip end-of-chapter questions and go straight to exercises, eliminating 'la posibilidad de una amplitud mayor de la mente del estudiante'
key_sources: José J. Lunazzi. (2009). "LA NUBE": LA MANERA MÁS EMOCIONANTE DE EXPERIMENTAR ESPEJOS PLANOS. Caderno Brasileiro de Ensino de Física V26 N2. https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.5259
